[Page 8]

The opening of the speech with this clause is a striking opening style, because of the strangeness of its style and because it instils awe in those who are warned. The intended meaning of "the people" (al-nas) is the polytheists of Makkah. "Iqtarab" (approached) is an intensive form of nearness. The form *ifti'āl*, which is normally used for reflexive meaning (*muṭāwaʿa*), is here used to affirm the act, meaning that its occurrence to them drew very near. In attributing "approaching" to "the reckoning" (ḥisāb) there is a metaphor of the type called *istiʿāra tamthīliyya* (a figurative image-metaphor), in which the state of the reckoning bearing down upon them is likened to a person who hastens to draw near the abodes of a people. Thus the abstract condition of the reckoning is depicted in a concrete form: that of a raider who presses on and hastens in attacking a people. He keeps pressing forward, striving to come close to their dwellings, while they are heedless of the reckoning seeking them, just as a people who are unaware and turn away from an enemy approaching them. Therefore the speech is a figurative image.

[Page 9]

The intended meaning of "the reckoning" is either the Day of Reckoning, and its "approaching" means that it is near in God's sight, because its occurrence is certain. Or it is near relative to the time that has passed of the duration of this world, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I and the Hour have been sent like these two." Or "the reckoning has drawn near" is a *kināya* (metonymy) for the approach of their death, because when they die they see the recompense of their deeds, and that is part of the reckoning. In this there is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) with a threat of the nearness of their destruction, which occurred through their annihilation on the day of Badr.

Or the intended meaning of "the reckoning" is being held accountable for sin, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 113]. According to this, "approaching" is also used in its literal sense, so this is the use of a word in both its literal and figurative meanings.

As for the lām in His saying "lil-nās" (for the people): if it is kept in its original meaning of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), then its mention is an emphasis of the meaning of the lām implied in the possessive construction in His saying "ḥisābuhum" (their reckoning). This is because its implied form is "a reckoning for them," and the pronoun refers back to "the people." So the phrase "lil-nās" becomes equivalent to the pronoun to which "ḥisāb" is attached, and it is as if it were said: "a reckoning has drawn near for the people, for them." Thus it is a verbal emphasis. Just as you say: "the departure of their people has drawn near for the tribe" (azifa lil-ḥayyi raḥīluhum); its origin is "the departure drew near for the tribe," then it became "azifa lil-ḥayyi raḥīluhum." From this is the Arabs' saying: "lā abā laka" (may you have no father), whose origin is "lā abāka," so the lām in "laka" became an emphasis of the meaning of the possessive. The poet said:

*Is it of death, which is inevitable that I will meet, that you frighten me, lā abāki?*

The underlying structure of the utterance is: "the reckoning has drawn near to the people" (iqtaraba lil-nāsi al-ḥisāb). The construction was arranged in this form by placing first what indicates the genitive complement, and defining "the people" with the definiteness of the genus, so that a kind of ambiguity arises, followed afterwards by clarification. Also, because of the emphasis given by placing the prepositional phrase first, the nearness is "for the people," so that the hearer knows that the intended meaning is the threat to the polytheists, since they are the ones who are often referred to as "the people" in the Qur'an. When the element was placed first, it was necessary to posit an elided genitive, so it became like "the reckoning has drawn near for the people, the reckoning," and the genitive was omitted because its explanatory element indicates it. Since the reckoning is the reckoning of the aforementioned people, the pronoun of the people was used so that it would refer back to the word "people," and another emphasis is achieved. This is a striking pattern of composing speech. It is also permissible for the lām to mean "from" (min) or "to" (ilā), attached to "iqtaraba," in which case the prepositional phrase is an adverbial complement (ẓarf laghw, a non-essential adverbial). Ibn Mālik gave as an example of the meaning of terminal point (intihāʾ al-ghāya) the saying: "I came near to you" (taqarrabtu minka).

The clause "wa-hum fī ghaflatin muʿriḍūn" (while they are heedless and turning away) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the people," meaning: the reckoning drew near to them while they were in their heedlessness and aversion. The intended meaning of "the people" is the polytheists, because they are the ones addressed by this speech, as is shown by what follows it.

Heedlessness (al-ghafla) is being oblivious to a thing and to the ways of knowing it. It was previously discussed under His saying: ﴿And indeed we were unaware of their studying﴾ [al-Anʿām: 156] in Sūrat al-Anʿām, and His saying: ﴿That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 146] in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.

Aversion (al-iʿrāḍ) is turning the mind away from being occupied with a thing. It was mentioned in His saying: ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 63] in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, and His saying: ﴿So turn away from them until they engage in a discourse other than it﴾ [al-Anʿām: 68] in Sūrat al-Anʿām. The particle "fī" (in) indicates a figurative sense of being within, which is the intensity of the attribute's firm hold over them, meaning: they are heedless in the utmost heedlessness, to the point that it is as if they are immersed in it or enclosed within its surroundings. This is because their heedlessness of the Day of Reckoning is rooted in them due to their prior disbelief. The meaning is: they are heedless of the reckoning and of its approach. Their aversion is their refusal to reflect on the verses of the Qur'an that remind them of the Resurrection and argue for it to them. Therefore the object of aversion is not the object of heedlessness, because one who turns away from a thing is not considered heedless of it. That is: when the call of the Messenger (ﷺ) to faith and his warning them of the Day of Resurrection came to them, they persisted in their heedlessness of the reckoning because of their turning away from the signs that remind of it. Thus their heedlessness of the reckoning was not uprooted from their souls, because they had disabled what by nature would uproot heedlessness from them, by turning away from the proofs that establish the Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 2:

﴿No reminder comes to them from their Lord, renewed, but they listen to it while they play,﴾ ﴿their hearts distracted.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3]

This sentence explains the statement ﴿and they are heedless, turning away﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1], clarifying how heedlessness and aversion have taken hold of them. When they hear in the Qur'an a reminder calling them to reflection and reasoning, they occupy themselves with play and idle diversion instead, so they do not grasp its meanings, and their share of it is only hearing its words. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and a cry: deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-dhikr (the reminder): the Qur'an. It is called "reminder" using the verbal noun form to indicate the intensity of its description as a reminder.

Al-muhdath (the renewed): the new, meaning that its revelation is new and recurring. This is a metonymy for their failure to benefit from the reminder each time it comes to them, such that they are always in need of the reminder being repeated and renewed, while their excuse is cut off. For had they heard a single reminder and paid it no heed, they would have fabricated for themselves an excuse, saying they were at that moment in heedlessness. But when the recurrence of its coming was repeated, it became clear to every fair-minded person that they turn away from it with deliberate aversion. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No reminder comes to them from the Most Merciful, renewed, but they turn away from it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 5], in Surat al-Shu'ara'. The meaning of "muhdath" here is not what stands opposite to "qadim" (eternal) in the terminology of the science of kalam (theology), since that does not fit the context of the composition.

Page 12

The question of the attribute of the speech of God, Exalted, has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God spoke to Musa directly﴾ [al-Nisa': 164], in Surat al-Nisa'. The clause "istama'uhu" (they listen to it) is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object pronoun in "ya'tihim" (comes to them), and this circumstantial clause is an exception from the general sense of circumstances, meaning: no reminder comes to them in any state except in the state of their listening. The clause "wa-hum yal'abun" (while they play) is a necessary circumstantial clause (hal lazima) relating to the subject pronoun in "istama'uhu," restricting the clause "istama'uhu." This is because the clause "istama'uhu" is a circumstance in that it is qualified by another circumstance, which is the intended purpose of the restriction; otherwise the statement would become praise of them. The benefit of this ordering between the two circumstantial clauses is to cut off their excuse, which is conveyed by His saying "muhdath," as you have understood.

And ﴿their hearts distracted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3] is a circumstantial clause relating to the subject in the clause ﴿while they play﴾, and it serves as a safeguard (ihtiras) for the clause "istama'uhu," meaning: listening without awareness accompanying it.

**Qur'an 21:3:** ﴿And those who did wrong conspired in secret, [saying], "Is this not but a human being like you? Will you then submit to magic while you see?"﴾

This is a resumed sentence (jumla mustaʼnafa). It may also be a conjunction (ʻatf) upon the sentence ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near for them﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 1] to its end, because both sentences are brought to mention the states of the polytheists' reception of the Prophet's ﷺ call, with denial, slander, and plotting to reject it. So "those who did wrong" are the intended referents of "the people" as mentioned before, and the plural waw (of the group) refers back to what the pronouns of absence refer to, which return to "for the people." The sentence ﴿And they conspired in secret﴾ is not a conjunction upon the sentence ﴿They listen to it while they play﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 2], because its content does not carry the sense of restricting what reminder comes to them.

"Those who did wrong" is a substitute (badal) for the plural waw, to strengthen the affirmation that they are the intended subject of the secret conference; and because the relative clause contains an indication of the cause of their secret consultation with what is mentioned, and that the cause of this is their disbelief and their wronging of themselves, and to censure the ugliness of what they are characterized by. The sentence ﴿Is this not but a human being like you?﴾ is a substitute for "the secret conference," because that is what they conferred about; it is therefore a full substitute (badal muṭābiq). It is not like the sentence ﴿They said, "Indeed, these two are certainly magicians"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63] within the sentence ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves and conspired in secret﴾ [Ta-Ha: 62] in Surat Ta-Ha, for that is a substitute of part from whole, because that saying was the last thing their secret conference resulted in.

The reason for their concealing that speech is that they intended that the Muslims not learn of what they plotted, so that the Messenger ﷺ would not take up the task of refuting them, since they knew that their argument in this was feeble, and they aimed by it to mislead the common people. Or they kept it secret from a group among whom they saw signs of acceptance of what the Prophet ﷺ had brought, when those who had embraced Islam had multiplied in Makkah, so they feared that people would continue entering Islam in succession; so they took aside a people who still remained upon polytheism and conferred with them about this, in order to introduce doubt into their hearts.

Al-Najwa (secret conference) is private, confidential conversation. Al-Israr (concealment) is keeping something hidden and a very covert speech. The two were previously combined in His words: ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret and their secret conference?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 78] in Surat Bara'a. And the reason for making "al-najwa" the object of "asarru" was previously discussed in His words ﴿And they conspired in secret﴾ in Surat Ta-Ha, meaning they made their secret conference the object of concealment and exaggerated in hiding it, because the nature of consultation on important matters is to keep it secret, lest an opponent learn of it and spoil it.

The interrogation in His words ﴿Is this not but a human being like you?﴾ is denunciatory (inkari), implying that they were addressing someone who was nearly about to believe in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ; i.e., "how can you believe in his prophethood when he is one of you?"

Likewise the interrogation in His words ﴿Will you then submit to magic?﴾ is denunciatory, and by "magic" they meant the speech he recites to you. The meaning: since he is a human like you, your acceptance of his prophethood is only due to a magic he has cast upon you, so you "submit to magic" by accepting what he calls you to.

"Coming" (al-ityan) is used figuratively or metaphorically for acceptance and following, because coming to something implies desire for it. It is also possible that "coming" here means attending the Prophet's ﷺ gatherings to hear his call, so they called it "coming," since most attendance at assemblies is by coming to them; and they called his speech magic, so they forbade those they conferred with from listening to him. This is like His words: ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and talk noisily during it, that you may overcome"﴾ [Fussilat: 26] in Surat Fussilat.

His words ﴿while you see﴾ are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "you submit to magic while your sight is sound." By this they meant self-evident knowledge, and they expressed it by sight, because perceptible things do not need reflection to be grasped.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 4:

﴿Say, "My Lord knows every word in the heaven and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾

God informed His Messenger of their secret conversation, so what they intended by concealing it was not achieved. After relating what they had confided to one another, He commanded him to inform them that God, who knows their secret conversation, knows every word in the heavens and the earth, whether spoken aloud or in secret. The definite article in "al-qawl" (the word) is for comprehensiveness (al-istighraq), and for this reason this is a concluding statement (tadhyil). He informed them, through His saying "and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," that He is characterized by perfect knowledge of things heard and of other things.

Page 15

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "qul" (Say) in the imperative form. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and Khalaf read "qala" (he said) in the past tense, and it is written this way in the Kufan codex, as stated by Abu Shamah. That is, the Messenger said it to them: God related what the Messenger said to them, and he said it on the basis of revelation. Thus it has the same meaning as the reading of the majority, "Say, My Lord knows the word," because when He commands him to say it, he has indeed said it.

He did not say "knows the secret" (al-sirr) in order to take into account the knowledge that what they said was of the category of secrecy, and that affirming His knowledge of every word necessarily entails affirming His knowledge of the secret and other things, according to common human usage. As for His saying in Surat al-Furqan: ﴿Say, He who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth has sent it down﴾ [al-Furqan: 6], there was no prior mention of concealment there, and the saying of those who disbelieved, ﴿This is nothing but a lie he has fabricated﴾ [al-Furqan: 4], came from them sometimes openly and sometimes secretly, so God informed them of His awareness of their secret. And it is understood from it, by way of implication (tariqat al-fahwa), that He is also aware of their open speech.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 5:

﴿Nay, they say: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet. Let him bring us a sign as the earlier ones were sent."﴾

"Bal" (بَلْ, "nay" / "rather") in its first occurrence is from the speech of God, the Exalted: it is a transitional idrab (إضراب, a shift from one statement to another) from relating the words of a group among them, ﴿Will you then approach magic while you see?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3], to relating another statement from among the sayings of the polytheists, namely their claim that what he reports and relates is dreams that he sees and then relates. Thus the pronoun in "qalu" (قالوا, "they said") refers to the body of the polytheists, not specifically to the first speakers.

The second "bal" may be part of the speech reported about them, a transitional idrab regarding what they describe the Qur'an as. The meaning: "Nay, he has invented it and fabricated it, not from dreams," i.e., it is a false speech.

Then they moved on and said, "He is a poet," meaning that his speech is poetry. So the third "bal" is an idrab from them concerning their own speech, and this indicates their confusion. This confusion arises from their hesitation regarding what they adopt as excuses against the Qur'an. This is the condition of the falsifier who is dumbfounded, that he wavers in his argument, as it is said: "Falsehood is confused" (al-batil lajlaj), i.e., it is ambiguous and wavering. It is also permissible that the second and third "bal" are like the first "bal," marking a transition in the reporting of their statements. The estimated sense is: "Nay, they said: 'He has invented it'; nay, they said: 'He is a poet'," and the verb of saying is omitted because the first saying indicates both. On this reading, the reported speech may be the words of several groups of polytheists, each group adopting a particular excuse.

Al-adghath (الأضغاث, "confused dreams") is the plural of dhigh (ضِغث, with a kasra on the dad), which is a bundle of sticks, grass, or mixed herbage, and then it was applied generally to any mixture, as in Surat Yusuf: ﴿They said: "Confused dreams"﴾. They meant that what he tells you of being given revelation, and of the reports of the Resurrection, the reckoning, and the Day of Judgment, is dreams that he sees.

They drew from their hesitation, or each group drew from its own statement, one single conclusion: the demand that he bring them a miracle, other than this Qur'an, that would indicate his truthfulness, of the kind that is related of the earlier messengers who came with it, such as the transformation of the staff into a serpent. It is part of their obstinacy to ask for a sign for which the claim that it is magic would be more plausible, since among the most famous works of sorcerers is the display of what appears to be extraordinary beyond the ordinary. Long ago, the people of Pharaoh said of the miracles of Musa that they were magic, unlike the sign of the miraculousness of the Qur'an.

The imperative lam (لام الأمر) entered upon the third-person verb with the sense of conveying the command to him, i.e., "So say to him: bring us a sign." The comparison in His words ﴿as the earlier ones were sent﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (حال) from the pronoun in "ya'tina" (يأتِنا), i.e., the state of this human being when he brings the sign, resembling the mission of the earlier ones. The likened (المشبَّه) is a person, and the likened-to (المشبَّه به) is the meaning of "mission," and this is widespread in Arabic speech. Al-Nabigha said:

*And I feared, until my fear increased not
beyond that of a wild goat from the crag of al-Mataratha, an intelligent one.*

That is, "in the state of fear of a wild goat," or the state of the sign being as the earlier ones were sent, i.e., with him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 6:

﴿Never did a town believe before them, which We destroyed. Will they then believe?﴾

It is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), answering their saying: ﴿As the earlier ones were sent [with signs]﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5]. The meaning is: the nations to whom the earlier ones were sent were not benefited by the signs that came to them, as you wished that the like of them would be given to you, yet they did not believe; and for this reason destruction became binding upon them. So your case, O polytheists, is like their case. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the earlier ones denied them﴾ [al-Isra': 59], in Surat al-Isra'.

Allah withheld the extraordinary signs from the polytheists of Makkah only because He intended to preserve them, so that among them there would be believers and their descendants would be the bearers of this religion in the world. Had the clear signs been sent down upon them, the way of Allah would have been that they be followed by the punishment of annihilation for those who do not believe in them.

"Ma" is negative. "Min" in His saying ﴿min qaryah﴾ [al-A'raf: 4] is redundant (za'idah), for the emphasis of the negation derived from the particle "ma". The object of "amanat" is omitted, indicated by the context, i.e., "no town believed in the signs." The clause "ahlaknaha" is an attribute of "qaryah," coming as a digression that implicitly warns that the polytheists too await destruction.

The town is mentioned here with its people intended by it, so that the description of its destruction may be predicated of it, because destruction struck the people of the towns and their dwellings alike. Therefore it is said "ahlaknaha" rather than "ahlaknahum," as in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿And those towns—We destroyed them﴾ [al-Kahf: 59]. The clause "afahum yu'minun" is made a consequence of the clause ﴿Never did a town believe before them﴾, accompanied by the interrogative of denial, meaning: they will not believe even if We bring them a sign as they have demanded, just as those before them did not believe, those whom they took as a model in their saying ﴿as the earlier ones were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5]. This is holding them to the necessary implication of their own saying.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 7:

﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of remembrance (ahl al-dhikr, those with knowledge of the earlier scriptures and laws) if you do not know.﴾

This is a conjunction of one answer upon another ('atf jawab 'ala jawab). The purpose is to refute their aim in saying, ﴿Is this not but a human like you?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3]. They meant that he is not fit to be singled out from them by a message from God, so He clarified their error in reasoning: the earlier messengers, whose messengership they acknowledged, were only humans, and messengership is nothing but revelation from God to whomever He chooses from among mankind.

His saying "men" (rijalan) implies that there were no female messengers, and this is agreed upon. The disagreement concerns the prophethood of women such as Maryam, sister of Musa, and Maryam, mother of 'Isa. Then he alluded to their ignorance and exposed their error, commanding them to ask the people of remembrance, meaning those who have knowledge of the books and of the earlier laws, such as the rabbis and monks. The clause ﴿So ask the people of remembrance﴾ and so on is a parenthetical clause placed between the conjoined clauses.

Addressing them directly after the discourse had been in the third person is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). Its rationale is that when the speech was explaining established facts, he turned away from them in stating it and made it a speech addressed to every listener, expressing them through third-person pronouns. But when the aim became to show their ignorance and to compel them to the proof against themselves, the speech was switched to the second person, to record it against them and to rebuke them for their ignorance.

[Page 19]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 8:

﴿We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal.﴾

Al-jasad: the body that has no life in it, and it is synonymous with al-juthha (the corpse). This is the statement of the verifiers among the imams of the language, such as Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, in his explanation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿So He brought forth for them a calf, a body (jasad) that lowed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88]. It has been discussed there earlier. From it is also the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We did tempt Solomon and placed upon his throne a body (jasad)﴾ [Sad: 34]. It was said that it was half of a boy without a soul, whom one of his wives bore. That is, We did not make them bodies in which souls were not infused such that the attributes of humans, the most distinctive of which is eating food, are negated from them. This is a refutation of what they said: ﴿What is this messenger that he eats food?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], together with their statement here: ﴿Is this not but a human like you?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 3].

The mention of "body" conveys mockery of the polytheists. For when they said: ﴿What is this messenger that he eats food?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and demanded that he bring what the earlier ones were sent with, the implication of their statements was that the earlier messengers were in the forms of human beings but did not eat food. Since eating food is one of the necessary features of life, it followed, from their saying "What is this messenger that he eats food?", that they must be holding that the nature of messengers is to be bodies without souls, and this is of extreme absurdity. As for His saying: ﴿nor were they immortal﴾, it is an added argument to establish their humanity, by means of what actually occurs of the incapacity of those messengers, as is known by observation, in order to cut off the excuses of the misguided. For if they claimed that the earlier messengers had been different from humans, then what would they do regarding the befalling of annihilation upon them? This is the aspect of the addition of ﴿nor were they immortal﴾. The negation of immortality from them is expressed with the form "ma kanu" (they were not), to establish the firm settling of non-immortality upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 9:

﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them, and We saved them and whomever We willed, and We destroyed the transgressors.﴾

"Thumma" (then) coordinates the sentence with the preceding sentences, so it indicates sequence in rank (al-tartib al-rutbi). The meaning is: and more important than what has been mentioned is that We fulfilled the promise to them, saving them and destroying those who denied them. The content of this is more important for both purposes: good tidings (al-tabshir) and warning (al-indhar). The good tidings are for the Messenger ﷺ and the believers, that God is true to His promise of victory, and the warning is for those who resemble the peoples of the earlier messengers.

The "promise" here means His promise to them of victory over those who denied them, as indicated by the words of the Most High: "and We saved them", which signals that it was a promise of punishment for their peoples. The discourse is thus led in the manner of honouring the earlier messengers, and it is an allusive threat against those who said: ﴿So let him bring us a sign as the earlier ones were sent [with signs]﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5]. In this there is a rebuke to the polytheists, meaning: if what the earlier ones brought impressed you, and you asked your messenger for the like of it, then your situation is like the situation of those to whom they were sent, so await what befell them, and let your messenger await what befell his predecessors. This is like His saying: ﴿Say: Wait, I am with you among those who wait﴾ [Yunus: 102] in Surat Yunus.

The word "al-wa'd" (the promise) is in the accusative after "sadaqnahum" by extension, through the removal of the preposition. The original usage is to say "sadaqnahum fi al-wa'd" (we were true to them in the promise), because "sadaqa" is not transitive except to one object. This elision is common in speech, and among it, in a proverb: "sadaqani sinna bakrihi" (he told me the truth about the age of his young camel).

The use of the imperfect form in His saying "man nashā'" (whomever We will) is ihtibak (interlocking ellipsis), and the implied meaning is: "and We saved them and whomever We willed, and We will save Our messenger and whomever We will of you." It is an expression of hope to them that they may believe, because among those who denied on the day this verse was revealed, there were those who later believed, up to the day of the conquest of Makkah. This is one of God's kindnesses to His servants, encouraging them to faith. For this reason He did not say "and We destroy the transgressors," but returned to the past tense, which narrates what befell the earlier nations. The intended purpose of mentioning those who were destroyed remains an allusion of threat and warning, that the same as what befell those may befall them, without explicitly stating the threat.

"Al-musrifun" (the transgressors) are those who exceed the limit in denial, persisting in it and continuing upon it until the punishment descended upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 10:

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder. Will you not then use your intellect?﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), an answer to their saying: ﴿So let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent [with signs]﴾ [al-Anbiya: 5]. It serves to awaken them to the fact that the sign which has come to them is greater than the signs with which the earlier ones were sent,

[Page 22]

and it is a rebuke for their minds, which did not perceive the greatness of the sign that has come to them, as the placement of this sentence in this place indicates.

Within this is also an affirmation (tahqiq) that the Qur'an is true, and a reminder of the benefits it contains, which they were heedless of, as was related about them at the beginning of the surah in the words of the Exalted: ﴿No reminder comes to them from their Lord, newly revealed, but they listen to it while playing﴾ [al-Anbiya: 2], ﴿their hearts distracted﴾ [al-Anbiya: 3], as the apparent meaning of the verse indicates.

For the purpose of this awakening, the sentence was introduced with what conveys affirmation: the oath-particle lam and the particle of certainty (qad). The sending down of the Book "to them", as the transitivity of the verb "anzalna" with the preposition "ila" requires, is the usual construction in which the object introduced by "ila" is the one to whom something is sent down. Thus the sending down was made "to them", because they stand in the position of one to whom it was sent down, given that the sending down was for their sake and their call. This is more eloquent than saying: "We have sent down for you." The indefinite form of "kitaban" is for magnification, indicating that it combined two great qualities: that it is a Book of guidance, and that it is a sign and a miracle for the Messenger ﷺ, such that no one can produce its like or anything close to it.

The word "dhikr" is used for reminding of what contains righteousness, and it is also used for reputation and renown, as in the words: "﴿The mention of your Lord's mercy to His servant Zakariyya﴾" [Maryam: 2]. This noun has been chosen here and made definite by its attribution to the pronoun of the addressees, so that the speech is directed at them, and so that both meanings of the word "dhikr" may be intended together: that the coming of the Qur'an containing the greatest guidance is a reminder to them of what achieves the perfection of their reform, and that its coming in their own language, among their own people, and through one of themselves, is a great renown for them, as the Exalted said: ﴿In clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 195], and He said: ﴿As We sent among you a Messenger from yourselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 151].

[Page 23]

The early scholars (al-salaf) explained this verse according to both meanings. In al-Tabari's tafsir here, a group said: the meaning of "in it is your reminder" is that it is honour, i.e., in it is your honour. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be intended: in it is your honour and your mention until the end of time, as great matters are mentioned. The Exalted's words ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44] have been explained in a similar way.

On both meanings, the statement of the Exalted "Will you not then use your intellect?" comes in the most fitting position as a consequence, because the rebuking interrogative denying their intellect applies to both meanings. Whoever is brought that by which he is guided and yet does not gain guidance is rebuked for his poor intellect, and whoever is brought that by which his glory and renown lie and yet pays it no heed is rebuked for his poor judgment in not valuing matters at their true worth, just as the reward for such a person would be multiplied. Also, it is a consequence of the persuasion through the sending down of the Qur'an as a sign surpassing the signs they asked for in the like, which is what is conveyed by the resumption and by the emphasis of the sentence with the oath and the particle of certainty. The Exalted said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51] in Surat al-'Ankabut, and that is due to its inimitability in both wording and meaning.

[Page 24]

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His saying ﴿They did not believe, before them, any town which We destroyed﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 6], or with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We destroyed the extravagant﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 9], and it is an allusive (taʿrīḍ) threat.

The appropriateness of its position is that, after He reported that He had fulfilled His promise to His messengers, which is a report that conveys the beginning of honouring the matter of the messengers and their victory, and of those who believed in them, it also mentions the destruction of those who denied the messenger, by way of consequence. Then He followed this with mention of the destruction of many nations of wrongdoers and a description of what befell them, so that this would be intended in itself, from the outset, out of concern for it, that it might strike their ears. Thus it is an allusive warning to the polytheists of extinction, by the rule of analogical equality (qiyās al-musāwāh), and that God will bring into being after them a believing community, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If He wills, He will take you away and bring a new creation﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 19], in Surah Ibrāhīm.

"Kam" (how many) is a noun that has the right of beginning the sentence, because its origin is an interrogative noun asking about number. Its use became common for reporting the abundance of a thing, in a figurative sense, because a great quantity is the kind of thing one asks about. The implied meaning is: We broke many towns. So "kam" here is informative (khabariyyah). It occupies a position of accusative governed by the verb "qaṣamnā" (We broke). In "kam", which indicates abundance of number, there is an indication that this abundance entails that the destruction of these towns was not left out. Together with the description of those nations as wrongdoers, that is, polytheists, as an indication of the cause of destruction, there arises from it, and from the noun of abundance, the meaning of generality. So the polytheists know the threat, that this will certainly befall them by the ruling of generality, and that this is not meant to refer to a specific town. What is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the intended town is Ḥaḍūrāʾ, with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ, a city in Yemen, whose people killed a prophet named Shuʿayb ibn Dhī Mahdam, in the time of Irmiyāʾ, the prophet of the Children of Israel, so God set Bukhtanṣar over them and he annihilated them, means only that this town is among those included in this verse. The implied meaning is: We broke many. The discussion of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [al-Anʿām: 6] has already been given in Surah al-Anʿām.

He applied the word "town" (qaryah) to its people, as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We brought into being after them another people﴾ indicates.

[Page 25]

The reason for choosing the word "town" here is similar to what we mentioned a moment ago in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They did not believe, before them, any town which We destroyed﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 6]. The particle "min" (from) in His saying, "min qaryah", is for specifying the kind (bayān al-jins), and it enters upon what has the sense of specification (tamyīz), and here it is a specification (tamyīz) because of the ambiguity of "kam".

Al-qaṣm: a severe breaking after which mending and benefit are not hoped for. It is borrowed for uprooting and strong destruction, like the destruction of ʿĀd, Thamūd and Sabaʾ.

The clause ﴿and We brought into being after them another people﴾ is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) between the clause ﴿and how many towns We broke﴾ and the clause ﴿when they perceived Our might﴾, etc. Thus the clause ﴿when they perceived Our might﴾, etc., is a consequent branch (tafrīʿ) upon the clause ﴿and how many towns We broke﴾. The pronoun in "minhā" (from it) refers to "qaryah" (town).

Al-iḥsās: perception through the senses, so it occurs by seeing what alarms them, or hearing sounds announcing destruction, such as thunderbolts and winds.

Al-baʾs: the intensity of pain and punishment. The particle "min" in His saying, ﴿from it they flee﴾, may be for origin (ibtidāʾ), meaning: going out from it. It may also be for causation, with the verb "yarkudūn" interpreted in the sense of "yahrubūn" (they flee), meaning: fleeing from the might which they perceived. So an elided modifier must be assumed, meaning: from Our might which they perceived in the town. That occurs with the appearance of signs of warning, such as earthquakes and thunderbolts.

Al-rakḍ: the quick pace of a horse. Its original meaning is striking with the foot, so running is called by it, because running requires strength in striking with the foot. The word "yarkudūn" in this verse is applied to the quick movement of people by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), likening the speed of their movement to the galloping of mares.

[Page 26]

"Minhā" (from it) is a stable adverbial phrase in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the independent nominative pronoun. The sudden "idhā" (suddenly) entered into the response of "lammā" (when), to indicate that they hastened to flee out of the intensity of their perception of the might, depicting the intensity of fear. The sudden "idhā" is not a connective of the response to the conditional, because this response does not need a connective. The sudden "idhā" may serve as a connective of the response in place of the connecting "fa" (then), where a connective is needed, because the meaning of suddenness is suitable for connection without necessarily being bound to it.

The clause "﴿Do not run﴾" is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ). It is an address to those who are running, by imagining them as present and witnessing at the time when their story is being recounted, as a reinforcement (tarshīḥ) of what required the bringing in of the particle of suddenness. This is like the saying of Mālik ibn al-Rayb:

"Desire called me, from the people of my love and my neighbours, at Dhū al-Ṭabasayn, so I turned back."

That is: when desire called him, that is, reminded him of his beloved while he was on a raid at Dhū al-Ṭabasayn, he turned back as one who is called by someone from behind him, so he imagined desire as a caller behind him. This clause may be a parenthetical clause between the clause "﴿when they perceived Our might﴾" and the clause "﴿They said: Woe to us, we were indeed wrongdoers﴾". It is also permissible to make the clause a quoted speech of an elided saying, addressed to them at that time, by their hearing it through a creation of God, exalted is He, or from the angels of punishment. This is what the exegetes (mufassirūn) explained, and it is made remote by the improbability that this would occur at every punishment that befell every town. Whichever it is, the speech is mockery directed at them.

Al-itrāf: giving luxury, which is prosperity and ease of living, that is: return to what you were given of comfort and to your dwellings.

[Page 27]

His saying, exalted is He, "﴿so that you may be questioned﴾", belongs to the mockery. The exegetes mentioned six possibilities regarding the meaning of "tusʾalūn" (you will be questioned). The most evident is: the meaning is: return to what you were in of blessings, so that you may see what it has come to, for perhaps a questioner will ask you about the condition of what befell you, so that you will know how to answer. This is because it is the custom of a traveller that those to whom he comes ask him about the condition of the lands he left, whether in fertility and plenty or the opposite. In this there is a completion of the mockery.

The clause "﴿They said: O woe to us﴾": if you make the clause "﴿Do not run﴾" a parenthetical clause as I have just established, then this clause is a resumed explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī) regarding the clause "﴿suddenly they are running from it﴾", as if a questioner asked what they say when they hurry off fleeing. This is because it is the custom of the fleeing, frightened person to utter words that show fear or regret about the causes that brought the terrors upon him, so it is answered that when they see the punishment they realise that they were wrongdoers, so they acknowledge their wrongdoing and produce lamentation and remorse with their saying: "﴿O woe to us, we were indeed wrongdoers﴾". If you make the clause "﴿Do not run﴾" a quoted speech of an elided saying, according to what the exegetes went to, then the clause "﴿They said: O woe to us, we were indeed wrongdoers﴾" is a response to the saying of one who said to them: "﴿Do not run﴾", in the manner of mockery directed at them, and the separation of the clause would be because it occurs in the position of dialogue, as we explained more than once, meaning: they said: We have known our sin, and the mockery against us is justified. Thus they confessed their sin. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they confessed their sin, so away with the companions of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 11], in Surah al-Mulk.

His saying, exalted is He, "﴿so that you may be questioned﴾", belongs to the mockery. The exegetes mentioned six possibilities regarding the meaning of "tusʾalūn" (you will be questioned). The most evident is: the meaning is: return to what you were in of blessings, so that you may see what it has come to, for perhaps a questioner will ask you about the condition of what befell you, so that you will know how to answer. This is because it is the custom of a traveller that those to whom he comes ask him about the condition of the lands he left, whether in fertility and plenty or the opposite. In this there is a completion of the mockery.

The clause "﴿They said: O woe to us﴾": if you make the clause "﴿Do not run﴾" a parenthetical clause as I have just established, then this clause is a resumed explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī) regarding the clause "﴿suddenly they are running from it﴾", as if a questioner asked what they say when they hurry off fleeing. This is because it is the custom of the fleeing, frightened person to utter words that show fear or regret about the causes that brought the terrors upon him, so it is answered that when they see the punishment they realise that they were wrongdoers, so they acknowledge their wrongdoing and produce lamentation and remorse with their saying: "﴿O woe to us, we were indeed wrongdoers﴾". If you make the clause "﴿Do not run﴾" a quoted speech of an elided saying, according to what the exegetes went to, then the clause "﴿They said: O woe to us, we were indeed wrongdoers﴾" is a response to the saying of one who said to them: "﴿Do not run﴾", in the manner of mockery directed at them, and the separation of the clause would be because it occurs in the position of dialogue, as we explained more than once, meaning: they said: We have known our sin, and the mockery against us is justified. Thus they confessed their sin. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they confessed their sin, so away with the companions of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 11], in Surah al-Mulk.

[Page 24]

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His saying ﴿They did not believe, before them, any town which We destroyed﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 6], or with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We destroyed the extravagant﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 9], and it is an allusive (taʿrīḍ) threat.

The appropriateness of its position is that, after He reported that He had fulfilled His promise to His messengers, which is a report that conveys the beginning of honouring the matter of the messengers and their victory, and of those who believed in them, it also mentions the destruction of those who denied the messenger, by way of consequence. Then He followed this with mention of the destruction of many nations of wrongdoers and a description of what befell them, so that this would be intended in itself, from the outset, out of concern for it, that it might strike their ears. Thus it is an allusive warning to the polytheists of extinction, by the rule of analogical equality (qiyās al-musāwāh), and that God will bring into being after them a believing community, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If He wills, He will take you away and bring a new creation﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 19], in Surah Ibrāhīm.

"Kam" (how many) is a noun that has the right of beginning the sentence, because its origin is an interrogative noun asking about number. Its use became common for reporting the abundance of a thing, in a figurative sense, because a great quantity is the kind of thing one asks about. The implied meaning is: We broke many towns. So "kam" here is informative (khabariyyah). It occupies a position of accusative governed by the verb "qaṣamnā" (We broke). In "kam", which indicates abundance of number, there is an indication that this abundance entails that the destruction of these towns was not left out. Together with the description of those nations as wrongdoers, that is, polytheists, as an indication of the cause of destruction, there arises from it, and from the noun of abundance, the meaning of generality. So the polytheists know the threat, that this will certainly befall them by the ruling of generality, and that this is not meant to refer to a specific town. What is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the intended town is Ḥaḍūrāʾ, with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ, a city in Yemen, whose people killed a prophet named Shuʿayb ibn Dhī Mahdam, in the time of Irmiyāʾ, the prophet of the Children of Israel, so God set Bukhtanṣar over them and he annihilated them, means only that this town is among those included in this verse. The implied meaning is: We broke many. The discussion of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [al-Anʿām: 6] has already been given in Surah al-Anʿām.

He applied the word "town" (qaryah) to its people, as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We brought into being after them another people﴾ indicates.

[Page 25]

The reason for choosing the word "town" here is similar to what we mentioned a moment ago in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They did not believe, before them, any town which We destroyed﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 6]. The particle "min" (from) in His saying, "min qaryah", is for specifying the kind (bayān al-jins), and it enters upon what has the sense of specification (tamyīz), and here it is a specification (tamyīz) because of the ambiguity of "kam".

Al-qaṣm: a severe breaking after which mending and benefit are not hoped for. It is borrowed for uprooting and strong destruction, like the destruction of ʿĀd, Thamūd and Sabaʾ.

The clause ﴿and We brought into being after them another people﴾ is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) between the clause ﴿and how many towns We broke﴾ and the clause ﴿when they perceived Our might﴾, etc. Thus the clause ﴿when they perceived Our might﴾, etc., is a consequent branch (tafrīʿ) upon the clause ﴿and how many towns We broke﴾. The pronoun in "minhā" (from it) refers to "qaryah" (town).

Al-iḥsās: perception through the senses, so it occurs by seeing what alarms them, or hearing sounds announcing destruction, such as thunderbolts and winds.

Al-baʾs: the intensity of pain and punishment. The particle "min" in His saying, ﴿from it they flee﴾, may be for origin (ibtidāʾ), meaning: going out from it. It may also be for causation, with the verb "yarkudūn" interpreted in the sense of "yahrubūn" (they flee), meaning: fleeing from the might which they perceived. So an elided modifier must be assumed, meaning: from Our might which they perceived in the town. That occurs with the appearance of signs of warning, such as earthquakes and thunderbolts.

Al-rakḍ: the quick pace of a horse. Its original meaning is striking with the foot, so running is called by it, because running requires strength in striking with the foot. The word "yarkudūn" in this verse is applied to the quick movement of people by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), likening the speed of their movement to the galloping of mares.

[Page 26]

"Minhā" (from it) is a stable adverbial phrase in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the independent nominative pronoun. The sudden "idhā" (suddenly) entered into the response of "lammā" (when), to indicate that they hastened to flee out of the intensity of their perception of the might, depicting the intensity of fear. The sudden "idhā" is not a connective of the response to the conditional, because this response does not need a connective. The sudden "idhā" may serve as a connective of the response in place of the connecting "fa" (then), where a connective is needed, because the meaning of suddenness is suitable for connection without necessarily being bound to it.

The clause "﴿Do not run﴾" is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ). It is an address to those who are running, by imagining them as present and witnessing at the time when their story is being recounted, as a reinforcement (tarshīḥ) of what required the bringing in of the particle of suddenness. This is like the saying of Mālik ibn al-Rayb:

"Desire called me, from the people of my love and my neighbours, at Dhū al-Ṭabasayn, so I turned back."

That is: when desire called him, that is, reminded him of his beloved while he was on a raid at Dhū al-Ṭabasayn, he turned back as one who is called by someone from behind him, so he imagined desire as a caller behind him. This clause may be a parenthetical clause between the clause "﴿when they perceived Our might﴾" and the clause "﴿They said: Woe to us, we were indeed wrongdoers﴾". It is also permissible to make the clause a quoted speech of an elided saying, addressed to them at that time, by their hearing it through a creation of God, exalted is He, or from the angels of punishment. This is what the exegetes (mufassirūn) explained, and it is made remote by the improbability that this would occur at every punishment that befell every town. Whichever it is, the speech is mockery directed at them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 15:

﴿So their claim did not cease until We made them as cut-down stalks, extinguished.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the statement ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we have been wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 14]. The noun "tilka" (that) is a demonstrative referring to the utterance implied by His words, ﴿They said, "Woe to us!"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 14], and its feminine form is due to the fact that it took on the feminine gender from the predicate referring to it, "their claim" (da'wahum), meaning: they continued repeating that phrase, calling down (yad'una) woe upon themselves by it.

Page 28

This interpretation strengthens the first explanation of His words, ﴿Do not flee, and return to that in which you were made affluent﴾ [al-Anbiya': 13], because it is the nature of the words that a fearful person says that he repeats them, since his judgment is clouded and he cannot find his way to producing other speech, unlike speech that is addressed as a response, for there is no reason to repeat it. The meaning is: they kept repeating that statement until they were all destroyed.

That utterance was called a "claim" (da'wa) because its intent was supplication (du'a') against themselves with woe, and supplication is called da'wa, as in His words, ﴿Their supplication therein is, "Glory be to You, O Allah"﴾ [Yunus: 10] in Surah Yunus. That is, their supplication with this continued to be repeated, and they did not cease from it until We made them like cut-down stalks, that is, We destroyed them.

The particle "hatta" (until) indicates the endpoint of what was implied by His words, ﴿So their claim did not cease﴾.

"Al-hasid" (cut-down) is a fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, that is, "the mowed" (al-mahsud). This form invariably takes the singular and masculine when it describes what it qualifies, as it does here.

"Al-hasd" means cutting crops and plants with a sickle, not by hand. The use of "al-hasid" for mown crops has become common, as a fixed noun.

"Al-khamid" is an active participle from "khamadat al-nar, yakhmudu" (the fire went out, it dies down), with the mim vowelled with damma, when its flame has ceased. They were likened to a crop that has been reaped, that is, after it had been standing upright on its stalk, green. Thus it implies their comparison, before their destruction, to a crop in beauty of appearance and splendour,

Page 29

just as they were likened to a crop in His words, ﴿like a seed that sends out its shoot, then strengthens it, so it grows thick and stands upon its stalk, pleasing the sowers﴾ [al-Fath: 29] in Surah al-Fath. And it is said of a young growing thing: "Allah caused it to grow well (anbatahu nabatan hasanan)," as He said, ﴿And He caused her to grow well a good growth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37] in Surah Al 'Imran. So to indicate both resemblances, the resemblance of radiance and the resemblance of ruin, the comparison of them at the time of their destruction to "hasid" (cut-down stalks) was preferred. Likewise, at the time of their destruction they were likened to an extinguished fire, which implies their comparison, before that, to a blazing fire in strength and force, just as they were likened to fire in His words, ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64] in Surah al-Ma'idah, and His words, ﴿Their likeness is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] in Surah al-Baqarah. Thus two eloquent comparisons arise, and they are not two implicit metaphors (isti'aratan makniyyatan), because the mention of the compared element in them prevents the reality of the metaphor from being established. This is contrary to the view of the two scholars al-Taftazani and al-Jurjani in their commentaries on the Miftah, who relied on the plural form of their pronoun in His words "ja'alnahum," and so considered this to be two implicit metaphors, since they were likened to a crop at the time of its disappearance and to a fire whose strength has gone, the compared element being omitted and indicated by a concomitant of each, namely mowing and extinguishing. So "hasidan" is, in meaning, a description of the pronoun in "ja'alnahum" accusative. Thus "hasid" here is a description that is not treated as a fixed noun, unlike the one in His words, ﴿and the grain of the harvest﴾ [Qaf: 9]. For this reason His words "﴿hasidan﴾" are not of the category of eloquent comparison, since they were not likened to a harvested crop; rather, it is affirmed of them that they are mown, as an implicit metaphor, like its counterpart in His words "﴿khamidin﴾", which is necessarily a metaphor, as its coming in the masculine plain form indicates, and the basis of metaphor is the forgetting of the comparison. This is an over-elaboration on their part, and I do not know what prompted the two of them to undertake this over-elaboration.

"﴿Hasidan khamidin﴾" is in the accusative because both are a second object, repeated for the verb "ja'ala" (to make), just as the subject is described by two or more predicates; for the two objects of "ja'ala" originally are the subject and the predicate, and the second of them is not a description of the first, as is evident.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verses 16–17:

Page 30
﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our presence, if We were to be doers.﴾

The Qur'an has frequently argued from the perfection of the order of the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, that God has wisdom in the creation of created things and in the creation of their systems, their laws and their natures, such that their states, their effects and the relation of some of them to others are proportionate and conform to what wisdom requires. For this reason God, may He be exalted, said in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ [al-Hijr: 85]. We have explained there the manner in which truth attaches to every kind and type of created thing, in a way that makes it unnecessary to repeat it here. The Qur'an often draws the minds' attention to the wisdom that required the connection between the creation of what is in the heavens and the earth being bound with truth, and the recompense of the responsible persons for their deeds, according to the law that the revealed laws (al-shara'i') established for them across their different generations, eras and lands, until the general, final law, the Shari'ah of Islam, encompassed them; and to the wisdom that required the creation of an everlasting life in which souls receive the recompense of what they had advanced in this transient life, a fitting recompense.

Therefore the verses that clarify the truth in creation are frequently followed by verses that mention recompense and reckoning, and vice versa, as in His saying, exalted is He, at the end of Surat al-Mu'minun: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]; and His saying at the end of al-Hijr: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth, and the Hour is surely coming, so forgive with gracious forgiveness﴾ [al-Hijr: 85]; and His saying

Page 31
﴿Indeed, those who stray from the way of God will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning﴾ [Sad: 26] ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain; that is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾ [Sad: 27] ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on the earth, or shall We make the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28] in Surat Sad; and His saying: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals﴾ [al-Dukhan: 37] ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38] ﴿We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39] ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is their appointed time, all of them﴾ [al-Dukhan: 40] in Surat al-Dukhan; and His saying: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term, yet those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 3] in Surat al-Ahqaf, along with other verses besides these.

Likewise, this verse is followed by the mention of the destroyed peoples, and the purpose of that is to awaken minds to reason from what is in the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them of subtle relations and of giving each creature what sustains it. So when that is the sunna of God in the creation of worlds, containers and contained, it is inferred from that that this sunna does not fail in the consequences of causes upon their causes concerning the deeds that the kind of responsible persons perform. Thus, when a failure of one cause to produce its cause appears to them, they are certain that it is a temporary failure. Then, when God informs them through the tongue of His laws that He has reserved the complete recompense for deeds until another day, they believe in it; and when He teaches them that they will not be separated from that by death, but that they have another life, and that God will resurrect them after death, they are certain of it; and when He informs them that He may hasten for them some of the recompense in the worldly life, they are certain of that too.

For this reason, the mention of the order of the creation of the heavens and the earth is frequently followed by the mention of the deferred recompense, the resurrection and the destruction of some unjust nations, or the mention of the resurrection and the deferred and immediate recompense is followed by the mention of the order of the creation of the heavens and the earth.

Page 32
It suffices you to note the sequence marked by the particle fa' in His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190] ﴿Those who remember God standing, sitting and on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191], these verses being the close of Surat Al 'Imran.

And for this reason the expression "and what is between them" has become regular, or nearly regular, after the mention of the creation of the heavens and the earth in such a context; because singling out what is between them for mention indicates concern with it, since the noblest of it is the human species, which is the object of lesson and reasoning and the locus of responsibility. The speech is therefore not built on making creation a play, with the aim of refuting the belief of one who holds that belief; rather it is built on negation, taking them to task for the necessary consequence of their heedlessness of the subtle details of God's wisdom, such that they were like those who say that this making is play.

Play (la'ib) is an action or speech not intended to achieve a benefit, whether attaining an interest or repelling a harm, nor to attain a gain or repel a damage, but is intended only to satisfy the soul when it inclines toward frivolity, as it is said: "The intelligent person must have a folly by which he lives." It is synonymous with 'abath (idle purposelessness) and lahw (diversion), and its opposite is jidd (earnestness). Play belongs to falsehood, since there is no wisdom in its doing; so its opposite is truth as well.

"La'ibin" (playing) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in "khalaqna" (We created), and it is a necessary state, since the meaning is not sound without it. The clause ﴿If We wished to take a pastime﴾ confirms the meaning of the clause ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾, confirming it by argument for the content of the clause and giving a reason for negating that the creation of the heavens and the earth is play, that is, purposeless, namely that play is not befitting to Us; or, on the assumption and for the sake of argument, if We wished for diversion,

Page 33
then what it would be used for would be found in the most noble places of the heavens, for they are most especially associated with God, the Exalted, since He made their inhabitants devoted servants to Him. Therefore it is expressed by the particle of place that is especially restricted, namely "ladun" (from the presence of), added to the pronoun of majesty, by His saying: "min ladunna" (from Us), meaning not the worlds that are particular to you, but rather in the world of the unseen, which is more especially associated with Us, since it is the world of the angels brought near. So the locative sense conveyed by "ladun" is a figurative locative sense. The addition of "ladun" to the pronoun of majesty indicates elevation and preference, as in His saying: ﴿a provision from Us﴾ [al-Qasas: 57] in Surat al-Qasas, and His saying: ﴿Grant us from Yourself mercy﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8] in Al 'Imran; meaning, if We wished to take a diversion, its taking would be in the world of your witnessing. This is an inference by customary implication, because the way of one who takes something for amusement is to keep it to himself and not permit others to share it, and this is based on what the minds of the addressees commonly hold, namely their assumption that the higher worlds are closer to God, the Exalted.

The clause ﴿if We were to be doers﴾: if you take "in" as conditional, its connection to the preceding clause is the connection of a condition to its omitted consequent, which is indicated by the response of "law" (if), namely the clause "la-attakhadhnahu" (We would have taken it), so it is a repetition of the implication. If you take "in" as a negative particle, the clause is a new sentence confirming the negation derived from "law", that is: We were not doers of diversion.

It suffices you to note the sequence marked by the particle fa' in His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190] ﴿Those who remember God standing, sitting and on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191], these verses being the close of Surat Al 'Imran.

And for this reason the expression "and what is between them" has become regular, or nearly regular, after the mention of the creation of the heavens and the earth in such a context; because singling out what is between them for mention indicates concern with it, since the noblest of it is the human species, which is the object of lesson and reasoning and the locus of responsibility. The speech is therefore not built on making creation a play, with the aim of refuting the belief of one who holds that belief; rather it is built on negation, taking them to task for the necessary consequence of their heedlessness of the subtle details of God's wisdom, such that they were like those who say that this making is play.

Play (la'ib) is an action or speech not intended to achieve a benefit, whether attaining an interest or repelling a harm, nor to attain a gain or repel a damage, but is intended only to satisfy the soul when it inclines toward frivolity, as it is said: "The intelligent person must have a folly by which he lives." It is synonymous with 'abath (idle purposelessness) and lahw (diversion), and its opposite is jidd (earnestness). Play belongs to falsehood, since there is no wisdom in its doing; so its opposite is truth as well.

"La'ibin" (playing) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in "khalaqna" (We created), and it is a necessary state, since the meaning is not sound without it. The clause ﴿If We wished to take a pastime﴾ confirms the meaning of the clause ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾, confirming it by argument for the content of the clause and giving a reason for negating that the creation of the heavens and the earth is play, that is, purposeless, namely that play is not befitting to Us; or, on the assumption and for the sake of argument, if We wished for diversion,

Page 33
then what it would be used for would be found in the most noble places of the heavens, for they are most especially associated with God, the Exalted, since He made their inhabitants devoted servants to Him. Therefore it is expressed by the particle of place that is especially restricted, namely "ladun" (from the presence of), added to the pronoun of majesty, by His saying: "min ladunna" (from Us), meaning not the worlds that are particular to you, but rather in the world of the unseen, which is more especially associated with Us, since it is the world of the angels brought near. So the locative sense conveyed by "ladun" is a figurative locative sense. The addition of "ladun" to the pronoun of majesty indicates elevation and preference, as in His saying: ﴿a provision from Us﴾ [al-Qasas: 57] in Surat al-Qasas, and His saying: ﴿Grant us from Yourself mercy﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8] in Al 'Imran; meaning, if We wished to take a diversion, its taking would be in the world of your witnessing. This is an inference by customary implication, because the way of one who takes something for amusement is to keep it to himself and not permit others to share it, and this is based on what the minds of the addressees commonly hold, namely their assumption that the higher worlds are closer to God, the Exalted.

The clause ﴿if We were to be doers﴾: if you take "in" as conditional, its connection to the preceding clause is the connection of a condition to its omitted consequent, which is indicated by the response of "law" (if), namely the clause "la-attakhadhnahu" (We would have taken it), so it is a repetition of the implication. If you take "in" as a negative particle, the clause is a new sentence confirming the negation derived from "law", that is: We were not doers of diversion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 18:

﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes. And woe to you for what you describe.﴾

"Bal" (بَلْ) is used here for a turning away (idrab) from taking play (lahw) and from the creation being mere play; it is an idrab of nullification and elevation (irtiqa'), meaning: rather, We deliberately aim at your falsehood and hurl the truth against it, out of disapproval of falsehood, far less than that We would do an act which is falsehood and play.

Page 34
The basic meaning of qadhf (قَذْف) is throwing one body onto another body. It is used here metaphorically for bringing forth whatever removes and nullifies a thing, whether a proof, a rebuke, an annihilation, or the creation of what overpowers it, because that is like throwing a nullified body with something that comes upon it to destroy or scatter it. So God nullifies falsehood by the truth: by making clear to people the nullity of falsehood through His messengers; by placing in their minds a perception for distinguishing between right and wrong; by empowering some of His servants over the falsifiers to root them out; and by creating creatures which He subjects to the nullifying of falsehood. God, Exalted, said: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], in Surat al-Anfal.

Al-dam' (الدَّمْغ) is the breaking of a hard hollow body. It is here a continuation (tarshih) of the metaphor of qadhf for bringing forth what nullifies, and it is also a metaphor, since dam' is used for the eradication and removal of falsehood as qadhf removes the body thrown. Thus both metaphors are of the borrowing of sensible things for intelligible things.

The particle of suddenness (fa-idha, فإذا) indicates the swiftness with which the truth annihilates falsehood upon its arrival, because the truth has a force; when it arrives and becomes clear, its effect is rapid. God, Exalted, said: ﴿He sent down water from the sky, and valleys flowed according to their measure, and the torrent carried a swelling foam﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17] up to His saying: ﴿Thus God strikes the truth and falsehood; as for the foam, it passes away as scum, but what benefits people remains on the earth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17], in Surat al-Ra'd.

Al-zahiq (الزّاهِق) is that which has come loose from its place and perished; its verb is like sami'a and daraba, and the verbal noun is al-zuhuq. It has preceded in His saying: ﴿and their souls depart while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 55], in Surat Bara'ah, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, falsehood was ever bound to vanish﴾ [al-Isra': 81], in Surat al-Isra'.

When their contention with clear proofs for nullifying their claims concerning the Messenger and the Qur'an had ended, beginning from His saying: ﴿And the wrongdoers conspired in secret﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3] up to His saying: ﴿as the earlier ones were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5], and what came between that of admonitions, awakenings and lessons, the discourse was concluded with censuring and threatening them with His saying: ﴿And woe to you for what you describe﴾, meaning: for what you describe Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an with.

Al-Waylu (الوَيْل) is a word of supplication for evil, and in the Qur'an it carries an implication, since waylun is the name of punishment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verses 19–20:

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And those near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire.﴾ ﴿They glorify [Him] night and day; they do not slacken.﴾

This is a continuation (ʿaṭf) of the sentence ﴿Had We wished to take a diversion, We would have taken it from Ourselves, if We were to do [such a thing]﴾ [al-Anbiya': 17], clarifying that everyone in the heavens and the earth is a servant of God Most High, created to accept His obligations and to carry out that for which they were created. It is also a transition (takhallus) toward refuting polytheism with a decisive argument, after the mention [in the preceding verses] of establishing the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the authority (ḥujjiyyah) of the Qur'an.

The lām in ﴿wa lahu﴾ indicates ownership (lil-milk), and the prepositional phrase with lām is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam). ﴿Man fi al-samawati﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the fronting of the prepositional phrase indicates exclusivity (lil-ikhtisas): meaning, to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and not to other than Him. This is a qaṣr of ifrād, a rebuttal of the polytheists who ascribed partners to God in divinity.

﴿Man fi al-samawati wa al-ard﴾ encompasses rational beings and others, and the relative pronoun that is predominantly used for rational beings is given precedence, because they are the primary intended referents. The phrase ﴿wa man ʿindahu﴾ may be conjoined (maʿṭūf) to ﴿man fi al-samawati wa al-ard﴾, in which case it is an instance of ʿaṭf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm (conjoining the specific to the general) for the sake of emphasis (lil-ihtimam) bihi. The aspect of emphasis is evident. In this case, the clause ﴿la yastakbirūna ʿan ʿibadatihi﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to the conjoined element.

It is also possible that ﴿man﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), with the clause ﴿la yastakbirūna ʿan ʿibadatihi﴾ as its predicate (khabar). The referent of ﴿man﴾ is a group, as indicated by the plural form in His saying ﴿la yastakbirūna﴾.

﴿Wa man ʿindahu﴾ refers to those brought near in the exalted realms, and they are the angels. On both readings regarding the position of the clause ﴿la yastakbirūna ʿan ʿibadatihi﴾, its intended purpose is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to those who are too proud to worship God and who worship idols, namely the polytheists.

Al-istiḥsār is a verbal noun like al-ḥusūr, which means fatigue. The sīn and tā' in it serve intensification in the description, as in al-istikbār, al-istinkār and al-istikhār. That is, there does not arise from them al-istiḥsār, which is the severe fatigue that their great labour would entail; that is, there does not occur from them what would, if others performed their work, cause them to become exhausted by its weight. Thus al-istiḥsār, which is strong ḥusūr, is used here because it suits the arduous work. Its negation is of the type of negating a restricted qualifier that came out in the manner of what is usual in such cases. Therefore it is not understood from the negation of strong ḥusūr that they may tire with weak ḥusūr. This meaning is what the scholars of rhetoric (ahl al-maʿānī) sometimes express by saying that the emphasis lies in the negation, not in the thing negated.

The clause ﴿yusabbihūna al-layla wa al-nahar﴾ explains the clause ﴿wa la yastaḥsirūn﴾, because one who does not tire of a deed does not abandon it; he persists in it and does not grow weary of it.

Al-layl and al-nahar are adverbs of time (ẓarfān). The principle regarding an adverb of time is that the event occurring in it encompasses it entirely; that is, they glorify [God] throughout the whole of the night and the day.

The glorification of the angels is through voices created in them, which the conveying of revelation or any other speech does not interrupt.

Al-futūr: cessation from an action.
