[Page 37]
﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who can raise the dead?﴾

"Am" (or) here is *munqati'a* (disjunctive, introducing a new statement) and *'atifa* (conjunctive), coordinating one sentence with the preceding one by way of *idrab intiqali* (a transitional shift, meaning a turn away from the previous topic). It is a shift from establishing the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ and the probative force of the Qur'an to refuting polytheism. It is a transition from the remainder of the previous theme, for which the listener was prepared by the *takhallus* (smooth transition, a thematic bridge) in the words of God Most High: ﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and those near Him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 19], as previously explained, to a theme devoted purely to refuting polytheism and refuting the plurality of gods. This transition came as *i'tirad* (an interjected digression) between the words ﴿They glorify Him night and day; they never tire﴾ [al-Anbiya: 20] and the words ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya: 23]. The transitional shift does not require that one never return to the theme that was left. "Am" indicates that the speech following it is cast in the form of a question, and it is an *istifham inkari* (rhetorical question of denial), denouncing their taking of gods.

The pronoun in "ittakhadhu" (they have taken) refers to the polytheists, who are evident from the context, as is the case with such pronouns. There are many parallels to this in the Qur'an. It is also permissible to regard it as an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person) from the pronoun in ﴿Woe to you for what you describe﴾ [al-Anbiya: 18], and it is permissible that it be consistent with the pronouns in ﴿Rather they say: confused dreams﴾ [al-Anbiya: 5] and what follows it.

Describing the gods as "from the earth" is a mockery of the polytheists and a display of the feebleness of their opinion. That is, they made for themselves gods from the world of the earth, or taken from parts of the earth, of stone or wood, implying that whatever is like this does not deserve to be worshipped. This is like what Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ [al-Saffat: 95], in the surah of al-Saffat.

The mention of the earth here is set in contrast with His words "and those near Him", because the intended meaning is the inhabitants of the heavens. The clause "﴿they can raise the dead﴾" is a second attribute of "gods".

[Page 38]
Its being joined with the *damir al-fasl* (separating pronoun, "hum") indicates restriction: that none other than those gods can raise the dead.

The intended meaning is the raising of the dead, that is, their resurrection. This is cast as mockery and as an *idmaj* (embedding) of proof of the resurrection by way of an indirect approach called *tajahul al-ma'arif* (feigned ignorance of what is known). It highlights their denial of the resurrection, which God informed them of through the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ, in the form of their denial that God is able to do it and that He is incapable of it. That is, the one more fitting to have power over the resurrection are their associates. Thus the occurrence of the resurrection is a matter that should not be disputed. If the disputants dispute it, they are disputing its attribution to God, and by this they aim to attribute it to their associates. This attribution is therefore denounced in this manner, which is full of subtle points. The polytheists did not claim for their gods that they raise the dead, nor do they acknowledge that the resurrection occurs; rather, they were treated as one who makes such a claim, as an artful way of imposing the argument. A parallel to this is His words, in the surah of al-Nahl, concerning the gods: ﴿They are dead, not living, and they do not know when they will be raised﴾ [al-Nahl: 21].

[Page 38]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Anbiya' (21), verse 22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted. Exalted is Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾

This clause explains the denial in His words, ﴿Or have they taken gods?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 21], and for this reason it is separated and not joined by a conjunction. The dual pronoun in "them" refers back to "the heavens and the earth" in His words, ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19]. The meaning is: had there been in the heavens and the earth other gods, and had not everyone in them been a possession of Allah and His servant, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted, and their order, by which they were created, would have been disrupted.

This is an argument against the creed of the polytheists, who claimed that Allah had made gods partners with Him in governing creation. That is, after He created the heavens and the earth, He set up partners for Himself on the earth. For this reason they used to say in the talbiyah during the Hajj: "Here I am, O Allah, no partner have You, except a partner who belongs to You; You possess him and what he possesses." This is part of the confused error which the leaders of disbelief devised for them through their ignorance and by promoting their misguidance upon the minds of the common folk.

Thereby it becomes clear that this verse is an argument for the impossibility of the existence of gods other than Allah after the creation of the heavens and the earth. This is because the polytheists did not deny that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth. He said: ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [al-Zumar: 38], in Surah al-Zumar, and He said: ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "They were created by the Mighty, the All-Knowing"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9], in Surah al-Zukhruf. So the verse is intended to establish the Oneness (tawhid), not to establish the existence of the Maker, since there is no dispute about this among those addressed. Nor is it intended to establish His sole possession of creation, since there is no dispute about that either. Rather, it is arranged in a manner suited to their false belief, in order to expose their error and to declare their falsehood.

Corruption (fasad) is the disruption of order and the absence of benefit from things. The corruption of the heavens and the earth is that they become unfit and disordered, such that the benefit derived from what is in them is nullified. From the soundness of the heaven is the order of its stars, the regularity of the times of their rising and setting, and the order of light and darkness. From the soundness of the earth is its being a cradle for movement, its producing of trees and crops, and its containing pastures, stones, minerals and timber. The corruption of each of these is the nullification of its sound order.

The way this argument is ordered is that if gods were multiple, it would necessarily follow that each god would be characterized by the known attributes of divinity, whose effects are known: absolute will and complete power over disposal. Further, plurality requires difference in the objects of their wills and their power, for if the gods were equal in the objects of their wills, then the plurality of gods would be pointless, since one of them would suffice. Also, if an existing thing comes into being, then if its coming into being is by the will of more than one, it would necessarily follow that two influencers act upon one influenced, and this is impossible, since two complete causes cannot act upon one effect. Therefore, it is certain that the plurality of gods entails difference in the objects of their dispositions, whether in kinds, in circumstances, or in places. So the god whose will does not take effect in some existing things is not a god with respect to those things which another has brought into being. It is certain that the objects of the wills of the gods would differ according to the differing interests of their subjects, their domains, or the conditions of their dispositions. Each one would be jealous of what is within his authority. Thus it is established that plurality entails difference of wills and the occurrence of dispute.

Since sameness in the reality of divinity requires equality in the strength of each god's power, and since it requires complete capability when the will is directed toward subduing the opposite, namely that nothing prevents him from eradicating his opponent, and since each of them repels from himself by attacking his opponent and corrupting his dominion and authority, it becomes necessary that whenever one of them turns to attack his opponent, he would destroy everything under the latter's authority. Thus, the corruption of what is in the heavens and the earth would continue at every dispute, as He said: ﴿And there was not with Him any god; otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91], in Surah al-Mu'minun.

Therefore, the observed continuance of the heavens and the earth, and their order across many eras and conditions, certainly indicates that their God is one, not many.

As for if one supposes a difference in the reality of divinity, this would require the superiority of some gods over others, and this is even more conducive to corruption, since mastery would belong to the strongest of them. He would bring all under his sway and corrupt whatever is in the possession of each weaker one, so corruption would be swifter.

[Page 39]

This argument, considered as directed at refuting a particular plurality, namely the plurality believed in by the idolaters of the Arabs and the Greeks, who claimed a plurality of gods according to the plurality of tribes and dispositions, and likewise what the Manichaeans of the Persians believed, who affirmed two gods, one of good and the other of evil, or one of light and the other of darkness, is a decisive proof.

As for considering the way the theologians (mutakallimun) followed in using this verse to refute the plurality of gods in principle with respect to the origination of the world, and which they called the "demonstration of mutual obstruction" (burhan al-tamanu'), it is a persuasive argument (dalil iqna'i), as Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani said in his commentary on al-Nasafiyya. He also said in al-Maqasid: "In some of its parts there is a weakness that is not hidden."

Its explanation is that agreement on the origination of the world may come from two wise ones or from wise beings, so the argument is not complete except by analogizing the gods to kings in common custom, and this is a persuasive analogy.

The reason it is called the demonstration of mutual obstruction is that the aspect of its indication of the impossibility of plurality of the god is the assumption that the gods would obstruct one another, i.e., one of them would prevent the other from executing his will. Delving into this is not our concern here.

What is looked at in the argument here is the necessity of the corruption of the heavens and the earth, not something else from premises external to the wording of the verse, such that the proof would become a decisive proof by them. This is because that has other proofs, such as His words: ﴿And there was not with Him any god; otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91]. This will come in Surah al-Mu'minun.

As for the argument by the demonstration of mutual obstruction, the theologians have two methods in its formulation, mentioned by the author of al-Mawaqif (al-Iji).

The first: the method of inferring the necessity of actual mutual obstruction, which is the well-known method. Its formulation is: if the world had two makers equal in power, then either their wills agree, in which case, if the acts are by both their wills, it would necessarily follow that two complete influencers act upon one influenced (with the letter tha' vowelled fath), which is impossible, since two complete causes cannot act upon one effect. And if the act is by one of the two wills rather than the other, it would necessarily follow the preference of one of them without a preponderating cause, since they are equal in attribute and in the one characterized by it. Or their wills differ, in which case mutual obstruction necessarily follows, meaning that each of them prevents the other from acting, since it is assumed that they are equal in power.

Objections are raised against the argument by this method in several matters. First, it does not follow that the two gods are equal in power; rather, it is intellectually possible that one of them is more powerful than the other. It was answered that absolute incapacity is contrary to divinity by self-evidence, as stated by 'Abd al-Hakim in the marginal notes on al-Baydawi.

Second, it is possible that the two gods agree that neither wills except what the other has not willed, so there is no necessary incapacity for the one who does not act.

Third, it is possible that the two gods agree upon bringing about the matter willed jointly rather than independently.

Fourth, it is possible that one of them delegates to the other the act, so there is no necessary incapacity of the delegator, because the non-bringing-about of a thing that is within power due to an impediment which the capable one himself willed is not called incapacity, especially since his purpose has been achieved, even if he did not do it himself.

The answer to these last three is that in all of them there is a deficiency in divinity, because divinity by its nature requires perfection in every state.

However, this answer does not take the demonstration out of the limit of persuasion.

The second method: al-Taftazani relied upon it in his commentary on the Nasafiyya creed. It is that the plurality of two gods necessarily entails the possibility of mutual obstruction between them, i.e., that one of them would prevent what the other wills, since plural beings may be subject to difference in will. If this possibility is necessarily attached to plurality, then if mutual obstruction occurs between them, when the will of one of them is directed at the existence of a specific person and the will of the other at his non-existence, then both wills cannot be realized together, because of the necessity of the joining of contradictories. If one of the two wills is realized, then the incapacity of the owner of the unrealized will necessarily follows, and incapacity necessitates origination, which is impossible. So the joining of contradictories or the origination of the god is necessary to plurality, and this is impossible. The necessary consequence of a necessary consequence is a necessity, so the first necessitated matter is impossible. Al-Taftazani said: "By this, the objections raised against the demonstration of mutual obstruction are dispelled."

I say: this method is refuted in that the possibility of mutual obstruction does not make the proof valid, because this possibility is impossible to occur, given the impossibility of disagreement arising between the two gods. This is based on the view that difference in will arises only from differing degrees of knowledge in grasping things, which is why disagreement is rare among the wise. We assume the two gods are equal in knowledge and wisdom, so their knowledge and wisdom require a similar revelation, and neither wills except what the other wills, so no mutual obstruction occurs between them. For this reason, al-Maqasid inferred the necessity of the occurrence of difference between them through the rule of customary necessity.

What remains is the consideration of how the act proceeds from them, and that is a transition to what the first method is built upon.

The possibility that the two gods agree on willing things whenever there is interest in them, on the basis that the two gods are wise and their wills do not differ, is a valid possibility; but in that case the plurality of gods becomes pointless, because the plurality of governors was only for seeking the manifestation of what is right when they differ. If they do not differ, there is no benefit in plurality. It is impossible to base the attribute of the highest of existents upon something that has no effect in reality. So the verse is a decisive proof.

[Page 40]

Then he retracted this in the commentary on al-Nasafiyya, verifying that it is a persuasive proof under both assumptions. The verifier al-Khayali said that it is not a decisive proof except with regard to examining the meaning of the locative (zarfiyya) in His words, "in them" (fihima), and he specified that the locative be the locative of influence, i.e., if an agent other than Allah were influencing them, meaning the heavens and the earth, the verse would be a decisive argument. 'Abd al-Hakim expounded this in his marginal notes on al-Khayali, and there is no need for us to reproduce his words here.

The exception in His words, ﴿except Allah﴾, is an exception from one of the two sides of the proposition, not from the judgment relation. That is, it is an exception from the subject of the judgment, not from the judgment itself. This is one of the places of exception, since the basis of exception is excluding from the excepted. Most often the exclusion is from the excepted in view of the judgment having applied to it before the exception, as in the case of the incomplete (mufarragh) and the accusative (mansub). It may also be in view of it before the judgment applied to it, as in the case other than the accusative and the incomplete. In that case it is said that "illa" here means "ghayr" (other than), and the excepted is parsed as a substitute (badal) for the excepted-from.

It follows from this argument the expression of the glorification of Allah, Exalted, above the saying which the argument refuted, in His words: ﴿Exalted is Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, i.e., above what they attribute to Him of the existence of a partner.

The manifest use of the Name Allah (ism al-jalalah) in a place where a pronoun would ordinarily stand serves to cultivate awe (li-tarbiyat al-mahabah).

Describing Him here as "Lord of the Throne" (Rabb al-'Arsh) serves as a reminder that He alone created the heavens, something they do not dispute. Rather, He is the Creator of the greatest of the heavens and what encompasses them, which is the Throne (al-'Arsh). This is an allusion (ta'rid) directed at them, obliging them to accept the necessary consequence of their own statement that He alone is the Creator: that the existence of partners with Him in what lies below that must likewise be negated.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 23:

Page 45
﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾
The most apparent view is that this sentence is a complementary circumstantial clause (hal) explaining the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They do not disdain to worship Him, nor do they tire. They glorify Him night and day, and they never slacken﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19], as was previously mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 21], and so on. The meaning is that those who are with Him, namely the angels who are closest to Him among the created beings, are, despite their nearness, questioned about what they do, while they do not question Him about what He does. That is, their nearness did not reach the point of presumption against Him or of setting themselves up to call His actions to account. Since the pronoun in the passive position (al-damir al-marfu' bi-l-niyabah 'an al-fa'il) indicates an agent that has been omitted for the purpose of generalization, meaning that no questioner questions God, exalted is He, about what He does, and since among those encompassed by the omitted agent are those with Him from among the closest ones, it is correct for this sentence to be a circumstantial clause (hal) of "those who are with Him," on the basis that the sentence ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ serves as a preparation for the sentence ﴿and they are questioned﴾. Moreover, placing it before the sentence ﴿and they are questioned﴾ was required by the context of speaking about His transcendence above partners, so it is a wonderful transition back to the rest of the states of those who are closest. The intended meaning is that those who are with Him, despite their nearness and elevated rank, are called to account by God for their deeds, so they fear falling short in the duties with which they have been charged; for this reason they neither tire nor slacken. By this you know that the pronoun in ﴿and they are questioned﴾ does not refer back to what the pronoun in "they describe" refers to, because for those the information that they are questioned is of no use, since no one doubts this knowledge; nor does it refer to ﴿gods from the earth﴾ [al-Anbiya': 21], because their questioning is not valid. That is what led us to regard the sentence ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "those who are with Him."

Page 46
The word "questioning" here means calling to account, seeking an explanation of the reason for an act, offering an excuse for performing some of what is done, and seeking deliverance from blame or reproach for what is done. It is like the questioning in the hadith: "Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock." Thus their being questioned is a metonymy (kinayah) for servitude, because the servant is liable to be held accountable for what he does and what he does not do, and is likely to err in some of what he does.
The intended meaning here is not the negation of questioning for consultation or seeking knowledge, as in His saying: ﴿They said: Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in al-Baqarah, nor questioning in supplication, nor questioning for benefit and deduction, like the questions of jurists or theologians about the wisdoms scattered in the legal rulings or in the cosmic order; because that is deduction and investigation, and is not directly questioning God, exalted is He, nor is it seeking deliverance from blame. In this there is a refutation of the divinity of the closest ones which the polytheists claimed, those who worshipped the angels and considered them daughters of God, exalted is He, by way of negating the distinctive attribute of the true God from them; for they are questioned about what they do, whereas it is the nature of a god that he is not questioned. And from the sentence ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ is derived a metonymy (kinayah) for the operation of God's acts, exalted is He, in accordance with wisdom, such that there is no room in them for the criticism of a critic, if the observer perfects contemplation of them or has what was hidden from him in them uncovered.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 24:

﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him? Say: "Bring your proof. This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me." But most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away.﴾

The clause ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him﴾ is an emphatic restatement of the clause ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth﴾ [al-Anbiya': 21]. This transition-turn (al-idrab al-intiqali) is reinforced with its like (ista'zaman) for the sake of its enormity (fazaatihi), and so that another argument may be built upon it, just as an argument was built upon its earlier counterpart. The first was followed by an argument of impossibility by way of reason ('aql), while this one is followed by an argument of invalidity, by the testimony of the revealed laws (shara'i') both earlier and later. So God instructed His Messenger ﷺ to say: "Bring your proof," that is, bring evidence that God has partners, from the testimony of the revealed laws and the messengers.

Al-burhan (proof) is the clear argument. It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿O people, there has come to you a proof from your Lord﴾ [al-Nisa': 174] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿This is the reminder of those with me﴾ refers to something assumed in the mind, which the predicate explains. The purpose of the demonstrative is to distinguish it and make it manifest, such that the addressee cannot deceive regarding it or its content, like His saying: ﴿This is the creation of God; so show me what those besides Him have created﴾ [Luqman: 11] in Surat Luqman. That is, the books of reminder (kutub al-dhikr), i.e., the religious books, are within people's reach, so look and see whether you find in any of them that God has partners, or that God permitted them to take gods.

The annexation of "dhikr" to "man ma'iya" is an annexation of the verbal noun to its object, and they are the ones being reminded, with the kaf pronounced with a fatha (al-mudhakkarun).

The companionship (ma'iyya) in His saying ﴿man ma'i﴾ is companionship of following, that is, those among the Muslims who are with me. So the referent of the relative "man" is the nations: that is, this is the reminder of the community that is with me, i.e., the reminder revealed for your sake. The annexation is thus an annexation of the verbal noun to its object, like His saying: ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 10]. What is meant by His saying ﴿This is the reminder of those with me﴾ is the Qur'an. As for His saying ﴿and the reminder of those before me﴾, its meaning is the reminder of the nations who came before me, and it encompasses all the well-known earlier books: the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the book of Luqman. This is like His saying: ﴿God bears witness that there is no deity but Him, and the angels and those of knowledge, upholding justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18] in Al 'Imran.

The argument is turned away from by describing it as fruitless among them, with His saying: ﴿But most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away﴾. That is, do not expect from them an acknowledgment of the invalidity of their polytheism, neither from the rational argument mentioned earlier nor from the argument of the testimony of the revealed laws mentioned second, for most of them do not know the truth and do not acquire its knowledge.

What is meant by their not knowing the truth is that they do not seek its knowledge, as indicated by the context of the consequence drawn from it in His saying: ﴿so they turn away﴾, that is, they turn away from reflecting on the evidences to which you call them to know and reflect upon.

This judgment was attributed to most of them rather than to all of them, either to record against them that a few of them know the truth and deny it, or as an allusion that a few of them have dispositions prepared to accept the truth. This is the state that comes over the soul when the breezes of divine success blow upon it, as happened to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab when he found the tablet with Surat Ta-Ha written in it at his sister's house, and he turned to its recitation with all his heart, and he had not finished the two before he resolved upon Islam.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 25:**

﴿We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me.﴾

When He had shown His Messenger that the obstinate deniers do not know the truth because of their aversion to receiving it, He turned to His Messenger ﷺ, strengthening his speech with the statement He had taught him to answer them with, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Bring your proof. This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me﴾ [al-Anbiya: 24]. This affirms its generality over the laws of all the messengers, whether the one to whom a scripture was sent or the one to whom no scripture was sent, and whether the one whose scripture has remained, like Musa, 'Isa and Dawud, or the one whose scripture has not remained, like Ibrahim.

[Page 49]

The mention of this sentence is not merely to confirm what precedes it of the verses on *tawhid* (affirmation of God's oneness). Although it does confirm them as a consequence of its intended purpose, it also shows God's concern with removing *shirk* (associating partners with God) from human souls and cutting off its roots, reforming their minds by removing from them the most monstrous folly and the most foolish opinion. No law has cut off the roots of *shirk* as Islam has cut them, to the point that *shirk* did not arise in this community.

The particle "min" in His saying, exalted is He: "﴿min rasulin﴾" (from a messenger) is added to emphasize the negation.

He made His command to them to worship Him a consequence of the proclamation, in what was revealed to them, that there is no god other than Him. Thus the entitlement to worship belongs exclusively to Him, exalted is He.

The majority of readers recite "illa yuha ilayhi" with a ya' (yuha) in the passive voice, while Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recite it with a nun (nuha) in the active voice. The exclusive exception construction (*al-istithna' al-mufarragh*) that follows is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verses 26–29:

﴿They say: "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants.﴾ ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not intercede except for one whom He approves, and they are fearful of Him in awe.﴾ ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him," We shall recompense him with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾

This is the conjunction of one story of their false claims to another story. When the discussion of their falsehood regarding the deities they took besides God had been completed, the speech moved on to explain another falsehood, which is their belief that God has taken a child. The tribe of Khuza'a, who were among the inhabitants of the outskirts of Mecca, claimed that the angels are the daughters of God, from among the chiefs of the jinn. Some of the Quraysh and other Arabs shared in this claim. This was already mentioned at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they attribute daughters to God, Glory be to Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 57] in the surah of al-Nahl.

The word "walad" (child) is a collective noun (ism jam'), whose singular is "mithluhu" (its like), meaning that He has taken children. "Walad" includes both male and female. Those who said "God has taken a child" meant that He had taken daughters, as He said: ﴿And they attribute daughters to God, Glory be to Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 57]. Since taking a child implies a deficiency in the one who necessarily exists, He followed their statement with the word "subhanahu" (Glory be to Him), exalting Him above that. Taking a child arises only from need, to complete a deficiency caused by the lack of a child, as He said in the surah of Yunus: ﴿They say: "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient﴾ [Yunus: 68]. Since what was meant by His saying ﴿And they say: "God has taken a son"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116] was that they claimed the angels to be God's daughters, the particle of disengagement (harf al-idrab, the particle marking a shift away from a prior statement) was followed by the information that they are servants, without mentioning the subject, because it is known. The implied meaning is: "Rather, the angels are honored servants," that is, God honored them by His pleasure with them, made them among His nearest servants, and preferred them over many of His righteous creatures.

As for "al-sabq" (precedence), its literal meaning is advancing ahead of another in running. Its use has become common figuratively for advancing in any action, and from it comes precedence in speech, that is, speaking before others, as in this verse. Negating it here is a kinaya (an indirect expression, implicature) for the absence of equality, that is, a kinaya for glorification and reverence. Its parallel in this regard is the prohibition of advancing in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1], for advancing carries the sense of precedence. So His saying ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ means that no speech issues from them before His speech, that is, they say nothing except what they are permitted to say, unless He says it first. This is general and includes the refutation of the claim of the polytheists that their objects of worship will intercede for them with God when God wants to punish them for their deeds. They say: "These are our intercessors with God," as He will explicitly deny later. The fronting of "bi-amrihi" (by His command) before "ya'malun" (they act) serves to express restriction (qasr, limitation of the predicate to a specified subject), that is, they do not act any act except by the command of God, Exalted is He. Just as they do not say a word He has not permitted, so too they do not perform any act except by His command.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ has a parallel that was mentioned in the surah of al-Baqarah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ is a specification by mention of part of what was included in His saying ﴿they do not precede Him in speech﴾, showing concern for it, because it is the matter on account of which they committed disbelief, when they made the deities intercessors for them with God.

The object of "irtada" (approved) has been deleted, because it is the returning pronoun of a relative clause (silla) governed by a verb. The implied meaning is: "for one whom He has approved," that is, whom He approved for intercession on his behalf, by permitting the angels to intercede for him, in order to show their honor with God, or in response to their asking forgiveness for those on earth, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And the angels glorify the praises of their Lord and ask forgiveness for those on earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5] in the surah of al-Shura. That asking forgiveness is among the things for which they were created, so it is not of the kind of precedence in speech.

Then their Lord increased their glorification by affirming it, with His saying: ﴿and they are fearful of Him in awe﴾, that is, they glorify Him with the glorification of one who fears His might and beware of opposing His command.

The "min" in His saying ﴿min khashyatihi﴾ (out of awe of Him) is causal (lil-ta'lil), and the prepositional phrase is a stable adverbial complement (zarf mustaqarr), and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the subject. "Mushfiqun" (fearful) is the predicate, that is, they are, because of His awe, that is, their awe of Him.

Al-ishfaq (fear) means anticipating something disliked and being wary of it.

The conditional in His saying ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him"﴾, etc., is a conditional on the basis of supposition, that is, if one of them were to say it, while knowing that they do not say it because of the firmly established intensity of their awe. The purpose of this conditional is an allusive rebuke of those who claimed divinity for them (the angels or others), that they attributed to them what they do not approve or say, and that they claimed for them what entails the Fire of Hell for its speaker, following the pattern of: ﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: "If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be lost"﴾ [al-Zumar: 65].

"In" (if) was replaced by "man" (whoever), the conditional particle, to indicate generality together with brevity. The demonstrative was introduced into the apodosis (jawab al-shart, the consequent of the conditional) to affirm the connection by attributing the conditional clause to its particle, to indicate that the content of the consequence is deserved by the one for whom the content of the condition is established. In this there is a refutation of the claim of the general body of Christians regarding the divinity of 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, and that they say about him what he did not say. Then He explicitly stated what the allusion implied, saying: ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, that is, a recompense like that, which is Hell, is what He gives to those who ascribe partners to God. Zulm (wrongdoing) here means shirk (association of partners with God).

Since what was meant by His saying ﴿And they say: "God has taken a son"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116] was that they claimed the angels to be God's daughters, the particle of disengagement (harf al-idrab, the particle marking a shift away from a prior statement) was followed by the information that they are servants, without mentioning the subject, because it is known. The implied meaning is: "Rather, the angels are honored servants," that is, God honored them by His pleasure with them, made them among His nearest servants, and preferred them over many of His righteous creatures.

As for "al-sabq" (precedence), its literal meaning is advancing ahead of another in running. Its use has become common figuratively for advancing in any action, and from it comes precedence in speech, that is, speaking before others, as in this verse. Negating it here is a kinaya (an indirect expression, implicature) for the absence of equality, that is, a kinaya for glorification and reverence. Its parallel in this regard is the prohibition of advancing in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1], for advancing carries the sense of precedence. So His saying ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ means that no speech issues from them before His speech, that is, they say nothing except what they are permitted to say, unless He says it first. This is general and includes the refutation of the claim of the polytheists that their objects of worship will intercede for them with God when God wants to punish them for their deeds. They say: "These are our intercessors with God," as He will explicitly deny later. The fronting of "bi-amrihi" (by His command) before "ya'malun" (they act) serves to express restriction (qasr, limitation of the predicate to a specified subject), that is, they do not act any act except by the command of God, Exalted is He. Just as they do not say a word He has not permitted, so too they do not perform any act except by His command.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ has a parallel that was mentioned in the surah of al-Baqarah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ is a specification by mention of part of what was included in His saying ﴿they do not precede Him in speech﴾, showing concern for it, because it is the matter on account of which they committed disbelief, when they made the deities intercessors for them with God.

The object of "irtada" (approved) has been deleted, because it is the returning pronoun of a relative clause (silla) governed by a verb. The implied meaning is: "for one whom He has approved," that is, whom He approved for intercession on his behalf, by permitting the angels to intercede for him, in order to show their honor with God, or in response to their asking forgiveness for those on earth, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And the angels glorify the praises of their Lord and ask forgiveness for those on earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5] in the surah of al-Shura. That asking forgiveness is among the things for which they were created, so it is not of the kind of precedence in speech.

Then their Lord increased their glorification by affirming it, with His saying: ﴿and they are fearful of Him in awe﴾, that is, they glorify Him with the glorification of one who fears His might and beware of opposing His command.

The "min" in His saying ﴿min khashyatihi﴾ (out of awe of Him) is causal (lil-ta'lil), and the prepositional phrase is a stable adverbial complement (zarf mustaqarr), and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the subject. "Mushfiqun" (fearful) is the predicate, that is, they are, because of His awe, that is, their awe of Him.

Al-ishfaq (fear) means anticipating something disliked and being wary of it.

The conditional in His saying ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him"﴾, etc., is a conditional on the basis of supposition, that is, if one of them were to say it, while knowing that they do not say it because of the firmly established intensity of their awe. The purpose of this conditional is an allusive rebuke of those who claimed divinity for them (the angels or others), that they attributed to them what they do not approve or say, and that they claimed for them what entails the Fire of Hell for its speaker, following the pattern of: ﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: "If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be lost"﴾ [al-Zumar: 65].

"In" (if) was replaced by "man" (whoever), the conditional particle, to indicate generality together with brevity. The demonstrative was introduced into the apodosis (jawab al-shart, the consequent of the conditional) to affirm the connection by attributing the conditional clause to its particle, to indicate that the content of the consequence is deserved by the one for whom the content of the condition is established. In this there is a refutation of the claim of the general body of Christians regarding the divinity of 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, and that they say about him what he did not say. Then He explicitly stated what the allusion implied, saying: ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, that is, a recompense like that, which is Hell, is what He gives to those who ascribe partners to God. Zulm (wrongdoing) here means shirk (association of partners with God).

[p. 53]

The majority of readers recited "awa-lam" (أوَلَمْ) with a *waw* after the hamza, which is the *waw* of conjunction (*wāw al-ʿaṭf*). The sentence is therefore coordinated, as an argument (*ʿaṭf al-istidlāl*), for the second creation by the first creation and the wonders it contains.

Ibn Kathir recited "a-lam yara" (ألَمْ يَرَ) without the conjunctive *waw*. Abu Shama said: "The *waw* was not established in the codices of the people of Mecca." I say: its meaning is that it was not established in the copy of the Qur'an that ʿUthman sent to Mecca. So the reciters of Mecca adhered to the transmission without the *waw* until Ibn Kathir recited with it, and other than his recitation was neglected.

The interrogative in both recitations is one of rebuke (*istifhām inkārī*), with the rebuke directed at their neglect of reflection (*naẓar*). The verb *ruʾya* (seeing) may be visual (*baṣariyya*) or cognitive (*ʿilmiyya*). The interrogative is suitable to be directed at either of them, because neglecting reflection upon observable things that indicate knowledge, knowledge of which would save one from entanglement in misguided beliefs, deserves rebuke. Rebuke is also fitting for failing to employ thought in the indication of things upon their necessary implications, so that no one falls into error. It may also be a rebuke mixed with affirmation (*taqrīr*), as we shall explain in detail.

*Ratq* means the joining and adhesion between the parts of a thing. *Fatq* is its opposite, namely separation and distancing between the parts.

Describing the heavens and the earth as *ratq* is a description by the verbal noun (*ikhbār bi-l-maṣdar*), for the sake of emphasizing the attainment of the attribute. Then the words of the Exalted, "*kānatā*" (they were), may mean that they were together one joined *ratq*, namely that the heavens and the earth were one compacted, connected body. It may also mean that each heaven was a *ratq* on its own, and the earth was a *ratq* on its own. The same possibilities apply to the words of the Exalted, "*fa-fataqnāhumā*" (then We parted them).

The reason He did not say something like "fa-ṣāratā fatqan" (then they became *fatq*) is that *ratq* is firmly established in them, as we have said, so that the great power to part them may be inferred from it. Also, the verb indicates the recency of the parting, which alludes to the origination of all existing things, and that none of them is eternal.

*Ratq* may be understood to mean meanings which, depending on their possibilities, give rise to corresponding meanings for *fatq*. If we take *ruʾya* as visual, then the *ratq* that is observed is what the observer sees of the absence of anything intervening between the parts of the heavens and the parts of the earth.

[p. 54]

*Fatq* is what the observer sees of the opposite of that, when he sees rain falling from the sky, sees lightning issuing from it, and sees thunderbolts falling from it. That is its *fatq*. And when he sees the earth split open by rainwater, and plants and trees springing forth from it after its dryness, all of this is observed and visible, indicating the disposal of the Creator. In this sense, admonition and divine favour are combined, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya said, namely that it is a sign indicating the greatness of power and an approximation to the manner of the revival of the dead, as the Exalted said: ﴿So We brought to life the earth after its death﴾ [Fāṭir: 9], in Surat Fāṭir.

If we take *ruʾya* as cognitive, then *ratq* may be understood with the same meaning as on the visual interpretation, and the interrogative would likewise be one of rebuke directed at their neglect of reflection upon observable things. It may also be understood to mean non-observable matters which nonetheless deserve the pursuit of knowledge, because they contain indications of the greatness of power and of divine oneness. Thus *ratq* and *fatq* may be understood in their literal senses, namely joining and separation. Furthermore, this possibility may be understood as referring to the sentence as a whole, meaning: the heavens and the earth were one *ratq*, that is, they were one mass, then the heavens separated from the earth, as indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water﴾ [Hūd: 7], in Surat Hūd.

On this possibility, *ratq* and *fatq* may also be distributed, meaning: the heavens were *ratq* in themselves, and the earth was *ratq* in itself, then God parted the heavens and parted the earth. This is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 9]; ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured therein its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 10]; ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and it was smoke, and He said to it and to the earth: Come willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come willingly﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 11]; ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and inspired in each heaven its command, and We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as protection. That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 12], in Surat Fuṣṣilat.

On these two possibilities, the interrogative is one of affirmation (*taqrīr*) concerning their turning away from listening to the verses that described the beginning of creation, and it is mixed with rebuke for that.

On all the possibilities, the aim of this is also to argue that He who created the heavens and the earth and brought them into being after non-existence is able to create creatures after their annihilation. The Exalted said: ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the like of them?﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 99].

It may be understood that *ratq* means non-existence and *fatq* means bringing into existence. On this possibility, the use of *ruʾya* for knowledge is evident, because the matter of their *ratq* in this sense is established among them. The Exalted said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: God﴾ [Luqmān: 25].

It may be understood that *ratq* means darkness and *fatq* means light. Thus existing things came into being in darkness, then God poured light upon them by bringing into existence in some bodies a light that illuminated existing things.

It may be understood that *ratq* means the unity of existing things when they were one substance, or were an ether (*athīr*) or a mist (*ʿamāʾ*), as came in the hadith: "He was in a *ʿamāʾ*." Then they were a single, high genus that should be called a created thing, and it was then a universal confined to one individual. Then God created from that genus parts, and gave each part its own inherent distinguishing features, so that each distinguished thing, by its reality, became a genus, and they became genera. Then He created in the genera distinguishing features by accidents affecting their realities, so they became species. This possibility is more in accord with the method of the philosophers, and they have agreed to name this differentiation *ratq* and *fatq*. Some of the Sufis, and the author of *Mirʾāt al-ʿĀrifīn*, made *ratq* a designation for the greatest element, meaning the total body. The total body is the greatest sphere, which is expressed as the Throne. This was mentioned by the Sufi sage Luṭf Allāh al-Arḍurūmī, author of *Maʿārij al-Nūr fī Asmāʾ Allāh al-Ḥusnā*, who died at the end of the twelfth century, and who entered Tunis in the year 1185 AH, in the introductions of his book *Maʿārij al-Nūr*, and in a treatise of his which he named *Risālat al-Fatq wal-Ratq*.

The apparent meaning is that the verse includes everything in which the meanings of *ratq* and *fatq* are realized, since there is no obstacle to considering a general meaning that gathers them all together. Thus the verse contains a sign that encompasses all people, and a sign specific to the people of reflection and knowledge. It is therefore among the scientific miracles of the Qur'an, to which we alluded in the introductions of this commentary.

* * *

﴿And We made from water every living thing. Will they not believe?﴾

This is an additional argument from what is more evident to the sight of eyes. In it is a lesson for people in most of its states, and it is a lesson for those who reflect on its subtleties in the formation of animals from moisture. This is the formation of procreation and the formation of all animals, for an animal is formed only from moisture and lives only in association with it. When moisture is absent from it, it loses life. For this reason, persistent fever leads to emaciation and then to death. Here *jaʿala* has the sense of *khalaqa* (created), taking one object, because it is not intended to mean transformation from one state to another.

"*Min al-māʾ*" (from water) is connected to "*jaʿalnā*" (We made), and "*min*" is for the starting point. The statement "*afalā yuʾminūn*" (will they not believe?) follows from this, as a rebuke for their not believing in the belief to which Muḥammad (ﷺ) called them, which is belief in the oneness of God.

[Page 57]

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains, lest it shake with them, and We made in it broad roads, that they might be guided.﴾

This is one of the effects of the splitting (fatq) of the earth itself, since God brought forth from it the mountains. That is a splitting of creation (fatq takwin), and He made in it the paths, meaning the easy lands in which a person can move about, the opposite of the mountains.

The rawasi (firm mountains) are the mountains, because they took root (rasat) in the earth, that is, they became firmly fixed in it. The mayd is agitation (al-idtirab), and it was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Nahl.

It was also mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Nahl that the meaning of "أنْ تَمِيدَ" is "أنْ لا تَمِيدَ" (that it should not shake), or "لِكَراهَةِ أنْ تَمِيدَ" (lest it shake). The meaning is: We placed in the earth wide roads. Since "فِجاجًا" means "wide," it functions in meaning as a description of "سَبِيلًا" (paths). When it was placed before the word it describes, it took the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl). The intended purpose is to complete the favour by subjugating the surface of the earth so that they may travel along it on broad roads. Had He willed, He could have made narrow passages between the mountains, like the narrow ways between...
