Corrected translation of the full passage:

The rawasi are the mountains, because they took root in the earth, that is, they became firmly fixed in it. The mayd is agitation, and it was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Nahl.

It was mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Nahl that the meaning of "أنْ تَمِيدَ" is "أنْ لا تَمِيدَ" (that it should not shake), or "لِكَراهَةِ أنْ تَمِيدَ" (lest it shake). The meaning is: We placed in the earth wide roads (fijaj). Since "فِجاجًا" means "wide," it functions in meaning as a description of "سُبُلًا" (paths). When it was placed before the word it describes, it took the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl). The intended purpose is to complete the favour by subjugating the surface of the earth so that they may travel along it on broad roads, and had He willed, He could have made the passages between the mountains narrow, like the narrow ways of... 

The fijaj is the plural of fajj, and the fajj is the wide road.

The subul is the plural of sabil, which means the road in general.

The clause "لَعَلَّهم يَهْتَدُونَ" (that they may be guided) is a new independent clause, expressing a hope (a performative, non-declarative utterance) for the guidance of the polytheists to the oneness of God, since these proofs are visible to them and clearly indicative. It is also possible that guidance here refers to guidance in travel, meaning: We made the paths clear and not obstructed by narrowness, so that they might be guided in their journeys. In that case this is another favour, namely God's arranging of things in a manner that suits humankind and sets right their affairs.

Thus His saying, "لَعَلَّهم يَهْتَدُونَ" (that they may be guided), belongs to speech addressed in a particular manner (al-kalam al-muwajjah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 32:

Page 58
﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling, yet they turn away from its signs.﴾
Since reflection upon the creation of the earth and what is in it was mentioned, it was appropriate, by way of correspondence (tibaq), to mention the creation of the sky immediately after it. However, the state of the earth's creation contains benefits for people. So he followed its mention with a reminder of favour (imtinan) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿lest it shake with them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 31], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿that perhaps they may be guided﴾ [al-Anbiya': 31]. As for the state of the sky's creation, no benefit is apparent in it, so no reminder of favour was mentioned after it. Instead, He mentioned their turning away from contemplating the signs of the sky's creation, which indicate consummate wisdom, and He followed this with His words, exalted is He: ﴿yet they turn away from its signs﴾. Thus a favour was incorporated (idmaj) within this, namely the preservation of the sky from some of the celestial bodies within it, or some of its parts, falling upon the earth and thereby destroying people or corrupting the earth and rendering its benefits inoperative. This is an incorporation of the favour within the course of the principal purpose, which cannot be dispensed with in taking heed.

The word saqf (ceiling), in its real meaning, is the covering of the top of a house placed upon its walls; the term saqf is not applied to the covering of a tent or pavilion. It is applied to the sky by way of the eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh), meaning: We made it like a ceiling, because the sky is not placed upon pillars from the earth. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God is the One who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2], and this was discussed earlier at the beginning of Surah al-Ra'd. The clause ﴿yet they turn away from its signs﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The signs of the sky are what the sky contains of the sun, the moon, the stars, and meteors, their courses, their risings and settings, their appearances and disappearances, and the ordering of all this upon a upright reckoning and a wondrous arrangement, all of which are indications of consummate wisdom.

Page 59
Therefore He named them signs (ayat). Likewise, what appears to us from the direction of the sky, such as clouds, lightning, and thunder.
﴿And He it is who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾ [al-Anbiya': 33]

Since in the bringing into being of these enumerated things here there are benefits for people, they were presented in the context of favour by being phrased as a nominal sentence whose two parts are both definite, to convey restriction (qasr). This is a restriction of particularization (qasr ifrad idafi), by treating the polytheist addressees as those who believe that their idols are partners with God in the creation of those things. For since they worshipped the idols, and worship is gratitude, it follows that they thank them, and since they have made them partners with God, it follows that they claim they are partners with God in the creation of what He created. Thus the argument moves to the refutation of their associating those idols with God in divinity.

Since the favour and the lesson lie in the bringing into being of the night and the day themselves, and of the sun and the moon themselves, and not in their bringing into being in a particular state, the verb of creation (khalq) is used here rather than the verb of making (ja'l).

The creation of the night is a part of the particulars of the creation of darkness, in which God brought beings into existence before the creation of the bodies that pour out light upon existents. For darkness is a non-existence (adam), while light is an existent quality and is the opposite of darkness, and non-existence precedes existence. So the state preceding the existence of the luminous bodies is darkness. The night is darkness that returns to the body of the earth when the rays withdraw from the earth. As for the creation of the day, it is by the creation of the sun and by its rays being directed toward the half of the earthly sphere facing the rays. Thus the creation of the day follows from the creation of the sun, the creation of the earth, and the earth's facing the sun's rays. Therefore, mention of the creation of the

Page 60
sun immediately after mention of the creation of the day has a strong correspondence, serving to draw attention to the source of the day's creation, as is well known. As for the mention of the creation of the moon, it is for correspondence with the creation of the sun, and as a reminder of the favour of bringing into being that which gives some light to people in some times of darkness. All of this is among the favours.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 33:

﴿Each in an orbit is swimming.﴾

It is a resumptive clause (mustaʼnafah) of explanatory type (istiʼnaf bayani). When He mentioned the opposite things, in terms of realities or times, mentioning some of them in general terms, namely the signs of the sky, and others in detail, namely the sun and the moon, the context stirred in the hearts of the listeners a question about the manner of their movement: how is it that they do not collide, or that there is no deviation from their appearing at their appointed time? So it was answered that each of the things mentioned has a space in which it travels, which does not meet the space of another's travel. The pronoun in "yasbahun" (they swim) refers to the generality of the signs of the sky and the particular of the sun and the moon, and the masculine plural pronoun was applied to them in consideration of the masculine gender of the names of some of them, such as the moon (al-qamar) and the star (al-kawkab).

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf that it was observed in it to describe them with swimming, which is among the actions of rational beings, so the pronoun of rational beings was also applied to them, meaning that this serves as a tarshih (complementary development) for the metaphor.

His words, exalted is He, "﴿in an orbit﴾" are a locative complement (zarf mustaqarr) predicated of "kull" (each), and "kull" is the subject, and its tanwin is a substitute for the genitive complement omitted, i.e., "kullu tilka" (each of those), so it is definite in estimation, and this is the purpose of the resumption, namely that it conveys that each of the things mentioned is situated in an orbit that does not collide with the orbit of another. It is known from the word "kull" and from the locative sense of "fi" that the word "falak" (orbit) is general, i.e., each of them has its own orbit, so they are many orbits.

The clause "yasbahun" (they swim) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

Al-sabh (swimming): it is a metaphor for movement in a wide expanse that has no intersecting paths in it, like the paths of the earth, and it is an approximation of the movement of the stars in the great expanse.

As for al-falak (orbit), the lexicographers explained it as the circuit of the stars, and likewise the exegetes explained it for this verse, and they did not mention that it is used in this sense in the speech of the Arabs. It is my strong opinion that it is one of the technical terms of the Qur'an, and from it the scholars of Islam took it, and it is the best way to express the imaginary circles by which the movement of a star is regulated, especially the movement of the sun and the movement of the moon. The more apparent view is that the Qur'an transferred it from falak al-bahr (the orbit of the sea), which is the rotating wave, by treating the collective noun as a singular; and the original root of all of that is falkat al-maghzal (the spindle whorl), with a fatha on the fa and sukun on the lam, which is a round piece of wood with a bent nail at its top into which the thread enters and is turned so that the thread is twisted.

Among the marvels of inimitability in this verse is that His words, exalted is He, "﴿kullun fi falak﴾" contain a figurative embellishment (muhassin badi'i), for its letters are read from its end in order just as they are read from its beginning, with lightness of composition, abundance of benefit, and its running as a proverb without discord or strangeness. Similar to it is His words, exalted is He, "﴿rabbaka fakabbir﴾" by dropping the conjunctive waw, and both verses are built upon seven letters. This type was named by al-Sakkaki the perfectly reversible inversion (al-maqlub al-mustawi), and he made it one of the kinds of a category he named inversion (al-qalb).

This category is specific to what inversion can achieve in the letters of its words. Al-Hariri named it in his Maqamat "what does not become invalid by reversal" (ma la yastahil bil-in'ikas), and built upon it the sixteenth maqama, and he composed examples in prose and verse; and in most of the examples he composed there is artificiality, discord and strangeness, and likewise what others composed, varying in that degree. The illustrations are mentioned in the books of rhetoric (badi'), so follow them up; and whenever they grow longer, they grow heavier.

The scholar al-Shirazi said in Sharh al-Miftah: "It is a type difficult in its path and rarely used." I say: They did not mention from it anything that occurred in the speech of the Arabs, so it is one of the innovations of the Qur'an.

The men of letters mention that al-Qadi al-Fadil al-Baysani visited al-'Imad the scribe, and when he mounted to leave from his presence, al-'Imad said to him: "Sir, so that the horses do not trip you (sir fala kaba bika al-furs)," and al-Qadi perceived that in it was the embellishment of inversion (muhassin al-qalb), so he answered him extemporaneously: "Dama 'ula al-'Imad" (may the exaltedness of al-'Imad endure), and in it is the embellishment of inversion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 34:

﴿We did not grant to any human before you immortality. So if you should die, would they be the immortals?﴾

The verses from the beginning of the surah were concerned with cataloguing the slanders of the polytheists against the Qur'an and the one who brought it, with their saying: ﴿Do you then approach magic while you see?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3], and their saying: ﴿Confused dreams! Rather, he has invented it! Rather, he is a poet!﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5]. Among their wishes, when the fabrication of slanders had exhausted them, was that they wished for the death of Muhammad (ﷺ), or hoped for it, or plotted for it. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet, for whom we await the misfortune of fate"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30] in Surat al-Tur, and God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you, or kill you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] in al-Anfal. The words of God, exalted is He, ﴿So if you should die, would they be the immortals?﴾ indicate that these people are the intended referents of the verse. Since their wishing for his death and their awaiting for him the misfortune of fate

Page 63

implies that those who wished this and awaited it for him were as though certain that they would die after him, so that their gloating would be complete, or as though they would never die at all, so that no one would gloat over them. The interrogative of denial was directed at them in the manner of allusion (ta'ridh), by treating them as one who claims that they are immortal.

In the verse there is also an indication that those among those who said that saying whom God did not decree Islam for will die before the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), and so will not gloat over him. For the Messenger (ﷺ) did not die until God destroyed the heads of those who opposed him and guided the rest of them to Islam. So in His words, ﴿We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾, there is the method of "answering according to the premise" (al-qawl bil-mujib), meaning: you will die as they said, but they do not see that, and they are in the state of those who claim that they are immortal; so they became certain that they await for you the misfortune of fate, from the extremity of their delusion. The inference was based on the first clause's premise, meaning: they are not immortal, such that they would be certain that they will witness your death. In the denial, which has the sense of negation, is a warning to them that none of them will witness his death.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 35:**

﴿Every soul shall taste death. And We test you with evil and with good as a trial. And to Us you will be returned.﴾

These are parenthetical clauses placed between the two conjoined clauses. The meaning of the first clause emphasizes the meaning of the clause it is conjoined to, which is ﴿We did not grant any human before you eternity﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 34]. The reason for repeating it is the difference in purpose: the first was to refute the polytheists, while this one is to instruct the believers. The word "tasting" (al-dhawq) is used metaphorically for any inner sensation, because tasting is a sensation of the tongue that is accompanied by swallowing, which reaches the inside.

Page 64

Tasting death means experiencing the pains of its preliminaries. As for after it has occurred, the body has no sensation.

By "soul" (nafs) is meant the souls that dwell in bodies, such as humans and animals. It does not include the angels, because applying the term "souls" to them is not customary in Arabic. Rather, it is a technical term of the philosophers (hukama'), and they use it only qualified by the description of "immaterial beings" (al-mujarradat), that is, those that do not inhere in bodies and do not come into contact with matter. As for applying "self" (nafs) to God Most High, it is a case of *mushakalah* (a figure in which a word is used because of its association with another word in the same context). This may be verbal, as in His saying: ﴿You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Your self﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116] in Surat al-Ma'idah; or it may be presumed, as in His saying: ﴿And God warns you of Himself﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28] in Al 'Imran.

The clause ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ is conjoined to the parenthetical clause, by virtue of the fact that tasting death presupposes that life has preceded it, and life is a period in which good and evil befall all living beings. So God Most High taught the Muslims that death is decreed upon every soul, lest they suppose that the Messenger ﷺ is immortal. Some of the Muslims were afflicted with something of this, among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). On the day the Prophet ﷺ passed away to the Highest Companion, he said: "The Messenger of Allah will certainly return and will cut off the hands and feet of some people." Then Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) arrived, and Allah strengthened him in that tremendous ordeal. He uncovered the face of the Prophet ﷺ, kissed him, and said: "You are good in life and in death. By Allah, Allah will not make you die twice."

The poet 'Abd Bani al-Hasḥas said, and excelled:

"I saw that the fates had left no one, Muhammad included, and none remaining except that death lay in wait for him."

Then God followed this with teaching them that life includes good and evil, and that the world is the abode of trial.

Page 65

*Al-balwa* (trial) means testing. It has been mentioned more than once before. The application of "trial" to what appears from people of endurance, weakness, gratitude, and disbelief, in response to the pleasures and pains they encounter, which are the things on which God Most High built the order of life, is a metaphorical usage. This is because the construction of the order upon them indicates the differences in people's conditions in how they handle these things and how they receive them. It resembles the testing of one who tests in order to know the conditions of those he tests.

*Fitnatan* (as a trial) is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), emphasizing the verb *nabluwakum* (We test you), because *fitnah* is synonymous with *balwa*. The clause ﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾ affirms the resurrection. Thus the verse combines death, life, and resurrection. The fronting of the prepositional phrase (*ilaynā*, "to Us") serves to observe the rhyme (*fāṣilah*) and to add emphasis to the assertion. As for the possibility of a restrictive meaning (*qaṣr*), it does not hold here, since the opposite of that is not a belief of those addressed, however one supposes them to be.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 36:

﴿When those who disbelieve see you, they take you not but in mockery: "Is this the one who mentions your gods?" while they are, at the mention of the Most Merciful, disbelievers.﴾

This is another description of what the polytheists would use to harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when they saw him. It is more specific than their harming him in his absence. When they see him, some of them say to others: ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾

Al-huzu' (with a damma on the ha' and a damma on the zay) is the verbal noun of hazi'a bihi, meaning he made him an object of play and amusement. The meaning of taking him as a huzu' is that they make him an object of mockery. This is an informing by the verbal noun for emphasis, or it is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, like khalq meaning makhluq (the created thing).

Allah's saying in Surat al-Kahf has already passed: ﴿And they took My signs and My messengers in mockery﴾ [al-Kahf: 106]. The clause ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ explains the clause ﴿they take you not but in mockery﴾, so it carries the sense of an implied saying, indicated by ﴿they take you not but in mockery﴾, because mockery is done by speech. Their taking him in mockery when they see him is restricted to mocking him, without mixing it with any other talk about his affair.

The interrogative is used for expressing wonder, and the demonstrative is used for belittling, by the indication of the mockery.

The phrase "mentions your gods" means he mentions them with evil, by the indication of the context, because they know what he mentions of their gods that displeases them. Mention can be with good or with evil, so when its object is not stated explicitly, one resorts to the context, as here in Allah's later saying: ﴿They said: "We heard a youth mention them"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 60]. Their speech is driven by rage and anger; therefore Allah followed it with the circumstantial clause ﴿while they are, at the mention of the Most Merciful, disbelievers﴾, meaning: they become angry that their gods are mentioned with what uncovers their true nature, in accordance with reality, while they are heedless of the mention of the Most Merciful, who is the one most worthy that they should mention Him. So the second mention is used for mention by praise and glorification, by the indication of the context. The most apparent view is that what is meant by the mention of the Most Merciful here is the Qur'an, that is, the reminder sent down from the Most Merciful. The connection is the transition from one mention to another. The meaning of their disbelief in the mention of the Most Merciful is their denial that the Qur'an is a sign indicating the truth of the Messenger (ﷺ), so they said: ﴿Let him bring us a sign as the earlier ones were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5]. Also, their disbelief in what the Qur'an brought of the affirmation of resurrection.

Allah the Exalted is referred to by the name "al-Rahman" as a rebuke against them, since they refused that al-Rahman be a name of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to whatever you order us?" And it increased them in aversion﴾ [al-Furqan: 60], in Surat al-Furqan.

The separating pronoun in Allah's saying ﴿they are disbelievers﴾ may convey restriction, meaning: they are disbelievers in the Qur'an specifically, not others among those of Makkah and other Arabs who embraced Islam, to indicate that these remain upon their disbelief despite the abundance of signs and warnings. It may also be that the separation is merely for emphasis, to affirm the continuance of their disbelief despite the manifestation of what should have turned them away from disbelief.

[Page 68]

The clause ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ is an interposition (i'tiraḍ) between the clause ﴿When those who disbelieve see you, they take you only in mockery﴾ [al-Anbiya': 36] and the clause ﴿I will show you My signs﴾. It serves as an introduction to the clause ﴿I will show you My signs﴾. As for the clause ﴿I will show you My signs﴾, it is an interposition between the clause ﴿When those who disbelieve see you, they take you only in mockery﴾ [al-Anbiya': 36] and the clause ﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 38]. This is because the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿When those who disbelieve see you, they take you only in mockery﴾ [al-Anbiya': 36] raise in the souls of the Muslims a question about how long the polytheists will be given respite. So the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten it﴾, came as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), interposed between the clauses that relate the statements of the polytheists and what follows from them. The address is to the Muslims who were impatient for the arrival of the threat that Allah, the Exalted, had promised to the deniers.

The reason for the placement of the two clauses is that mentioning the mockery of the polytheists toward the Prophet ﷺ stirs the anger of the Muslims against them, so they wish that the threat would descend upon the deniers quickly. Therefore they were addressed with patience and told not to seek to hasten their Lord, because He knows best what wisdom requires regarding the timing of the threat's arrival, and what benefits for the religion lie in delaying its descent.

The most important of these benefits is giving the people respite so that many of them may enter Islam. The preferable view is that the first clause serves as a preparation for the second.

Al-'ajal (العجل) means haste, and the phrase ﴿created of haste﴾ is a metaphor for the firm establishment of this attribute in the natural constitution of humankind. The intensity of this attribute's constancy is likened to the material of creation being described by it, because the weakness of patience in man is a consequence of reflecting on what is loved and what is hated. When the intellect considers something beloved, it hastens its attainment out of the impulse of love; and when it considers something disliked, it hastens its removal out of the impulse of aversion. Human conditions are never free of these two, so man is naturally hasty, as though he were created from haste. Similar to this is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And man has ever been hasty﴾ [al-Isra': 11], and His words: ﴿Indeed, man was created anxious﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19]. Furthermore, people vary in this haste according to their varying depth of reflection and their disbelief, but they nevertheless are never free of it. As for those who interpreted al-'ajal (العجل) as "clay" and claimed that it is a Himyarite word, they have strayed far, and how far from felicity they are.

The clause ﴿I will show you My signs﴾ is the intended purpose of the interposition. It is a new resumption, and its meaning is a promise that they will see the signs of Allah in the support of the religion. This is what occurred on the day of Badr of victory and the destruction of the leaders of polytheism, and what occurred after it of the days of Islam in which victory was the outcome for the Muslims.

From this promise follows a prohibition against seeking to hasten it, meaning: you must leave that matter to what Allah determines and postpones, for "every term has a Book" (cf. al-Ra'd: 38). This is a prohibition against excessive indulgence in this attribute and against its consequences that lead to doubt about the threat. The ya' of the first person has been deleted from the word تَسْتَعْجِلُونِ (tasta'jiluna) for lightness while its vowel remains; when one pauses upon it, the vowel of the nun is dropped.

[Page 69]

Qur'an 21:38–40: "They say, 'When is this promise, if you are truthful?' Were those who disbelieved to know the time when they will not be able to ward the Fire off their faces or off their backs, and they will not be helped. Rather, it will come upon them suddenly and bewilder them, so they will not be able to repel it, nor will they be given respite."

The mention of the Muslims' impatience for God's promise of victory over the disbelievers was followed by the mention of its counterpart on the side of the polytheists: that they asked about the time of this promise in mockery. Thus the two statements arose and the two situations differed. The words of the Exalted, "They say, 'When is this promise?'" (Qur'an 21:38), are coordinated (ʿaṭfan) with the clause "I will show you My signs" (Al-Anbiya' 21:37). This expresses another of their statements, by which they received the call of the Prophet ﷺ with mockery and obstinacy. The mention of this statement here is to express the Muslims' impatience for victory. With this consideration, it is connected to the clause "When those who disbelieve see you, they take you not except in mockery" (Al-Anbiya' 21:36), and it is permissible that it be coordinated with it.

They addressed the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims with the plural pronoun. For the sake of this statement, the Muslims would hasten the threat against the polytheists.

Their interrogative was used in mockery, as a *majāz mursal* (a figurative usage based on a non-metaphorical relation), with the indication of "if you are truthful," because the polytheists were certain that the promise would not be fulfilled. By "the promise" is meant what the Qur'an threatened them with: the victory of His Messenger and the uprooting of his opponents. To this verse and its like refers the saying of the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Badr, when he stood over the well in which the corpses of the polytheists had been buried and called them by their names: "We have found that which our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found that which your Lord promised you to be true?" (Al-A'raf 7:44).

[Page 70]

That is, what our Lord promised us of victory, and what He promised you of destruction and the punishment of the Fire. The clause "If only those who disbelieved would know" is a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*) for explanation, because the Muslims were awaiting, from the report of the statement "They say, 'When is this promise, if you are truthful?'", what their answer would be to their mockery. The essential answer is that it is certainly going to happen, and there is no way to deny it.

The answer to *law* ("if only") is omitted. Its estimated meaning is: "Since they were in what they were upon of disbelief and mockery of your Messenger and your religion, and the like of that which the context allows." It may be derived from the indication of the statement of the Exalted, "When those who disbelieve see you, they take you not except in mockery" (Al-Anbiya' 21:36). The omission of the answer of *law* is frequent in the Qur'an. Its purpose is to make its kind terrifying, so that the soul of the listener goes in every direction.

Here, *ḥīn* is a noun in the accusative as an object (*mafʿūl*), not as a time adverb (*ẓarf*). It is thus one of the inflecting time nouns. That is, if they knew its time and were certain of its occurrence, they would not have denied it or the one who warned them of it, and they would not have considered its delay a proof of its falsity. The clause "they will not ward off" is the sentence that *ḥīn* is annexed to. The pronoun in "they will not ward off" has two possibilities. One of them, which appears to me, is that the pronoun refers to the angels of punishment, and the referent of the pronoun is known from the context. Parallels to this referent are numerous in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. The meaning of "ward off" (*kaff*) in this case is holding back, which is its literal sense: that is, when the angels do not hold back the scorching of the Fire from the faces of the polytheists. This verse has the same meaning as the statement of the Exalted in Surat al-Anfal: "If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs, and [saying], 'Taste the punishment of the burning!'" (Al-Anfal 8:50). That is a striking with whips of fire. What is here is a warning of what they will face on the day of Badr, just as the verse of al-Anfal is a narration of what they met on the day of Badr.

[Page 71]

The mention of the faces and the backs is for the purpose of humiliating and frightening them, because the faces are the most honoured of the limbs for people, as 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"We expose to the swords, when we meet, faces that are not exposed to slaps."

And because people disdain being struck on the backs, since striking them is a humiliation and a disgrace; it is called *kasʿ*.

The second possibility is that the pronoun in "they will not ward off" refers to those who disbelieved, and "ward off" (*kaff*) means repelling and shielding, as a *majāz* by the relation of necessity (*ʿalāqat al-luzūm*). That is: when they are unable to push the Fire away from their faces with their hands, nor from their backs, that is, when the Fire encompasses them from the front and from behind. The mention of the backs after the faces is a precaution (*iḥtirāz*) against this possibility, to repel the illusion that they might ward it off from their backs if their hands were not occupied with warding it off from their faces. This second possibility is the one on which all the commentators whose books we have have relied. However, the first possibility is more preferable in meaning, because it is perfectly suited to the present disbelievers who are being rebuked, and to their denial of the threat of destruction in their statement "When is this promise?", and to the statement of the Exalted, "I will show you My signs," as has preceded.

The statement of the Exalted, "nor will they be helped," is coordinated with "they will not ward off." That is: the scorching of the Fire will not be held back from them, or they will not be able to repel the scorching of the Fire from themselves, nor will they find a helper to aid them. Thus they are in the snare of punishment. In this there is an allusion that the defeat of Badr will befall them, so they will be unable to escape it, nor will they find a helper from their allies.

"Bal" (rather) here is for a transitional turning away (*iḍrāb intiqālī*), from amplifying what has been prepared for them to the threat that this will befall them suddenly and abruptly. This is more severe on the souls, because they are not prepared for it nor settled upon it, as Kuthayyir said:

"I said to her, 'O Izza, every calamity, when the soul has once settled itself for it, becomes humbled.'"

[Page 72]

If the intended meaning is the punishment of the Hereafter, then the negation of a helper is a denial of them in their statement: "These are our intercessors with God" (Yunus 10:18). The subject of "it will come upon them" is a pronoun referring to the promise. The verb is marked with the feminine sign according to the first possibility mentioned earlier in the statement of the Exalted: "when they will not ward off the Fire from their faces," with regard to the event or something similar. This is an allusion that it will be in that which has a feminine noun, like "the event" (*al-waqʿa*) and "the raid" (*al-ghazwa*). As for the second possibility mentioned earlier, which the other commentators, as far as we have seen, followed, the reference is to the promise as the Hour or the Resurrection, or the time (*ḥīn*) in the sense of the Hour.

*Al-badghah* is the sudden arrival, which is the occurrence of something unexpected.

*Al-bahth* is the sudden overpowering that prevents resistance. It is said: "He bewildered him, so he was bewildered." The Exalted said in Surat al-Baqarah: "So the one who disbelieved was bewildered" (Al-Baqarah 2:258), that is, he was overcome. This is the meaning of the consequence in the statement of the Exalted, "so they will not be able to repel it." The statement of the Exalted "nor will they be given respite" means they will not be delayed. In it is a warning to them that they were given respite for a long time, perhaps they would desist from their error. How closely this state fits what happened to them on the day of Badr. The Exalted said: "Even if you had made an appointment together, you would have differed about the appointment, but [it was so] that God might accomplish a matter that was to be done" (Al-Anfal 8:42). And He said: "And He made you appear few in their eyes, that God might accomplish a matter that was to be done" (Al-Anfal 8:44).

There is no doubt that the mockers, such as Abu Jahl, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, 'Utba ibn Rabi'a and Umayya ibn Khalaf, were among those whom the punishment of the sword overtook suddenly, and their supporters from the Quraysh were among those whom it bewildered. As for if the pronoun in "it will come upon them" is intended to refer to the Hour and the Resurrection, then it comes suddenly upon those who are of the same kind as the polytheists, or the Trumpet and the Resurrection will come upon them suddenly. As for those mockers, they had passed away for centuries.

[Page 70]

That is, what our Lord promised us of victory, and what He promised you of destruction and the punishment of the Fire. The clause "If only those who disbelieved would know" is a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*) for explanation, because the Muslims were awaiting, from the report of the statement "They say, 'When is this promise, if you are truthful?'", what their answer would be to their mockery. The essential answer is that it is certainly going to happen, and there is no way to deny it.

The answer to *law* ("if only") is omitted. Its estimated meaning is: "Since they were in what they were upon of disbelief and mockery of your Messenger and your religion, and the like of that which the context allows." It may be derived from the indication of the statement of the Exalted, "When those who disbelieve see you, they take you not except in mockery" (Al-Anbiya' 21:36). The omission of the answer of *law* is frequent in the Qur'an. Its purpose is to make its kind terrifying, so that the soul of the listener goes in every direction.

Here, *ḥīn* is a noun in the accusative as an object (*mafʿūl*), not as a time adverb (*ẓarf*). It is thus one of the inflecting time nouns. That is, if they knew its time and were certain of its occurrence, they would not have denied it or the one who warned them of it, and they would not have considered its delay a proof of its falsity. The clause "they will not ward off" is the sentence that *ḥīn* is annexed to. The pronoun in "they will not ward off" has two possibilities. One of them, which appears to me, is that the pronoun refers to the angels of punishment, and the referent of the pronoun is known from the context. Parallels to this referent are numerous in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. The meaning of "ward off" (*kaff*) in this case is holding back, which is its literal sense: that is, when the angels do not hold back the scorching of the Fire from the faces of the polytheists. This verse has the same meaning as the statement of the Exalted in Surat al-Anfal: "If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs, and [saying], 'Taste the punishment of the burning!'" (Al-Anfal 8:50). That is a striking with whips of fire. What is here is a warning of what they will face on the day of Badr, just as the verse of al-Anfal is a narration of what they met on the day of Badr.

[Page 71]

The mention of the faces and the backs is for the purpose of humiliating and frightening them, because the faces are the most honoured of the limbs for people, as 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"We expose to the swords, when we meet, faces that are not exposed to slaps."

And because people disdain being struck on the backs, since striking them is a humiliation and a disgrace; it is called *kasʿ*.

The second possibility is that the pronoun in "they will not ward off" refers to those who disbelieved, and "ward off" (*kaff*) means repelling and shielding, as a *majāz* by the relation of necessity (*ʿalāqat al-luzūm*). That is: when they are unable to push the Fire away from their faces with their hands, nor from their backs, that is, when the Fire encompasses them from the front and from behind. The mention of the backs after the faces is a precaution (*iḥtirāz*) against this possibility, to repel the illusion that they might ward it off from their backs if their hands were not occupied with warding it off from their faces. This second possibility is the one on which all the commentators whose books we have have relied. However, the first possibility is more preferable in meaning, because it is perfectly suited to the present disbelievers who are being rebuked, and to their denial of the threat of destruction in their statement "When is this promise?", and to the statement of the Exalted, "I will show you My signs," as has preceded.

The statement of the Exalted, "nor will they be helped," is coordinated with "they will not ward off." That is: the scorching of the Fire will not be held back from them, or they will not be able to repel the scorching of the Fire from themselves, nor will they find a helper to aid them. Thus they are in the snare of punishment. In this there is an allusion that the defeat of Badr will befall them, so they will be unable to escape it, nor will they find a helper from their allies.

"Bal" (rather) here is for a transitional turning away (*iḍrāb intiqālī*), from amplifying what has been prepared for them to the threat that this will befall them suddenly and abruptly. This is more severe on the souls, because they are not prepared for it nor settled upon it, as Kuthayyir said:

"I said to her, 'O Izza, every calamity, when the soul has once settled itself for it, becomes humbled.'"

[Page 72]

The verb is marked with the feminine sign according to the first possibility mentioned earlier in the statement of the Exalted: "when they will not ward off the Fire from their faces," with regard to the event or something similar. This is an allusion that it will be in that which has a feminine noun, like "the event" (*al-waqʿa*) and "the raid" (*al-ghazwa*). As for the second possibility mentioned earlier, which the other commentators, as far as we have seen, followed, the reference is to the promise as the Hour or the Resurrection, or the time (*ḥīn*) in the sense of the Hour.

*Al-badghah* is the sudden arrival, which is the occurrence of something unexpected.

*Al-bahth* is the sudden overpowering that prevents resistance. It is said: "He bewildered him, so he was bewildered." The Exalted said in Surat al-Baqarah: "So the one who disbelieved was bewildered" (Al-Baqarah 2:258), that is, he was overcome. This is the meaning of the consequence in the statement of the Exalted, "so they will not be able to repel it." The statement of the Exalted "nor will they be given respite" means they will not be delayed. In it is a warning to them that they were given respite for a long time, perhaps they would desist from their error. How closely this state fits what happened to them on the day of Badr. The Exalted said: "Even if you had made an appointment together, you would have differed about the appointment, but [it was so] that God might accomplish a matter that was to be done" (Al-Anfal 8:42). And He said: "And He made you appear few in their eyes, that God might accomplish a matter that was to be done" (Al-Anfal 8:44).

There is no doubt that the mockers, such as Abu Jahl, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, 'Utba ibn Rabi'a and Umayya ibn Khalaf, were among those whom the punishment of the sword overtook suddenly, and their supporters from the Quraysh were among those whom it bewildered. As for those mockers, they had passed away for centuries.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but those who ridiculed them were engulfed by what they used to mock.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the sentence ﴿I will show you My signs﴾ [al-Anbiya': 37], serving as reassurance (taṭmīn) to the Prophet (ﷺ) and consolation (tasliyah) for him. The connection of its conjunction with the sentence ﴿If only those who disbelieved knew, at the time when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces﴾ [al-Anbiya': 39], and what follows it to its end, is evident. The like of this verse has already been mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

[Page 74]

After the Messenger ﷺ was consoled for their mockery of the threat, he was commanded to remind them that their delusion through being granted respite was from God, an act of mercy toward them, as is His way with His mercy toward His creatures. He was to tell them that when His punishment descends upon them, they will find no one to protect them from the punishment besides Him, and their gods will not prevent it from them. The interrogative ("who") is one of denial and rebuke, meaning: none will protect you from Him. So how can you be ignorant of this? It is a reminder to them, since they had forgotten His blessings.

The mention of "the night and the day" is for comprehensiveness (istee'ab) of times, as if it were said: who will protect you at all times?

The night is mentioned first because it is the time of fears, since darkness aids the causes of harm in reaching their aims, whether from humans, animals, or bodily ailments.

The mention of the day after it is for comprehensiveness.

The meaning of "from the Most Merciful" is: from His might and His punishment. After this conditional sequence, three successive transitions (idrab, "a shift from one statement to another") come, in the gradual manner that is characteristic of idrab.

The first idrab is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, but they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord.﴾ This is an ascent from the rebuke, which was meant for correction, to despair of their reform, that they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord. Thus no benefit is hoped from them through the calamities. That is: postpone the question and the rebuke, and leave them until, when they become entangled in the punishment, they will know that they have no protector.

Then He made a second idrab with "am" (the disjunctive am, munqati'a), which is a sister of "bal" while also indicating interrogation, for the purpose of rebuke. He said: ﴿Or do they have gods who protect them from besides Us?﴾ That is: rather, do they have gods? The interrogative is one of denial and rebuke, meaning: they have no gods that protect them from besides Us. This is a refutation of their belief that they had taken the idols as intercessors. The clause ﴿They are unable to help themselves﴾ is a resumptive, parenthetical clause (isti'naf, mu'taridha). The pronoun in "yastatee'oona" refers to the gods, and the pronoun of rational beings was applied to them in imitation of what the Arabs do in their speech. The meaning: how could they help them when they cannot even help themselves? Nor are they supported by God through acceptance.

Then He made a third idrab, by which He moved to uncovering the cause of their delusion. Out of their ignorance of it, they reckoned themselves secure from God's seizing them with punishment, and this emboldened them to mock the threat. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, We have granted these people and their fathers enjoyment﴾ [al-Anbiya: 44]. That is: what they continue to enjoy of blessing is only a granting of enjoyment and respite, just as We granted their fathers enjoyment before them. Just as their fathers had appointed terms which they reached, so too will these people have theirs. But the terms differ according to what God knows of wisdom regarding their extent, until the lifespans of their forebears became long. This is an allusion that the lifespans of these people will not reach the lifespans of their fathers, and that God will bring upon them destruction for their denial, at a term He knows.

The address was first directed to them with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: who will protect you﴾, then He turned away from them from the mode of direct address (khitab) to the mode of third person (ghaiba). This is because what was directed at them, namely the denial that anyone could protect them from God's punishment, made them deserving of being turned away from, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea, until when you are in ships and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice in it﴾ [Yunus: 22], the verse in Surat Yunus.

The word "yusbahoon" may be the present form of "sahibahu" (to accompany, keep company with, and cling to), and companionship requires support and backing. Thus the subject that has replaced the agent in the passive form may be God, exalted is He, meaning: God does not accompany them, that is, He does not support them. In this case His saying "from Us" is connected to "yusbahoon" with the meaning of "min" of connection (ittisaliyya), that is: companionship connected to Us, meaning a firm companionship. This is a negation of what the polytheists believed in their saying: ﴿We worship them only so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. It is also possible that the omitted subject is omitted for the purpose of generality, meaning: no companion will accompany them, that is, no protector will shelter them, for proximity (jiwar) requires the protection of the neighbour. In this case His saying "from Us" is connected to "yusbahoon" with the meaning of "min" that carries the sense of "ala" (against), as in His saying: ﴿Who will help us against the might of God if it comes upon us?﴾ [Ghafir: 29]. Or the word may be the present form of "asbahahu" (with a hamza), meaning to protect and preserve him, that is, from evil. The indication by "these people" refers to those present in minds, namely the disbelievers of Quraysh.
