Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 44:

﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts? Are they then the victors?﴾

This is a consequence of their denial of the victory of the Muslims, and their regarding the delay of the promise as proof of its non-occurrence, to the point that they said: ﴿When will this promise be, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 38], mockingly and in denial. Then, when He warned them of what would befall them in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If only those who disbelieved knew the time when they will not be able to avert from their faces the Fire﴾ [al-Anbiya': 39], up to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that which they used to ridicule﴾ [al-Anbiya': 41], this is a branch of all of that, an interrogative expressing wonder at their failure to perceive the signs of the promise's connection with what is promised, as evidence of its nearness through the occurrence of its signs.

The seeing (ru'yah) is cognitive ('ilmiyyah), and the sentence takes the place of the two objects, because it is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: marvel at their failure to perceive the diminution of their land from its outlying parts, and that this is from the handiwork of God, may He be exalted, by the directing of a special providence, since it does not proceed according to the usual dominant course. Whoever reflects will know that it is among the wondrous handiwork of God, may He be exalted. That suffices as evidence for the veracity of the Messenger (ﷺ), for the truth of what he promised them, and for his Lord's care for him, as the verb "na'ti" indicates. The "coming" (al-ityan) is a depiction of the state of the raider who goes to the land of a people, killing and capturing, as already mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So God came at their structures from the foundations﴾ [al-Nahl: 26]. The definiteness in "al-ard" (the land) is definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), that is, the land of the Arabs, as in His saying, may He be exalted, in Surah Yusuf: ﴿I will not leave the land﴾ [Yusuf: 80], meaning the land of Egypt.

Page 77

And al-nuqsan (diminution): reducing the quantity of something.

And al-atraf: plural of tarf (with a fatha on the ta' and the ra'). It is that by which a body ends on one of its sides. Its opposite is the middle (al-wasat).

The intended meaning of the land's diminution is the diminution of those upon it from among the people, not the diminution of its area, because this surah is Meccan; at that time none of the land of the polytheists was in the possession of the Muslims, and the observed evidence is the indicator.

The intended meaning is the decrease in the number of polytheists through the entry of many of them into Islam, from among those of Mecca who embraced Islam, and those of them who emigrated to Abyssinia, and those from Medina who embraced Islam, if the verse was revealed after the conversion of the people of the first or second 'Aqaba, so the number of Muslims that day exceeded two hundred. A parallel to this sentence has preceded at the end of Surah al-Ra'd.

The sentence ﴿Are they then the victors?﴾ is a consequence of the sentence expressing wonder at their failure to perceive this state. The interrogation is denunciatory, meaning: how can they suppose that they have prevailed over the Muslims and gained power to argue against them?

The choice of the nominal sentence in His saying, "Are they then the victors?", rather than the verbal one, is because its two components, being definite, indicate restriction (qasr), meaning: they are not the victors, rather the Muslims are the victors, for if the polytheists were the victors, their number would not be diminishing, and their city would not have been emptied of a great many of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 45:

﴿Say: I only warn you by the revelation, but the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned.﴾

This is an independent resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i), intended to cover all that preceded it of their mocking demand for the promise, in their sarcastic words, ﴿And they say: When will this promise be?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 38],

Page 78

and of the threat directed at them in His words, ﴿If only those who disbelieved knew﴾ [al-Anbiya': 39], etc.; and of their reminder of the Creator and their being alerted to the falsehood of their gods in His words, ﴿Say: Who protects you by night and day?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 42], up to His words, ﴿until life lengthened for them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 44]; and of the argument against them by the appearance of the glimmers of the victory of the Muslims and the approach of the promise, in His words, ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its edges?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 44]. This was followed by God's command to His Messenger to address them by defining the essence of his call, which is restricting it to warning them of what will befall them in this world and the Hereafter, a warning through the revelation sent down to him from God, the Exalted, which is the Qur'an. That is: do not turn away from it, do not seek from me any sign other than this, do not ask about the fixing of the terms of the arrival of the threat, and do not think that you can anger me by your turning away and your deep immersion in your disbelief.

Thus the statement is a restriction (qasr) of a described subject to a quality, and its restriction to what is connected with that quality, following its connected element, so it stands in place of two restrictions. No example of this from the speech of the Arabs before the Qur'an has become clear to me.

This statement entails a withdrawal from them after the delivery of the message, in establishing the proof against them; for this reason it was appended with His words, ﴿and the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned﴾. The conjunction "wa" (and) is for coordination with ﴿I only warn you by the revelation﴾, a coordination of resumption upon resumption, because an appended conclusion (tadhyil) is of the kind of resumption.

The definite article in "al-Summ" (the deaf) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq). "Deafness" is used metaphorically for not benefiting from meaningful speech, likening the non-benefit from what is heard to the non-entry of speech into the ear-canal of the one addressed. It has preceded in His words, ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18] in Surat al-Baqarah. Included in its generality are the polytheists who turn away from the Qur'an, and they are the intended target of the appended statement, so that their inclusion in the ruling is by way of inferring the particular from the general.

The restriction of the non-hearing to the time of turning away upon hearing the warning is to denounce their turning away from the warning, because it is a turning away that leads them to ruin, so it is more grievous than the non-hearing of good tidings or narration; and because the appended statement follows many warnings.

The word "al-du'a'" (the call) was chosen because it corresponds to the purpose, since the Prophet ﷺ was a caller, as He said, ﴿I call to God with insight﴾ [Yusuf: 108]. The more apparent view is that the clause ﴿and the deaf do not hear the call﴾ is speech addressed to the Messenger ﷺ and is not part of what he was commanded to say to them.

The majority read "wa la yasma'u" with a ya' at its beginning and "al-summu" in the nominative. Ibn 'Amir read "wa la tusmi'u" with a ta' at the beginning, dammed, and "al-summa" in the accusative, addressed to the Messenger ﷺ; this reading is explicit in the separation of the clause from the speech commanded to be said to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 46:

﴿And if a breath of your Lord's punishment should touch them, they would surely say: "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾

It is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿Say: I only warn you by revelation﴾ [al-Anbiya: 45], and the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: warn them that they will regret when the first of the punishment reaches them in the Hereafter. This is a transition from warning them of the punishment of this world to warning them of the punishment of the Hereafter. The conditional is emphasized with the lam of oath (lam al-qasam) to confirm the occurrence of the consequent.

Al-mass (المَسّ): contact with the outer surface of the body.

Al-nafḥah (النَّفْحَةُ): a single instance of a small gift, from the verb nafaḥa, said when one gives something: "nafahahu bi-shay'" (he gave him something).

Page 80
In the root n-f-ḥ it is said that it is a small, meager gift. With the form of the singular noun in it, the indefiniteness, and the attribution of touching to it rather than to another verb, there are four intensifications of minimization. So what do you think of a punishment whose small portion moves the one it strikes to acknowledge that he deserves it and to express his astonishment at the bad state of his own soul?

Al-waylu (الوَيْلُ) was explained at the words of the Most High: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at the words of the Most High: ﴿And woe to the disbelievers because of a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim: 2] at the beginning of Surat Ibrahim.

The meaning of "Indeed we were wrongdoers" is: indeed we were transgressors against ourselves, in that we turned away from reflecting on the truthfulness of the Messenger's ﷺ call. Thus, zulm (wrongdoing) in this verse is meant as shirk (polytheism), because their polytheism is well known among them, so it is not something they would fail to recognize when a breath of the punishment touches them.

[Page 81]

﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least. Even if it be the weight of a mustard seed, We shall bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners.﴾

It is permissible for the *waw* to be conjunctive, joining this sentence to the sentence ﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord touches them﴾ [al-Anbiya; 21:46], and so on, for the reason of their saying, "Indeed, we were wrong-doers." It also serves to show that they will be recompensed for all that they had committed of disbelief and denial of the Messenger. This is shown by way of mentioning the general after the specific in the two forms of recompense. Thus it resembles a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) because of the generality of His saying, ﴿so no soul will be wronged in the least﴾, and it resembles the thing being recompensed because of His saying, ﴿Even if it be the weight of a mustard seed, We shall bring it forth﴾.

It is also permissible for the *waw* to be a *waw al-hal* (circumstantial), referring to His saying, "your Lord," and for the first-person plural "We" of exalted majesty to be an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person), in keeping with the fitting of the recompense to the deeds, as one says: "He rendered to him the measure, a *sa'* for a *sa'*." For this reason, His saying, ﴿so no soul will be wronged in the least﴾, is built upon it.

It is also permissible for the sentence to be parenthetical (*mu'taridah*), and for the *waw* to be parenthetical (*i'tiradiyyah*).

The original meaning of *al-wad'* (placing) is setting something down and fixing it in a place; it is the opposite of raising. It is also applied to making a thing and designating it for a use, and in that sense it is figurative.

*Al-mizan* (the scale) is the name of an instrument for weighing. It has many forms that vary with customs, but they all share the feature of having two pans (*tabaqayn*) balanced in weight, called *kiftatayn* (with a *kasra* on the *kaf* and a shadda on the *fa'*). They may be made of wood or iron; if they are made of brass, they are called *sanjatayn* (with a fatha on the *sad* and a sukun on the *nun*). Each pan is suspended by strings from an end that is joined to a rod of iron or hard wood, with a loop at each of its two ends to which one of the pans is tied. This rod is called *shahin* (the beam), and it is laid out extended. At its middle, equidistant, is a loop by which the weigher's hand holds it. Sometimes they made that loop elongated, of metal, and set in it a thick metal needle hanging from a small metal loop fixed at the middle of the beam. When the beam is raised, that needle moves. If it coincides with the middle of the long loop, perfectly aligned, the balance of the weight is known; if it leans, the imbalance is known. This needle is called *lisan* (the tongue). When one wishes to weigh two things to know whether they are equal or one is heavier, each is placed in a pan. The pan holding the heavier one descends and the other, holding the lighter, rises. If they balance, the two things weighed are equal.

When one wishes to know the weight of a thing in itself, without comparing it to something else, they took pieces of metal (brass, copper, iron, or stone) of fixed, agreed-upon quantities, such as the *dirham*, the *uqiyyah* and the *ratl*. They made these a measure of the weight of what is weighed, so that its quantity may be known, to prevent fraud in exchange. Their unit is the *mithqal*, which is also called *al-sanj* (with a fatha on the unpointed *sin* and a sukun on the *nun* after it, followed by a *jim*).

[Page 82]

*Al-qist* (with a kasra on the *qaf* and a sukun on the *sin*) is a noun in the sense of the object, and it is a verbal noun whose verb is *aqsata* (with a hamza). It was discussed earlier in His saying, ﴿standing firm in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran; 3:18], in the surah of Al 'Imran.

The scholars of the early generations (*al-salaf*) differed over whether *al-mawazin* (the scales) here is meant literally or figuratively. The majority held that it is literal, and that God will set up on the Day of Gathering scales for weighing the deeds of His servants, resembling the familiar scale. Some of them held that each person has his own scale by which his deeds are weighed; this is the apparent sense of the plural form in this verse and in His saying, ﴿As for him whose scales are heavy﴾ [al-Qari'ah; 101:6], ﴿he will be in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Qari'ah; 101:7], in the surah of al-Qari'ah. Others held that there is one scale in which the deeds of the servants are weighed one by one, and that it is in the hand of Gabriel. On this view the plural refers to the things weighed in it, so as to agree with the reports stating that it is a general scale.

All agree that it is suited to the greatness of that Day and is not like the scale of this world, but resembles it in form, approximately. On this interpretation, *al-wad'* is used in its literal meaning, namely setting up and establishing.

Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak held, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that the scale mentioned in the Qur'an is a parable for justice in recompense, as in His saying, ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾ [al-A'raf; 7:8], in the surah of al-A'raf. Al-Tabari inclined to this view. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: "*Al-mawazin*: the sound reckoning and the recompense for deeds with fairness, without anyone being wronged." End of quotation.

That is, it is used metaphorically for justice in recompense, because it resembles the scale in securing justice in dealings, as in His saying, ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the Balance﴾ [al-Hadid; 57:25].

*Al-wad'* here is a *tarshih* (a metaphor that develops a metaphor) and a metaphor for manifestation.

The Ash'arites (*al-Ash'ariyyah*) held that the scale is to be taken in its outward sense.

The Mu'tazilites had two positions on this. One group said the scale is literal, and another group said it is figurative. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned both views in *al-Kashshaf*, which shows that both views are attributed to their leading scholars, and this is stated explicitly in *Taqrir al-Mawaqif*.

In *al-Maqasid*: "Attributing to the Mu'tazilites, without qualification, the view that the literal reality of the scale is denied is a deficiency on the part of some theologians." End of quotation.

I say: perhaps he meant by this al-Nasafi in his creed.

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said in his book *al-'Awasim min al-Qawasim*: "The Qur'an alone mentions the scale, while the Sunnah alone mentions the Path (*al-sirat*) and the Basin (*al-hawd*). Since this matter is so, people have differed about it. Some said: the deeds are literally weighed in a scale with two pans and a beam, and the records of good and evil deeds are placed in the two pans, and God creates the weight in them according to His knowledge of them. Others said: the report about weighing refers only to God's informing the servants of the measures of their deeds." Al-Tabari and others transmitted from Mujahid that he inclined to this view.

It is not impossible that the scale and the weighing are in their outward sense, but the question remains about how deeds, which are accidents, are weighed. Here, whoever halts, let him halt, and whoever walks on, let him walk. Whoever holds to halting should halt at the first position. Whoever wishes to proceed will find a path of three meanings: a scale, a weighing and a thing weighed. If he proceeds along the path of the scale and the weighing and finds it sound in every term, until he reaches the specification of the thing weighed without it becoming clear to him, he should not turn back in retreat, abandoning what he has affirmed. Rather, he should keep what came before in its reality and soundness, and strive to interpret this and clarify it." End of quotation.

[Page 83]

I say: both views are acceptable, and all agree that the names of the states of the Hereafter are only an approximation to us through what we are familiar with. God is capable of everything. The power of God is not known through such investigations, nor is His action denied by analogy to what is customary and familiar.

It appears to me that the consistent use of the plural form *al-mawazin* in the three verses in which the scale is mentioned indicates that the weighing in them is meant in its figurative sense. Its explanation by the word "*al-qist*" in this verse makes that preference stronger.

The mention of weighing has already occurred in His saying, ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾ [al-A'raf; 7:8], in the surah of al-A'raf.

*Al-qist* means justice. It is said *al-qistas* (the scale or balance), a word arabicized from the Roman, that is, Latin, language.

Al-Bukhari transmitted this from Mujahid at the end of his *Sahih*.

So, on the view that the scales are literal instruments for weighing in the Hereafter, the word *al-qist*, which is a verbal noun meaning justice, is for the scales, with an elided modifier, that is, "the scales of justice." On the view that the scales are about justice, the word *al-qist* is a substitute for *al-mawazin*, making it a stripping of the figurative (*tajrid ba'da al-tarshih*). It is also permissible for it to be an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), since it is a verbal noun suited to that function.

The *lam* in His saying, "for the Day of Resurrection" (*li-yawm al-qiyamah*), may be a *lam* of cause with an elided modifier, that is, "for the sake of the Day of Resurrection," meaning the recompense on the Day of Resurrection. It may also be a *lam* of time, in the sense of *'inda* (at), which is the close temporal sense, as one says: "It was written for three nights passed of such-and-such month," and as in His saying, ﴿So divorce them at their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq; 65:1]. That is: We set up the scales at the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 85]

The linking of ﴿so no soul will be wronged in the least﴾ to the setting up of the scales is a linking of cause to effect, or effect to cause. *Al-zulm* (wrong) is the opposite of justice, and therefore the negation of wrong is linked to the affirmation of the setting up of justice. *Shay'an* (in the least) is in the accusative as an absolute object: "some of wrong." Its occurrence in the context of negation indicates the emphasis of generality, that is: some of wrong. Its occurrence in the context of negation also indicates the emphasis of generality from the verb *tuzlamu* (is wronged), which also occurs in the context of negation: that is, a soul will not be wronged by a diminishment of good that it deserved, nor by an addition of something it did not deserve. Thus wrong applies to both conditions, and so does the thing.

This sentence is a comprehensive word, with many meanings in concise wording. The genus of wrong is negated and negated of every soul, so it indicates that there is no remaining wrong without recompense.

The sentence ﴿Even if it be the weight of a mustard seed﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The *in* is a concessive particle indicating that what follows is something whose ruling might be supposed not to apply. When it is explicitly stated that the ruling covers it, it is known that its covering of what is other than it is by way of a fortiori reasoning. This conditional is often introduced by *law* (even if), as in His saying, ﴿So there will not be accepted from any of them the fill of the earth in gold, even if he offered it as ransom﴾ [Al 'Imran; 3:91], in Al 'Imran. It is also introduced by *in*, as here, and in the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

*Beauty is not in a wrapper, know this, even if you are clothed in a mantle.*

This was discussed earlier in the surah of Al 'Imran.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read *mithqal* with the accusative, taking it as the predicate of *kana* (was), and its subject is a pronoun referring back to *shay'an*. The answer of the condition is elided, indicated by the preceding sentence.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read *mithqal* with the nominative, taking *kana* as complete (*tamma*) and *mithqal* as its subject.

[Page 86]

The meaning of the two readings converges in outcome, which is this: if a soul has the weight of a mustard seed of good or of evil, it will be brought into the scale of its deeds and will be recompensed for it. On the first reading the sentence ﴿We shall bring it forth﴾ is a new sentence. On the second reading it is either the answer to the condition, or a new sentence with the answer of the condition elided. The pronoun in *bihā* (with it) refers back to *mithqal habbah* (the weight of a grain). Its pronoun took the feminine gender because its antecedent is feminine by addition, namely *habbah* (grain).

*Al-mithqal* is that which equals a thing in weight, that is, heaviness, so the *mithqal* of a grain is its measure.

*Al-habbah* is one of the seeds of plants that come out of the spike, or in the husks like pods, or in pods like pulses.

*Al-khardal* (mustard) is fine grains like sesame seed, which are the seeds of a tree known among the Arabs as *al-khardal*, and whose name in botany is *sinabis* (mustard). It is of two kinds, wild and cultivated, and grows in India, Egypt and Europe. Its tree has a thin stem that reaches about one metre in height, and its leaves are large. It produces yellow flowers from which its seeds form, emerging in small husks full of this grain. They come out green, then turn black, like small carobs. When this grain is crushed, a fragrant smell arises, which, when brought close to the nose and smelled, makes the eyes water. When its paste is placed on the skin, after a moment it causes a burning and heat, and then the skin cannot bear it for long, and it leaves the spot on the skin very red because blood gathers beneath the surface. For this reason its paste mixed with water is used as a medicine placed on a site afflicted by congestion of blood, such as pleurisy and chest colds.

[Page 87]

The clause ﴿And We suffice as reckoners﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause ﴿And if there is the weight of a mustard seed﴾. The object of *kafā* (suffice) is omitted, and it is indicated by His words ﴿so no soul will be wronged in the least﴾. The implied sense is: "And We suffice people in the matter of their reckoning." The meaning of "We suffice them as reckoners" is that they will not look to any other reckoner who could equal Us. This is an assurance to people that no one will be repaid with something he does not deserve, and it contains both a warning against punishment and an encouragement toward reward.

The plural pronoun in His words ﴿reckoners﴾ (*ḥāsibīn*) is understood in light of the pronoun of majesty in His words ﴿by Us﴾ (*binā*). The *bā'* (with) is extra (*zā'idah*), for emphasis. The underlying structure is: "We suffice the people." This *bā'* commonly enters after the verb *kafā* and most often falls on its subject, as here and in His words ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ [al-Nisā' 4:79] in Surat al-Nisā'. It may also enter on its object, as in the hadith: «Sufficient is it a sin for a man that he narrates everything he hears.»

The word *ḥāsibīn* is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) or as a specification (*tamyīz*) for the implied subject of *kafā*. Similar instances of this construction have occurred more than once before, including His words ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ [al-Nisā' 4:79] in Surat al-Nisā'.

This is a continuation of the previous passage, linked (*'atf*) to the sentence beginning ﴿Nay, they say: [it is but] confused dreams﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5], up to His words ﴿Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent [with signs]﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5]. Its purpose is to establish the proof against the polytheists through rational and persuasive arguments and admonitions, and then through the evidence of historical witness and the circumstances of earlier nations.

These accounts bear witness to the comparison between what was given to the Prophet ﷺ and what was given to his predecessors among the messengers and prophets, and that he was not an innovator among the messengers in his call to monotheism. That is the call for which the polytheists denied him, along with what is interwoven in this of mention of the obstinacy of peoples, the firmness of feet, and the support from the King, the All-Knowing. In this there is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ regarding what he encounters from his people: that this is the practice (*sunnah*) of the earlier messengers, as He, exalted, said: ﴿The practice [We applied] to those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [al-Isra': 77], in the surah of al-Isra'. Thus in these verses come reports about the circumstances of the earlier messengers.

In presenting the reports of these messengers and prophets there is also an elaboration of what the surah was built upon, from His words: ﴿We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed﴾ [al-Anbiya': 7], and the verses following it; then His words: ﴿We sent not before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya': 25]; then His words: ﴿Say: I only warn you by revelation﴾ [al-Anbiya': 45]. Its connection with all of that is a firm connection. For this reason it is followed by His words: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down. Will you then deny it?﴾

Mention begins with Musa and his brother together with their people, because the accounts of that are recorded in a book present with its people, which the Arabs know; and because the effect of Musa's bringing of the Law (*shari'ah*), peace be upon him, is the widest effect for establishing the order of a community that is second in greatness to the Law of Islam.

The opening of the narrative with the emphatic oath particle (*lam al-qasam*) is for emphasis, given that the polytheists stand in the position of those who deny that story, through the ignorance of some of them of it, the heedlessness of some of them toward it, and the forgetting of some of them of it. The point of comparison in this narrative is the support of the Messenger ﷺ with a manifest Book, and the people's receiving of that Book with aversion and denial.

*Al-Furqan* (the criterion): that by which truth is distinguished from falsehood, whether by speech or by action. God, exalted, named the Day of Badr "the Day of al-Furqan," because it was the beginning of the manifestation of the strength and victory of the Muslims. So it is permissible that *al-Furqan* is intended to mean the Torah, as in His words ﴿And We gave them both the clear Book﴾ [al-Saffat: 117], in the surah of al-Saffat.

The report about *al-Furqan* by attributing its bringing to the Divine Name (*damir al-jalalah*) is to alert that it was nothing more than a gift from God, exalted, and a revelation, just as Muhammad ﷺ was given the Qur'an. So how do they deny the giving of the Qur'an while they know that Musa, peace be upon him, came only with its like? In this is an alert to the greatness of that given thing.

It is also permissible that *al-Furqan* is intended to mean the miracles that distinguish the miracle from magic, as in His words ﴿And We sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority﴾ [Ghafir: 23], in the surah of Ghafir. And it is permissible that it is intended to mean the Law that distinguishes justice from injustice, as in His words ﴿And when We gave Musa the Book and the criterion, that perhaps you would be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 53], in the surah of al-Baqarah.

On the aforementioned possibilities, possibilities arise regarding His words that follow: ﴿And a light and a reminder for the God-conscious﴾. It is not necessary that some of these attributes be a division of others; rather they are overlapping attributes, so the totality of what was given to Musa and Harun embodies these three attributes.

*Al-Diya'* (light): radiance. It is used figuratively for guidance and knowledge, and this usage is common, and it is what is intended here. God, exalted, has said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], in the surah of al-Ma'idah.

*Al-Dhikr* (reminder): its origin is a thing coming to mind after heedlessness of it. It is also applied to the Book in which the mention of God is found. So His words (*li-l-muttaqin*, "for the God-conscious") may be such that the speech in it is for emphasis, so that the noun governed by the preposition *li-* is in the sense of the object, i.e., those who have attained God-consciousness (*taqwa*), that is, complying with His commands and avoiding what He has forbidden, because it reminds them of what they do not know and of what they forget of what they have known, and renews in their souls the watchfulness of their Lord. It is also permissible that the *lam* is for causation, i.e., a reminder for the sake of the God-conscious, that is, a Book from which the God-conscious benefit, not others of the misguided.

He described them with what increases the meaning of "the God-conscious" by clarification, in His words ﴿who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾. This is in the manner of His words ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], in the surah of al-Baqarah.

The *ba'* in His words (*bi-l-ghayb*, "in the unseen") is in the sense of *fi* ("in").

*Al-Ghayb* (the unseen): what is hidden from people's eyes. That is, they fear their Lord in private; they do not intend by that show-off, nor for fear of worldly deterrents or blame from people.

*Al-Ishfaq*: anticipation of a fearful event. The meaning of being apprehensive of the Hour is apprehension of its terrors; so they prepare for it its provision through God-consciousness to the extent of their ability. In this there is an allusion to those who were not guided by the Book of God, exalted, by the implication of the converse meaning of His words ﴿who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾. Whoever is not guided by the Book of God is not among those who fear their Lord in the unseen, and these are Pharaoh and his people.

He has followed this allusion with the mention of the intended purpose of the speech arising from it, which is the contrast, in His words ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down. This is a continuation of the previous passage, linked (*'atf*) to the sentence beginning ﴿Nay, they say: [it is but] confused dreams﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5], up to His words ﴿Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent [with signs]﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5]. Its purpose is to establish the proof against the polytheists through rational and persuasive arguments and admonitions, and then through the evidence of historical witness and the circumstances of earlier nations.

These accounts bear witness to the comparison between what was given to the Prophet ﷺ and what was given to his predecessors among the messengers and prophets, and that he was not an innovator among the messengers in his call to monotheism. That is the call for which the polytheists denied him, along with what is interwoven in this of mention of the obstinacy of peoples, the firmness of feet, and the support from the King, the All-Knowing. In this there is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ regarding what he encounters from his people: that this is the practice (*sunnah*) of the earlier messengers, as He, exalted, said: ﴿The practice [We applied] to those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [al-Isra': 77], in the surah of al-Isra'. Thus in these verses come reports about the circumstances of the earlier messengers.

In presenting the reports of these messengers and prophets there is also an elaboration of what the surah was built upon, from His words: ﴿We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed﴾ [al-Anbiya': 7], and the verses following it; then His words: ﴿We sent not before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya': 25]; then His words: ﴿Say: I only warn you by revelation﴾ [al-Anbiya': 45]. Its connection with all of that is a firm connection. For this reason it is followed by His words: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down. Will you then deny it?﴾

Mention begins with Musa and his brother together with their people, because the accounts of that are recorded in a book present with its people, which the Arabs know; and because the effect of Musa's bringing of the Law (*shari'ah*), peace be upon him, is the widest effect for establishing the order of a community that is second in greatness to the Law of Islam.

The opening of the narrative with the emphatic oath particle (*lam al-qasam*) is for emphasis, given that the polytheists stand in the position of those who deny that story, through the ignorance of some of them of it, the heedlessness of some of them toward it, and the forgetting of some of them of it. The point of comparison in this narrative is the support of the Messenger ﷺ with a manifest Book, and the people's receiving of that Book with aversion and denial.

*Al-Furqan* (the criterion): that by which truth is distinguished from falsehood, whether by speech or by action. God, exalted, named the Day of Badr "the Day of al-Furqan," because it was the beginning of the manifestation of the strength and victory of the Muslims. So it is permissible that *al-Furqan* is intended to mean the Torah, as in His words ﴿And We gave them both the clear Book﴾ [al-Saffat: 117], in the surah of al-Saffat.

The report about *al-Furqan* by attributing its bringing to the Divine Name (*damir al-jalalah*) is to alert that it was nothing more than a gift from God, exalted, and a revelation, just as Muhammad ﷺ was given the Qur'an. So how do they deny the giving of the Qur'an while they know that Musa, peace be upon him, came only with its like? In this is an alert to the greatness of that given thing.

It is also permissible that *al-Furqan* is intended to mean the miracles that distinguish the miracle from magic, as in His words ﴿And We sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority﴾ [Ghafir: 23], in the surah of Ghafir. And it is permissible that it is intended to mean the Law that distinguishes justice from injustice, as in His words ﴿And when We gave Musa the Book and the criterion, that perhaps you would be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 53], in the surah of al-Baqarah.

On the aforementioned possibilities, possibilities arise regarding His words that follow: ﴿And a light and a reminder for the God-conscious﴾. It is not necessary that some of these attributes be a division of others; rather they are overlapping attributes, so the totality of what was given to Musa and Harun embodies these three attributes.

*Al-Diya'* (light): radiance. It is used figuratively for guidance and knowledge, and this usage is common, and it is what is intended here. God, exalted, has said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], in the surah of al-Ma'idah.

*Al-Dhikr* (reminder): its origin is a thing coming to mind after heedlessness of it. It is also applied to the Book in which the mention of God is found. So His words (*li-l-muttaqin*, "for the God-conscious") may be such that the speech in it is for emphasis, so that the noun governed by the preposition *li-* is in the sense of the object, i.e., those who have attained God-consciousness (*taqwa*), that is, complying with His commands and avoiding what He has forbidden, because it reminds them of what they do not know and of what they forget of what they have known, and renews in their souls the watchfulness of their Lord. It is also permissible that the *lam* is for causation, i.e., a reminder for the sake of the God-conscious, that is, a Book from which the God-conscious benefit, not others of the misguided.

The *ba'* in His words (*bi-l-ghayb*, "in the unseen") is in the sense of *fi* ("in").

*Al-Ghayb* (the unseen): what is hidden from people's eyes. That is, they fear their Lord in private; they do not intend by that show-off, nor for fear of worldly deterrents or blame from people.

[Page 92]

The story of Musa and Harun is followed by the story of Ibrahim, concerning what was revealed to him about resisting polytheism (shirk) and making clear the proof of its falsehood. Ibrahim was the first model, before the coming of Islam, of resisting polytheism. He resisted it with argument, with force, and by proclaiming monotheism (tawhid). He built for monotheism a sanctuary in Makkah, which is the Ka'bah, and on Mount Nabu in the land of the Canaanites, where at that time there was a city called Luza. Then he built Bayt Il near the site of the city of (Jerusalem), in the place where the temple of Sulayman was later erected. Thus the story of Ibrahim with his people is a witness to the falsehood of polytheism, which resembled the state of the polytheists of Makkah, whom Muhammad (ﷺ) came to eradicate.

In mentioning the story of Ibrahim there is a rebuke (tawarruk) of the polytheists of Makkah, since they were in the condition that their forefather Ibrahim had denounced in his people, and that is sufficient as a proof against them. Also, the law of Ibrahim is the most famous law after the law of Musa.

The emphasis on the report about him with the lam of oath is for the reason we explained just before, in the emphasis on the report about Musa and Harun. It is that the Arabs, by opposing the law of their father Ibrahim, were placed in the position of one who denies that Ibrahim was given right guidance and direction. Likewise the report that Ibrahim was given right guidance, with the giving attributed to the pronoun of the Majesty (Allah), is for the same reason established in the story of Musa and Harun: to draw attention to the magnitude of that right guidance which he was given.

Al-rushd means guidance and sound judgment, and its opposite is al-ghayy (error). It was discussed earlier in His saying, ﴿There is clear distinction between right guidance and error﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256], in Surat al-Baqarah. The idafah (construct) of "al-rushd" to the pronoun of Ibrahim is an idafah of the verbal noun to its object, meaning "the guidance with which he was guided." The benefit of the idafah here is to draw attention to the greatness of this guidance, i.e., guidance befitting him. Also, the guidance of Ibrahim was a proverbial example among the Arabs and others. That is, he is the one whose renown you know, which has spread to the East and the West. So what do you think of a guidance given to him from Allah, the Exalted? Since the idafah was in the sense of the lam, it indicated exclusivity, as if he alone had it. This hints that Ibrahim was singled out in guidance among his people. The added emphasis and magnification is provided by the parenthetical clause at the end, His saying, ﴿and We were fully aware of him﴾, meaning: We gave him great guidance with knowledge from Us about Ibrahim, that is, about his being worthy of that guidance. This divine knowledge is connected to the great disposition by which he was the object of Allah's praise in many places in His Qur'an. That is, He knew from his inner nature qualities with which He was pleased and which He praised, so he merited by them to be taken as a close friend (khalil). This is like His saying, ﴿And We chose them with knowledge over the worlds﴾ [al-Dukhan: 32], and His saying, ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

As for His saying "from before" (min qablu), it means before We gave Musa and Harun the Criterion (al-Furqan), a light and a reminder. The reason for mentioning this (the giving of Ibrahim's guidance before Musa and Harun) is to draw attention to the fact that the giving of the Reminder to Musa and Harun happened only because their law had remained known and studied.

"When he said" (idh qala) is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by the verb "We gave" (atayna). That is, his being given guidance occurred at the time when he said to his father and his people, ﴿What are these images﴾ etc. That was the guidance with which he was given, i.e., at the time when revelation descended to him with the call to the oneness of Allah, the Exalted. That was the first thing with which revelation began.

The people of Ibrahim were of the Chaldeans (al-Kaldan). He lived in a land called Kawthi, with a thā' at its end followed by an alif, which is called in the Torah (Ur of the Chaldees). It is also said that it is Urfa in al-Ruha. Then he and his father and family settled in Harran, and Harran is Harran. Afterwards it was among the lands of the Chaldeans, as is required by Chapter 12 of Genesis, because of His saying in it: "Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father's house." His father died in Harran, as in Chapter 16 of Genesis. So it is certain that the call of Ibrahim was from Harran, because from Harran he went out to the land of Canaan. Harran is famous for being the city of the Sabians, and in it is a great temple of the Sabians. The people of Ibrahim were Sabians who worshipped the stars and made for them embodied images.

The interrogative in His saying, ﴿What are these images﴾, applies to the description in His saying, ﴿to which you are devoted﴾. So it is as if he said: "What is your worship of these images?" But it was phrased in the form of directing the question to the essence of the images, in order to leave the question about the reality of the images vague at the beginning of the speech, as a hint that there is no fit between their reality, expressed by "images," and their description as objects of worship, expressed by their devotion to them. This is from the feigned ignorance (tajahul al-arif) that he used as a preparation for their being judged wrong after they hear his answer. They thought he was a questioner seeking information, and for this reason they answered his question with their saying, ﴿We found our fathers worshipping them﴾. The nature of a question with "what" (ma) is that it asks for an explanation of the essence of what is asked about.

The pointing to the images is to add clarity to their meaning, which indicates their lowness from the rank of divinity. Expressing them as "images" strips them of independent existence.

The idols that the Chaldeans, the people of Ibrahim, worshipped were Ba'l, which was the greatest of them. It was made of gold, and it was the symbol of the sun in the era of Semiramis. They also worshipped symbols of the stars. There is no doubt that they worshipped the idols of the people of Nuh: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr, either under those names or under other names. The archaeological evidence has shown that among the idols of Assyria, the brothers of the Chaldeans, there was an idol named Nasrukh, which is certainly an eagle (nasr).

The making of devotion (ukuf) predicated to their pronoun indicates that Ibrahim had not previously participated with them in that, so that it would be known from it that he was in a position of rejecting them. This is because the use of the nominal sentence in His saying, ﴿You are devoted to them﴾ conveys the sense of their constancy in that. The verb "ukifuna" implicitly contains the meaning of worship, and therefore it is followed by the lam to indicate constant worship of them.

In answering him, they brought what they imagined would persuade him, namely that worshipping those idols was the custom of their fathers. They thought he would be like them, sanctifying the deeds of the fathers without examining whether they agreed with the truth. For this reason he did not delay in answering them: ﴿You and your fathers were certainly in clear error﴾, emphasizing this with the lam of oath.

In His saying, ﴿You were in error﴾ (kuntum fi dalal), the use of the verb "to be" and the particle of place (fi) hints at their being firmly established in error and immersed in it, to indicate that it was manifest error without any doubt. He emphasized this by describing it as "clear" (mubin). When they mentioned their fathers to him, he included the fathers with them in the judgment of error without leniency, by joining the fathers to them in that, so that they would know that they have no excuse for following their fathers, and their fathers have no excuse for establishing that for them, because the reality of those idols contradicts the reality of divinity and the deservingness of worship. And because they denied that what their fathers were upon was error, and were certain that their fathers were upon the truth, they doubted Ibrahim's state: whether he spoke in earnest and this was his belief. So they said, ﴿Have you come to us with the truth?﴾, expressing it with "the truth," which is the opposite of play, and that is what is called earnestness. The meaning is: "Is it with the truth according to your belief, or did you intend it as jest?" So they asked him and inquired: ﴿Have you come to us with the truth, or are you one of the players?﴾ The ba' is for accompaniment. The intended meaning of play here is the play of speech, which is called jest. They intended, by interpreting his words as jest, to be gentle with him and to avoid attributing falsehood to him, seeking to win his favor, since they saw the strength of his argument.

He turned from describing him with the attribute of "player" to describing him as belonging to the group of players, as an exaggeration of his speech's deep immersion in the domain of jest, such that the one who says it is firmly established in play and counted among the group described as players.

In his answer to them, he turned away from their saying, ﴿or are you one of the players?﴾, to negate that he is one of the players, and to affirm that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. That is, those images are not lords, since there is no dispute that they did not create the heavens and the earth. Rather, they are made, carved from stones, as in the other verse: ﴿He said: Do you worship what you carve?﴾ [al-Saffat: 95]. Since the creation of the heavens and the earth is not attributed to them, as is undisputed among you, they are carved from parts of the earth, so they are nothing but created, made things, not lords and not creators. The plural pronoun in His saying, ﴿He created them﴾, certainly refers to the heavens and the earth. So Ibrahim's answer was a negation of their saying, ﴿or are you one of the players?﴾, together with the basis of the negation, by establishing the proof that he came to them with the truth. There is no "method of the wise style" (al-uslub al-hakim) in it, as al-Tibi thought.

His saying, ﴿And I am of those who bear witness to that﴾, is an announcement to them that he was sent by Allah to establish the religion of monotheism, because the messenger of every nation is a witness over it, as He said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41]. There was not at that time anyone among his people who bore witness to the falsehood of the divinity of their idols. So it is determined that the intended meaning of "those who bear witness" is that he is one of those who testified to the oneness of Allah in divinity across different times or regions.

They thought he would be like them, sanctifying the deeds of the fathers without examining whether they agreed with the truth. He emphasized this by describing it as "clear" (mubin). When they mentioned their fathers to him, he included the fathers with them in the judgment of error without leniency, by joining the fathers to them in that, so that they would know that they have no excuse for following their fathers, and their fathers have no excuse for establishing that for them, because the reality of those idols contradicts the reality of divinity and the deservingness of worship. And because they denied that what their fathers were upon was error, and were certain that their fathers were upon the truth, they doubted Ibrahim's state: whether he spoke in earnest and this was his belief. So they said, ﴿Have you come to us with the truth?﴾, expressing it with "the truth," which is the opposite of play, and that is what is called earnestness. They intended, by interpreting his words as jest, to be gentle with him and to avoid attributing falsehood to him, seeking to win his favor, since they saw the strength of his argument.

He turned from describing him with the attribute of "player" to describing him as belonging to the group of players, as an exaggeration of his speech's deep immersion in the domain of jest, such that the one who says it is firmly established in play and counted among the group described as players.

that al-Walid is more deserving of the excuse.

[Page 97]

For this reason he did not delay in answering them: ﴿You and your fathers were certainly in clear error﴾, emphasizing this with the lam of oath.

In His saying, ﴿You were in error﴾ (kuntum fi dalal), the use of the verb "to be" and the particle of place (fi) hints at their being firmly established in error and immersed in it, to indicate that it was manifest error without any doubt. He emphasized this by describing it as "clear" (mubin). When they mentioned their fathers to him, he included the fathers with them in the judgment of error without leniency, by joining the fathers to them in that, so that they would know that they have no excuse for following their fathers, and their fathers have no excuse for establishing that for them, because the reality of those idols contradicts the reality of divinity and the deservingness of worship. And because they denied that what their fathers were upon was error, and were certain that their fathers were upon the truth, they doubted Ibrahim's state: whether he spoke in earnest and this was his belief. So they said, ﴿Have you come to us with the truth?﴾, expressing it with "the truth," which is the opposite of play, and that is what is called earnestness. The meaning is: "Is it with the truth according to your belief, or did you intend it as jest?" So they asked him and inquired: ﴿Have you come to us with the truth, or are you one of the players?﴾ The ba' is for accompaniment. The intended meaning of play here is the play of speech, which is called jest. They intended, by interpreting his words as jest, to be gentle with him and to avoid attributing falsehood to him, seeking to win his favor, since they saw the strength of his argument.

He turned from describing him with the attribute of "player" to describing him as belonging to the group of players, as an exaggeration of his speech's deep immersion in the domain of jest, such that the one who says it is firmly established in play and counted among the group described as players.

In his answer to them, he turned away from their saying, ﴿or are you one of the players?﴾, to negate that he is one of the players, and to affirm that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. That is, those images are not lords, since there is no dispute that they did not create the heavens and the earth. Rather, they are made, carved from stones, as in the other verse: ﴿He said: Do you worship what you carve?﴾ [al-Saffat: 95]. Since the creation of the heavens and the earth is not attributed to them, as is undisputed among you, they are carved from parts of the earth, so they are nothing but created, made things, not lords and not creators. The plural pronoun in His saying, ﴿He created them﴾, certainly refers to the heavens and the earth. So Ibrahim's answer was a negation of their saying, ﴿or are you one of the players?﴾, together with the basis of the negation, by establishing the proof that he came to them with the truth. There is no "method of the wise style" (al-uslub al-hakim) in it, as al-Tibi thought.

His saying, ﴿And I am of those who bear witness to that﴾, is an announcement to them that he was sent by Allah to establish the religion of monotheism, because the messenger of every nation is a witness over it, as He said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41]. There was not at that time anyone among his people who bore witness to the falsehood of the divinity of their idols. So it is determined that the intended meaning of "those who bear witness" is that he is one of those who testified to the oneness of Allah in divinity across different times or regions.

It may also carry the sense of emphasis for that, like an oath, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Al-Farazdaq bears witness when he meets his Lord
that al-Walid is more deserving of the excuse.

[Page 97]

Then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, moved from changing the evil by speech to changing it by hand, announcing his resolve to do so in His saying, ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plan against your idols after you turn away, retreating﴾, emphasizing his resolve with an oath. So the waw is coordinating the oath clause with the preceding declarative clause.

The ta' (in "ta-llahi") is specific to an oath about a matter that is wondered at, and it is specific to the name of Allah. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿They said: By Allah, you will not cease remembering Yusuf﴾ [Yusuf: 85].

He called his breaking of the idols "plan" (kayd) by way of metaphor, or by implied mushakalah (correspondence), because the addressees believed that they claimed the idols could defend themselves, so that he could not touch them with harm except by way of plotting (kayd). Plotting (kayd) is devising a way to inflict harm in a form that is not hateful to the one harmed. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿Indeed, your plotting is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28] in Surat Yusuf. He restricted his plotting to after the departure of the addressees only to indicate that he would inflict harm on the idols at the first opportunity to do so. This is part of his resolve, peace be upon him, because hastening to change the evil, although it is by hand, is a stance of resolve, and he could not do that while the worshippers of the idols were present. If he had tried to break them in their presence, his action would have been futile. The purpose of changing evil is to remove it as far as possible, and for this reason removing it by hand is only possible when one has the capacity to do so.

"Retreating" (mudbirin) is a circumstantial clause emphasizing its governing verb. Its like has been mentioned more than once before, including at His saying, ﴿Then you turned away, retreating﴾ [al-Tawbah: 25] in Surat Bara'ah.

[Page 92]

The story of Musa and Harun is followed by the story of Ibrahim, concerning what was revealed to him about resisting polytheism (shirk) and making clear the proof of its falsehood. Ibrahim was the first model, before the coming of Islam, of resisting polytheism. He resisted it with argument, with force, and by proclaiming monotheism (tawhid). He built for monotheism a sanctuary in Makkah, which is the Ka'bah, and on Mount Nabu in the land of the Canaanites, where at that time there was a city called Luza. Then he built Bayt Il near the site of the city of (Jerusalem), in the place where the temple of Sulayman was later erected. Thus the story of Ibrahim with his people is a witness to the falsehood of polytheism, which resembled the state of the polytheists of Makkah, whom Muhammad (ﷺ) came to eradicate.

In mentioning the story of Ibrahim there is a rebuke (tawarruk) of the polytheists of Makkah, since they were in the condition that their forefather Ibrahim had denounced in his people, and that is sufficient as a proof against them. Also, the law of Ibrahim is the most famous law after the law of Musa.

The emphasis on the report about him with the lam of oath is for the reason we explained just before, in the emphasis on the report about Musa and Harun. It is that the Arabs, by opposing the law of their father Ibrahim, were placed in the position of one who denies that Ibrahim was given right guidance and direction. Likewise the report that Ibrahim was given right guidance, with the giving attributed to the pronoun of the Majesty (Allah), is for the same reason established in the story of Musa and Harun: to draw attention to the magnitude of that right guidance which he was given.

Al-rushd means guidance and sound judgment, and its opposite is al-ghayy (error). It was discussed earlier in His saying, ﴿There is clear distinction between right guidance and error﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256], in Surat al-Baqarah. The idafah (construct) of "al-rushd" to the pronoun of Ibrahim is an idafah of the verbal noun to its object, meaning "the guidance with which he was guided." The benefit of the idafah here is to draw attention to the greatness of this guidance, i.e., guidance befitting him. Also, the guidance of Ibrahim was a proverbial example among the Arabs and others. That is, he is the one whose renown you know, which has spread to the East and the West. So what do you think of a guidance given to him from Allah, the Exalted? Since the idafah was in the sense of the lam, it indicated exclusivity, as if he alone had it. This hints that Ibrahim was singled out in guidance among his people. The added emphasis and magnification is provided by the parenthetical clause at the end, His saying, ﴿and We were fully aware of him﴾, meaning: We gave him great guidance with knowledge from Us about Ibrahim, that is, about his being worthy of that guidance. This divine knowledge is connected to the great disposition by which he was the object of Allah's praise in many places in His Qur'an. That is, He knew from his inner nature qualities with which He was pleased and which He praised, so he merited by them to be taken as a close friend (khalil). This is like His saying, ﴿And We chose them with knowledge over the worlds﴾ [al-Dukhan: 32], and His saying, ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

As for His saying "from before" (min qablu), it means before We gave Musa and Harun the Criterion (al-Furqan), a light and a reminder. The reason for mentioning this (the giving of Ibrahim's guidance before Musa and Harun) is to draw attention to the fact that the giving of the Reminder to Musa and Harun happened only because their law had remained known and studied.

"When he said" (idh qala) is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by the verb "We gave" (atayna). That is, his being given guidance occurred at the time when he said to his father and his people, ﴿What are these images﴾ etc. That was the guidance with which he was given, i.e., at the time when revelation descended to him with the call to the oneness of Allah, the Exalted. That was the first thing with which revelation began.

The people of Ibrahim were of the Chaldeans (al-Kaldan). He lived in a land called Kawthi, with a thā' at its end followed by an alif, which is called in the Torah (Ur of the Chaldees). It is also said that it is Urfa in al-Ruha. Then he and his father and family settled in Harran, and Harran is Harran. Afterwards it was among the lands of the Chaldeans, as is required by Chapter 12 of Genesis, because of His saying in it: "Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father's house." His father died in Harran, as in Chapter 16 of Genesis. So it is certain that the call of Ibrahim was from Harran, because from Harran he went out to the land of Canaan. Harran is famous for being the city of the Sabians, and in it is a great temple of the Sabians. The people of Ibrahim were Sabians who worshipped the stars and made for them embodied images.

The interrogative in His saying, ﴿What are these images﴾, applies to the description in His saying, ﴿to which you are devoted﴾. So it is as if he said: "What is your worship of these images?" But it was phrased in the form of directing the question to the essence of the images, in order to leave the question about the reality of the images vague at the beginning of the speech, as a hint that there is no fit between their reality, expressed by "images," and their description as objects of worship, expressed by their devotion to them. This is from the feigned ignorance (tajahul al-arif) that he used as a preparation for their being judged wrong after they hear his answer. They thought he was a questioner seeking information, and for this reason they answered his question with their saying, ﴿We found our fathers worshipping them﴾. The nature of a question with "what" (ma) is that it asks for an explanation of the essence of what is asked about.

The pointing to the images is to add clarity to their meaning, which indicates their lowness from the rank of divinity. Expressing them as "images" strips them of independent existence.

The idols that the Chaldeans, the people of Ibrahim, worshipped were Ba'l, which was the greatest of them. It was made of gold, and it was the symbol of the sun in the era of Semiramis. They also worshipped symbols of the stars. There is no doubt that they worshipped the idols of the people of Nuh: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr, either under those names or under other names. The archaeological evidence has shown that among the idols of Assyria, the brothers of the Chaldeans, there was an idol named Nasrukh, which is certainly an eagle (nasr).

The making of devotion (ukuf) predicated to their pronoun indicates that Ibrahim had not previously participated with them in that, so that it would be known from it that he was in a position of rejecting them. This is because the use of the nominal sentence in His saying, ﴿You are devoted to them﴾ conveys the sense of their constancy in that. The verb "ukifuna" implicitly contains the meaning of worship, and therefore it is followed by the lam to indicate constant worship of them.

Page 98
The two attached pronouns in (jaʻalahum) and (lahum) refer to the idols, which are treated as if they were rational beings, while the pronoun in (laʻallahum) refers to the people of Ibrahim. The context directs similar pronouns to their proper referents, like the two plural pronouns in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they cultivated it more than they cultivated it﴾ [al-Rum: 9].
And al-judhadh, with a dammah on the jim in the reading of the majority, is a collective noun (ism jamʻ) of judhadhah, which is fuʻalah from al-jadhdh, meaning cutting, like qulamah and kunasah; that is, he broke them and made them into fragments.

al-Kisa'i read jidhadhan with a kasrah on the jim, as a verbal noun (masdar); so it is from the expression by the verbal noun for emphasis.

It was said: the idols were seventy idols arranged in rows, and with them was a great idol, which was opposite the door of the house of the idols. After he broke them, he placed the axe on the neck of the greatest idol, mocking them. The meaning of ﴿that they might return to it﴾ is the hope that the people would return to consulting the greatest idol, so that it would inform them who broke the rest of the idols, because he knows that their ignorance makes them greedy to consult the great idol. Perhaps what is meant is consulting its attendants, so that they would tell them what they receive from its alleged revelation.

The pronoun in (lahum) refers to the idols from his saying (aṣnamakum). The plural pronoun for rational beings was applied to the idols, imitating the sense of Ibrahim's speech, because his people reckoned the idols to be rational. Similar is the pronouns in His saying after it, ﴿Rather, the greatest of them did it; so ask them, if they can speak﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63].

Page 99
This act which Ibrahim performed he performed after he had argued with his father and his people about worshipping the idols and the stars, and saw their obstinate refusal of clear proof, as mentioned in Surat al-An'am.
The saying of his people, ﴿Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is of the wrongdoers,﴾ indicates that it had not occurred to them that the greatest of the gods had done that. These people are a group who had not heard Ibrahim's threat to plot against their idols, and those who said "We heard a young man mention them" are those before whom Ibrahim threatened the idols in their hearing.

al-Fata: the male whose youth has become strong; it may apply to people and to camels, and its feminine is fatah. They sometimes use it as a word of praise indicating the completion of a man's praiseworthy qualities.

al-Dhikr: speaking with words.

The object of (yadhkuruhum) is omitted, because context indicates it; that is, he mentions them with a threat, and this is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 36], as has passed. The position of the two clauses (yadhkuruhum) and (yuqalu lahu) is in the position of a qualifier for (fata). And in their saying ﴿called Ibrahim﴾ there is an indication that those who were appointed to investigate the matter did not know Ibrahim, or that the witnesses intended to belittle him by saying he is unknown and is merely called or named Ibrahim, that is, he is not one of the known people.

(Ibrahim) is in the nominative as the deputy subject of (yuqal), because the verb of saying, when built into the passive, often carries the meaning of calling or naming; therefore the benefit is obtained from its transitivity to a bare noun, although the nature of the verb of saying is that it transitively takes only a clause or a noun that carries the sense of a clause, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿No! It is a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100].

Page 100
The meaning of ﴿before the eyes of the people﴾ is in the sight of the people. The preposition of elevation is used figuratively, since sight is firmly settled in it, until the seen thing is as if contained within the eyes. The meaning of (yashhadun) is that perhaps they may bear witness against him that he is the one who threatened the idols with plotting.

There occurs here the omission of a sentence required by the indication of implication (dalalat al-iqtida'). The implied meaning is: "So they brought him, and said, 'Did you do this to our gods?'"

صفحة ١٠١
For he did not claim that he had witnessed it, but he spoke in a way that conveys his supposition of it, since none of the idols remained intact except the greatest. In allowing that this chief of theirs who smashed them might be the one, there is an indication of the proof of the absence of a plurality of gods, for he made them imagine that their chief was angry at those idols sharing in his divinity. This is a gradual step toward the proof of God's oneness. Thus Ibrahim, in denying that he was the doer, intended to lay upon them the burden of proof against the divinity of the great idol, and against the divinity of the smashed idols a fortiori, with the intention that they would acknowledge all of this as false and become certain that he was the one who smashed the idols, and that if they were gods they would have defended themselves, and if their chief were the chief of gods he would have defended his entourage and allies. For this reason he said, ﴿So ask them, if they can speak﴾, mocking them and implying that what cannot speak or express itself is unfit for divinity.

The pronoun in "ask them" includes all the idols, both those that were smashed and those that remained standing. Although the people knew that the idols had not spoken before, Ibrahim intended to convince them that such a great event requires that they speak and identify who did it to them. This is analogous to the reasoning of the scholars of kalam that the miracle indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger, since God does not break habit to confirm a liar; thus His creating something beyond habit at the Messenger's challenge is evidence that God intended to confirm him.

As for what is related in the Sahih from Abu Hurayra that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Ibrahim did not lie except three lies, two of them concerning God, Mighty and Majestic: his saying, ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his saying, ﴿Rather, this one, their chief, did it﴾. And while he was one day with Sarah, he came upon one of the tyrants, and it was said to him: 'Here is a man with a woman among the most beautiful of people.' So he sent for him and said, 'Who is this?' He said, 'My sister.' Then he came to Sarah and said, 'O Sarah, there is no believer on the face of the earth except me and you, and this one asked me, and I told him you are my sister, so do not contradict me.'" . . . And he related the hadith.

Its meaning is that he lied in his answer to the words of his people, ﴿Did you do this to our gods?﴾, when he said, ﴿Rather, this one, their chief, did it﴾, because "bal" when it follows a question conveys the negation of what is asked about. So their words, ﴿Did you do this?﴾, were a question about his being the smasher of the idols; when he said "bal," he negated that about himself, and this negation contradicts reality and his belief, so it is a lie. Yet lying is blameworthy and forbidden, and it is permitted out of necessity, as Ibrahim said. This reversal was a preparation for the proof, with the intention that the truth would become clear to them in the end. For this reason he said, ﴿Do you then worship, besides Allah, that which neither benefits you at all nor harms you?﴾, and so on.

As for the statement, ﴿this one, their chief, did it﴾, it is not a lie, even though it contradicts reality and the speaker's belief, because speech and reports are established by their endings and what follows them, like speech followed by a condition or an exception. When he intended to warn them of the error of worshipping the idols, he prepared for that with a statement that proceeds on the basis of supposition and assumption. It is as if he said: "If this were a god, he would not have been content with aggression against his partners. When the aggression against them occurred in the presence of their chief, it became necessary that he be the doer." Then he advanced in the argument by negating divinity from all of them with his saying, ﴿if they can speak﴾, as has been explained.

The meaning of the hadith, then, is that these were lies at the outset, and that upon reflection their purpose becomes evident. The reason for the prohibition of lying is the deception of the addressee and what results from a false report, namely that actions proceed on the assumption that reality is other than it is. When a statement is followed by truth, it is not lying, but rather allusion, jest, or the like.

As for what occurs in the hadith of intercession, where Ibrahim says, "I am not fit for that," and mentions lies he told, its meaning is that he mentions having spoken words contrary to reality without God's permission by revelation; but he committed a statement contrary to reality out of the necessity of argument according to his own reasoning, and he feared that his reasoning would not coincide with the correct aim of God, so he feared God's rebuke and freed himself from that position.

صفحة ١٠٣
His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So they returned to themselves﴾, may mean that some of them returned to others, that is, some of them turned to address one another and turned away from addressing Ibrahim, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿then greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61], and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa: 29]; that is, some of them said to others, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers."
The plural pronouns are intended distributively, as in: "The people rode their animals." It may also mean that each one returned to himself, that is, he set aside consideration of the accusation against Ibrahim and reflected on Ibrahim's defense. Thus it became clear to each of them that Ibrahim was innocent, so some of them said to others, ﴿Indeed, you are the wrongdoers﴾, and the plural pronouns remain on their usual basis. The sentence conveys restriction, that is, "you are the wrongdoers, not Ibrahim," because you attached the accusation to him, that he wronged our idols, while the apparent course was that we should ask them about who did this to them; and it appears that the doer was their chief.

The "returning to themselves," according to the two previous possibilities, is a metaphor for the mind being occupied with something after it had been occupied with another, as a man returns to his house after going out to another place. The verb "nukisu" is passive, that is, "nakasahum nakis" (someone turned them over), and since there was no doer of that overturning except themselves, the verb was made passive and came to mean "they overturned upon their heads." This is an image.

Naks is turning the top of a thing to its bottom and its bottom to its top. It is said: "The thief was crucified upside down," that is, with his head placed directly on the ground, which is the most hideous posture of the crucified. Since the normal posture of the human body is to stand upright on its feet, when it is inverted its standing becomes as if on its head. So his saying here, ﴿they were turned back upon their heads﴾, is an image for the change of their opinion from the right course, just as they said, ﴿Indeed, you are the wrongdoers,﴾ and then returned to repeating error, in the state of those whose conditions have changed from standing on their feet to standing on their heads, overturned. This is the depiction of the intelligible by the sensible, and its purpose is reproach.

The preposition "ʿala" indicates elevation, that is, their bodies were raised above their heads, by their bowing down very intensely so that their heads did not appear. The verse admits other possibilities, which al-Zamakhshari (Kashshaf) indicated.

The meaning: then their opinions changed after they had nearly acknowledged Ibrahim's argument, and they returned to obstinacy and defense of the idols. So they said, ﴿You know well that these do not speak﴾, that is, you know that these idols do not speak, so what did you intend by your saying, ﴿So ask them, if they can speak﴾, except to disclaim your offense?

The clause "You know well..." to its end is the quoted speech of an elided verb, indicated by ﴿so they said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers"﴾. The clause ﴿these do not speak﴾ conveys the strengthening of the attribute of lacking speech, because of the absence of its instrument, which is the tongues. The verb "you know" is suspended from governing because of the negation particle after it. When they acknowledged that the idols cannot speak, Ibrahim seized the opportunity to guide them, building upon their admission that they do not speak, with a rhetorical question of denunciation of their worship of them, adding that those idols neither benefit nor harm; and he made their inability to benefit or harm entail their inability to speak, because speech is the means of conveying meaning, and whoever cannot convey meaning is evidently lacking intellect and its concomitants of knowledge, will, and power.

"Uff" is a verb-noun expressing annoyance, derived from the sound of one who is vexed breathing out from the tightness of his breath with anger. The tanwin of "uff" is called tanwin of indefiniteness, and what is meant by it is magnification, that is, a strong annoyance at you. It was mentioned in Surat al-Isra: ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ [al-Isra: 23]. The lam in "lakum" indicates the one on whose account the annoyance is expressed, that is, "Uff for your sake and for the idols you worship besides Allah."

صفحة ١٠٥
The explicit mention of the Name of Majesty is for added clarity and to make the worship of other than Him more repugnant.
He based upon the denunciation and annoyance a rhetorical question of denunciation concerning their failure to reflect upon the clear proofs of reason and the senses, saying, ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾
