This is a gradual step toward the proof of God's oneness. Thus Ibrahim, in denying that he was the doer, intended to lay upon them the burden of proof against the divinity of the great idol, and against the divinity of the smashed idols a fortiori, with the intention that they would acknowledge all of this as false and become certain that he was the one who smashed the idols, and that if they were gods they would have defended themselves, and if their chief were the chief of gods he would have defended his entourage and allies. For this reason he said, ﴿So ask them, if they can speak﴾, mocking them and implying that what cannot speak or express itself is unfit for divinity.

The pronoun in "ask them" includes all the idols, both those that were smashed and those that remained standing. Although the people knew that the idols had not spoken before, Ibrahim intended to convince them that such a great event requires that they speak and identify who did it to them. This is analogous to the reasoning of the scholars of kalam that the miracle indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger, since God does not break habit to confirm a liar; thus His creating something beyond habit at the Messenger's challenge is evidence that God intended to confirm him.

As for what is related in the Sahih from Abu Hurayra that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Ibrahim did not lie except three lies, two of them concerning God, Mighty and Majestic: his saying, ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his saying, ﴿Rather, this one, their chief, did it﴾. And while he was one day with Sarah, he came upon one of the tyrants, and it was said to him: 'Here is a man with a woman among the most beautiful of people.' So he sent for him and said, 'Who is this?' He said, 'My sister.' Then he came to Sarah and said, 'O Sarah, there is no believer on the face of the earth except me and you, and this one asked me, and I told him you are my sister, so do not contradict me.'" . . . And he related the hadith.

Its meaning is that he lied in his answer to the words of his people, ﴿Did you do this to our gods?﴾, when he said, ﴿Rather, this one, their chief, did it﴾, because "bal" when it follows a question conveys the negation of what is asked about. So their words, ﴿Did you do this?﴾, were a question about his being the smasher of the idols; when he said "bal," he negated that about himself, and this negation contradicts reality and his belief, so it is a lie. Yet lying is blameworthy and forbidden, and it is permitted out of necessity, as Ibrahim said. This reversal was a preparation for the proof, with the intention that the truth would become clear to them in the end. For this reason he said, ﴿Do you then worship, besides Allah, that which neither benefits you at all nor harms you?﴾, and so on.

As for the statement, ﴿this one, their chief, did it﴾, it is not a lie, even though it contradicts reality and the speaker's belief, because speech and reports are established by their endings and what follows them, like speech followed by a condition or an exception. When he intended to warn them of the error of worshipping the idols, he prepared for that with a statement that proceeds on the basis of supposition and assumption. It is as if he said: "If this were a god, he would not have been content with aggression against his partners. When the aggression against them occurred in the presence of their chief, it became necessary that he be the doer." Then he advanced in the argument by negating divinity from all of them with his saying, ﴿if they can speak﴾, as has been explained.

The meaning of the hadith, then, is that these were lies at the outset, and that upon reflection their purpose becomes evident. The reason for the prohibition of lying is the deception of the addressee and what results from a false report, namely that actions proceed on the assumption that reality is other than it is. When a statement is followed by truth, it is not lying, but rather allusion, jest, or the like.

As for what occurs in the hadith of intercession, where Ibrahim says, "I am not fit for that," and mentions lies he told, its meaning is that he mentions having spoken words contrary to reality without God's permission by revelation; but he committed a statement contrary to reality out of the necessity of argument according to his own reasoning, and he feared that his reasoning would not coincide with the correct aim of God, so he feared God's rebuke and freed himself from that position.

صفحة ١٠٣
His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So they returned to themselves﴾, may mean that some of them returned to others, that is, some of them turned to address one another and turned away from addressing Ibrahim, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿then greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61], and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa: 29]; that is, some of them said to others, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers."
The plural pronouns are intended distributively, as in: "The people rode their animals." It may also mean that each one returned to himself, that is, he set aside consideration of the accusation against Ibrahim and reflected on Ibrahim's defense. Thus it became clear to each of them that Ibrahim was innocent, so some of them said to others, ﴿Indeed, you are the wrongdoers﴾, and the plural pronouns remain on their usual basis. The sentence conveys restriction, that is, "you are the wrongdoers, not Ibrahim," because you attached the accusation to him, that he wronged our idols, while the apparent course was that we should ask them about who did this to them; and it appears that the doer was their chief.

The "returning to themselves," according to the two previous possibilities, is a metaphor for the mind being occupied with something after it had been occupied with another, as a man returns to his house after going out to another place. The verb "nukisu" is passive, that is, "nakasahum nakis" (someone turned them over), and since there was no doer of that overturning except themselves, the verb was made passive and came to mean "they overturned upon their heads." This is an image.

Naks is turning the top of a thing to its bottom and its bottom to its top. It is said: "The thief was crucified upside down," that is, with his head placed directly on the ground, which is the most hideous posture of the crucified. Since the normal posture of the human body is to stand upright on its feet, when it is inverted its standing becomes as if on its head. So his saying here, ﴿they were turned back upon their heads﴾, is an image for the change of their opinion from the right course, just as they said, ﴿Indeed, you are the wrongdoers,﴾ and then returned to repeating error, in the state of those whose conditions have changed from standing on their feet to standing on their heads, overturned. This is the depiction of the intelligible by the sensible, and its purpose is reproach.

The preposition "ʿala" indicates elevation, that is, their bodies were raised above their heads, by their bowing down very intensely so that their heads did not appear. The verse admits other possibilities, which al-Zamakhshari (Kashshaf) indicated.

The meaning: then their opinions changed after they had nearly acknowledged Ibrahim's argument, and they returned to obstinacy and defense of the idols. So they said, ﴿You know well that these do not speak﴾, that is, you know that these idols do not speak, so what did you intend by your saying, ﴿So ask them, if they can speak﴾, except to disclaim your offense?

The clause "You know well..." to its end is the quoted speech of an elided verb, indicated by ﴿so they said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers"﴾. The clause ﴿these do not speak﴾ conveys the strengthening of the attribute of lacking speech, because of the absence of its instrument, which is the tongues. The verb "you know" is suspended from governing because of the negation particle after it. When they acknowledged that the idols cannot speak, Ibrahim seized the opportunity to guide them, building upon their admission that they do not speak, with a rhetorical question of denunciation of their worship of them, adding that those idols neither benefit nor harm; and he made their inability to benefit or harm entail their inability to speak, because speech is the means of conveying meaning, and whoever cannot convey meaning is evidently lacking intellect and its concomitants of knowledge, will, and power.

"Uff" is a verb-noun expressing annoyance, derived from the sound of one who is vexed breathing out from the tightness of his breath with anger. The tanwin of "uff" is called tanwin of indefiniteness, and what is meant by it is magnification, that is, a strong annoyance at you. It was mentioned in Surat al-Isra: ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ [al-Isra: 23]. The lam in "lakum" indicates the one on whose account the annoyance is expressed, that is, "Uff for your sake and for the idols you worship besides Allah."

صفحة ١٠٥
The explicit mention of the Name of Majesty is for added clarity and to make the worship of other than Him more repugnant.
He based upon the denunciation and annoyance a rhetorical question of denunciation concerning their failure to reflect upon the clear proofs of reason and the senses, saying, ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verses 68–69:**

﴿They said: "Burn him, and support your gods, if you are going to act."﴾ ﴿We said: "O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham."﴾

When he (Abraham) overcame them with the overwhelming argument, they found no means of rescue except by destroying him. Likewise, when the proof of its falsehood strikes the falsehood of the one who upholds error, he becomes angry at the one who holds the truth, and he has no refuge left but to oppose him and to take revenge on him, just as the polytheists of Quraysh did with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when they were unable to counter him. Abraham's people chose that his destruction be by burning, because fire is the most terrifying and most horrible punishment.

Al-tahriq (burning) is an intensified form of harq (burning), meaning burning that destroys.

The saying concerning his burning is attributed to all of them, because they accepted this proposal and asked their king, Nimrod, to burn Abraham, and he ordered his burning, since the infliction of punishment by destroying lives belongs only to the rulers of peoples. It has been said that the one who proposed the opinion of burning Abraham was a man of the people, a Kurd named Hinun, and the people approved of it; and the one who ordered the burning was Nimrod. Thus the imperative in their words "burn him" is used in the sense of consultation.

It appears that this saying was a secret plot among them, without Abraham being present, and that they devised it to surprise him with it, fearing that he would flee, in accordance with the words of the Exalted: ﴿And they intended a plot against him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 70].

As for this Nimrod, they say that he was the son of Kush, son of Ham, son of Noah. This is not correct, because of the great distance between the time of Abraham and the time of Kush. The correct view is that Nimrod was from the descendants of (Kush), and it is possible that the word "Nimrod" was a title for the king of the Chaldeans and not a proper name. What is presumed in history is that the king of the city of Ur in the time of Abraham was (Alghaa ibn Ukhraj), who is the one mentioned earlier at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Supporting the gods means avenging them by destroying their enemy.

The meaning of ﴿if you are going to act﴾ is: if you are going to give support. This is an incitement and a kindling of their zeal.

The clause ﴿We said: "O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham."﴾ is separated from the one before it, either because it came as a response to their saying "burn him," so it resembles the clauses of dialogue, or because it is a resumption answering a question that arises from the story of the conspiracy to burn him, and by this a further clause must be supposed, namely: so they threw him into the fire; We said: "O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham." Allah manifested this as a miracle for Abraham, when He directed to the fire the will to deprive it of the power to burn, and to make it cool and safe, if the statement is taken literally; or He removed from Abraham's temperament the effect of the fire's heat, if the statement is taken as an eloquent metaphor, meaning: be like coolness in not burning what is thrown into you, by your heat.

As for its being "safe," this is literally and undoubtedly true. The mention of "safe" after "cool" serves as a safeguard, because coolness, if it persists and grows intense, may be harmful; so the mention of safety follows the mention of coolness for this reason. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Had He not said that, its coolness would have destroyed him." He mentioned "cool" and then followed it with "safe," and did not limit himself to "cool," in order to show the wondrous workmanship of power, since He turned the fire into coolness. And "for Abraham" is governed by both "cool" and "safe." This is more emphatic in bringing about the benefit of both for him. It is also permissible for it to be connected to the verb "be."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 70:

Page 107
﴿And they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers.﴾

Calling their resolve to burn him a "scheme" (kayd) implies that they plotted this in secret from him, and perhaps their aim in this was that he would not flee the city, so that the victory for their gods would not be complete.

Al-akhsarun (the greatest losers): this is an intensive form of al-khasir (the loser). It is an elative form (ism al-tafdil) from which the sense of comparison has been removed.

The definiteness of the two parts of the sentence (al-akhsarin, "the greatest losers," with the definite article on both the predicate and its object) conveys restriction (qasr). It is a restriction for emphasis, as though their loss could not be matched by any other loss, and as though they alone were characterized by the description of "the greatest losers," so that this description does not apply to anyone else. By "loss" (khasara) is meant failure (khayba), and their failure is called a loss by way of metaphor (isti'arah), likening the failure of their purpose to burn him to the failure of a merchant in his trade, as the words of the Exalted indicate: ﴿And they intended a scheme against him﴾, that is, "so they failed with a great failure." This is because there was gathered for them, through their failure, that Ibrahim was safe from the effect of their punishment, even though what they had prepared for punishment became a miracle and a confirmation for Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

As for the severity of the loss implied by the elative form, it is in what befell them after that of punishment, since God empowered over them a punishment, as the words of the Exalted in Surat al-Hajj indicate: ﴿Then I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them, and how was My rejection?﴾ [al-Hajj: 44]. The people of Ibrahim were counted among them, but I have not seen anyone interpret that seizing in an acceptable way. The apparent view is that God empowered over them the Assyrians, who took their lands, and the kingdom of the Chaldeans came to an end and was succeeded by the Assyrians. History has established that the Elamites, from the people of Susa, dominated the lands of the Chaldeans during the lifetime of Ibrahim, around the year 2286 BC.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verses 71–73:

﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds.﴾ ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous.﴾ ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat; and they were worshippers of Us.﴾

Page 108

This is a second deliverance after his deliverance from the harm of the Fire: it is his deliverance from being settled among a people who were his enemies, unbelievers in his Lord and theirs, and it is a deliverance from the abode of polytheism and corruption of belief. This was by God making his emigration easy for him from the lands of the Chaldeans to the land of Palestine, which is the land of Canaan.

The emigration of Abraham was the first emigration on earth for the sake of religion. Abraham took with him Lot, the son of his brother (Haran), because he had believed in what Abraham brought. Sarah, the wife of Abraham, was also with them, and her companionship was understood from the fact that a man does not emigrate except with his wife.

Lot is in the accusative as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), not as a direct object (maf'ul bihi), because Lot was not himself threatened by the enemies, so that the act of deliverance (al-inja') would attach to him.

The verb (najjaynahu) implies the meaning of bringing out (al-ikhraj), so it is followed by the preposition (ila).

As for "the land," it is the land of Palestine, and God described it as one which He blessed for all the worlds, that is, for the people, meaning its inhabitants, because God created it a land of fertility, abundant living and security. It is mentioned in the Torah that God said to Abraham: "It flows with milk and honey."

Blessing (al-barakah) is abundance of good and benefit. It was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 96] in Surat Al 'Imran.

The gift of Isaac to him is an increase granted to him in old age, after his wife Sarah had despaired of childbearing.

Page 109

The gift of Jacob is an increase to Isaac, son of Abraham, during the lifetime of Abraham, and Abraham seeing him as a righteous adult.

Al-nafilah is an additional gift that was not promised. Abraham had asked his Lord, saying ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 100], meaning a son, and Ishmael was born to him, as in Surat al-Saffat. Then Isaac was born to him without request, as in Surat Hud, so he was an additional gift; and Jacob was born to Isaac, so he too was an additional gift.

"Nafilah" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) whose governing verb is (wahabna), so it is a state of Isaac and Jacob; the rule for circumstantial phrases following plural nouns is that they refer back to all of them.

The tanwin of (kullan) is a substitute for the genitive complement omitted (iwad 'an al-mudaf ilayhi). The meaning is: and We made each of them righteous, that is, We made their souls righteous. What is intended is Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, since they are the ones the preceding discussion was about. As for Lot, he was mentioned by way of accompaniment and will be singled out for mention after this verse.

The repetition of the verb (ja'ala) in His saying ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾, rather than saying "and leaders who guide," by coordinating (a'immah) with (al-salihin), is for the sake of emphasis on this noble making, namely, making them guides for people after having made them righteous in themselves. The verb is repeated so that it may have greater stability, and because repeating the verb entails repeating the first object, so that repetition serves as a means to mentioning the first object again; and in that repetition there is the care that there is in the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, as becomes apparent to the sensitive taste.

Al-a'immah is the plural of imam, which means a model and one who acts as he acts. The original sense of imam is the pattern according to whose form a thing is made, for good or for evil.

Page 110

The clause (yahduna) in the position of a circumstantial state restricts the meaning of leadership, meaning that they were leaders of guidance and direction. His saying (li-amrina) means that they were guiding by God's command, which is revelation, in addition to the making.

In al-Kashshaf: "In this is that whoever is fit to be a model in the religion of God, guidance is incumbent upon him; he is commanded with it, and it is not for him to neglect it or be slack about it. The first part of that is that he be guided himself, because the benefit of his guidance is more general, and souls are more inclined to be guided by one who is guided." End of quotation. This guidance is the purification of people's souls, their reform, and the spreading of faith, and it includes the matters of faith and its branches and its manners.

As for His saying ﴿And We revealed to them the doing of good deeds﴾, this is the establishment of the laws of religion among people, of acts of worship and dealings. His saying "the doing of good deeds" encompasses them.

(Fi'l al-khayrat) is a verbal noun (masdar) in construct with (al-khayrat), and it is necessarily construed as an object-genitive, since al-khayrat are the things done, not the doers. So the verbal noun here stands in the position of a passive verb, because the intended thing is its object, while the agent is secondary to it, meaning that they themselves should do, and their people should do, good deeds, so that good deeds become the object for all people. The agent is omitted for generality together with brevity, since the object requires it. Treating the verbal noun as the verbal noun of a passive verb is permissible when the context indicates it. This is what the practice of al-Zamakhshari suggests. Al-Akhfash, however, permitted it without condition. It is also possible that (fi'l al-khayrat) is itself what was revealed, meaning: and We revealed to them this speech, so the verbal noun stands in place of the verb and is meant as a command, the sense being: "Do good deeds," as in His saying ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

Page 111

The specification of the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat by mention after the inclusion of good deeds of them is an honouring of their status, because through prayer is the righteousness of the soul, since prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing, and through zakat is the righteousness of society, by meeting the need of the needy. This is a pointer to the basis of the ḥanifiyyah with which Abraham, peace be upon him, was sent.

The meaning of the revelation concerning the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat is that the command to do these was revealed to them, as is clear. Then He singled them out by mentioning what they were distinguished by over the rest of people: the constant devotion to God, Exalted is He, as indicated by the verb of being, which conveys the firmness of the attribute, and as indicated by the placing of the prepositional phrase before its object, showing that they devoted worship to God alone, never worshipping anyone else, as the rank of prophethood requires, being protected from worshipping other than God from the time of accountability, as Joseph said ﴿It is not for us to associate anything with God﴾ [Yusuf: 38], and as God, Exalted is He, said in praise of Abraham ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 78:**

﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field, when the sheep of the people grazed in it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment.﴾ ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon, and to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79]

This begins the enumeration of a group of prophets who were not messengers (rusul). In singling them out for mention, what has been observed is the distinction that God bestowed upon each of them, in keeping with the mention of what God favoured Moses and Aaron with, namely the giving of the Book resembling the Qur'an, and what followed that. After Moses, among the Children of Israel, there was no era with a distinction like that of David and Solomon, since the affairs of the community of the Children of Israel had evolved from being governed by prophets, from the time of Joshua son of Nun, and then, after the death of Samson until the rise of Saul, the son-in-law of David, by the disorder that befell them. Saul was a king whose authority was confined to commanding the army, and was not a prophet. As for the management of affairs, it belonged to the prophets and to judges such as Samuel.

David was the first among the prophets of the Children of Israel in whom prophethood and kingship were combined. The kingdom of Israel, in David's time, reached a great degree of might and strength and the subjugation of enemies. David was given the Psalms (al-Zabur), which contain wisdom and admonition, and so it was a completion of the Torah (al-Tawrah), which had been a teaching of law. Thus the time of David completed wisdom and the subtleties of speech.

Solomon was given wisdom, and craftsmen and innovators were subjected to him. Thus the state of Israel in his time completed the grandeur of order, wealth, wisdom and commerce. In their story there is therefore a lesson. That story was arranged within this noble thread: the thread of the giving of the criterion (al-Furqan), guidance, rectitude, direction to good, judgment and knowledge.

In the story of David and Solomon there is an alert to the principle of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning, the exertion of the jurist to reach a ruling), and to the jurisprudence of judgment. For this reason David and Solomon were singled out for some detail of their accounts. Thus "David" is coordinated with "Noah" in His saying "and Noah", meaning: We gave David and Solomon judgment and knowledge when they judged... to the end of the verse. So "when they judged" (إذْ يَحْكُمانِ) is connected to the omitted "We gave" (آتَيْنا), meaning: the time of their judging in the matter of the field was a manifestation of their judgment and their work.

"Judgment" (الحُكْم) means wisdom (الحِكْمَة), which is prophethood. "Knowledge" (العِلْم) means the root of understanding. "When the sheep... grazed" (وإذْ نَفَشَتْ) is connected to "they judged" (يَحْكُمانِ).

This case which the verse contains is a manifestation of justice and of the utmost precision of the jurisprudence of judgment, and of the combining of interests and details among the levels of ijtihad, and of the variety of the ways of judging by the truth, even though the truth is attained by the one who is right. Its import is that it is the jurisprudence in the religion which the messengers before had brought.

Its summary is that David sat to judge between the people, and his son Solomon at that time was a youth, so he would sit outside the door of the house of judgment. Two men brought a dispute to David: one of them was a worker in a field belonging to a group, in crops or a vineyard, and the other was a shepherd of sheep belonging to a group. The sheep entered the field by night and destroyed what was in it. David ruled that the sheep should be given to the owners of the field, since the value of those sheep equalled the value of what had been lost from that field. When he gave this judgment and the two litigants went out, the matter was related to Solomon, and he said: "If I were the judge, I would have judged otherwise than this." This reached David, so he summoned him and said: "By what would you judge?" He said: "I saw what was more gentle to all." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "That the owners of the sheep should take the field, and their worker should tend it and restore it for a full year until it returns to what it was, and return it to its owners; and that the owners of the field should take the sheep, which are to be handed over to their shepherd, so that they benefit from their milk, their wool and their offspring during that period. Then, when the field is complete and returns to its former state, each party is given back what was theirs." David said: "You have been granted success, my son." And he judged between them accordingly.

The meaning of "the sheep... grazed in it" (نَفَشَتْ فِيهِ) is that they entered it by night. They said: al-Nafsh is the straying of livestock for grazing by night. The sheep are attributed to "the people" (القَوْم) because they belonged to a group of people, as is taken from His saying, exalted is He, "the sheep of the people" (غَنَمُ القَوْمِ). Likewise, the field was a partnership among persons, as is taken from what Ibn Kathir reported in his commentary from Masruq, from the transmission of Ibn Abi Hatim. This is also the apparent sense of the exposition of al-Kashshaf. As for what came in other reports concerning mention of two men, it is to be understood that the two who attended the dispute were the shepherd of the sheep and the worker of the field.

Know that what is implied by the coordination of David and Solomon with Abraham, and by His saying "and We were witnesses to their judgment", that is, knowing, and by His saying, exalted is He, "and to each We gave judgment and knowledge" [al-Anbiya: 79], and what is implied by the occurrence of the two judgments in one case and at one time, is that the two judgments were not from a revelation from God; rather, they were from knowledge which David and Solomon were given. That is judgment by ijtihad, and it applies according to the correct opinion regarding the permissibility of ijtihad for the prophets and for our Prophet (ﷺ), and its occurrence in various matters.

The judgment of David was correct, because it rests on imposing compensation for damages upon those who were negligent in the matter of the sheep, and the basis of compensation is that it be immediate restitution; so that judgment was correct. It suffices you that it agrees with what the Sunnah has brought concerning the destruction caused by livestock.

The judgment of Solomon was correct, because it rests on giving the right to its rightful owners together with showing kindness to those whose rights are held by deferring their enjoyment of their property for a time. So it resembles reconciliation (al-sulh). Perhaps the owners of the sheep had no other livelihood, as is usually the case, and both litigants were content with Solomon's judgment, because both disputants were people of equity, not of oppression. Had they not been content, the matter would have reverted to the judgment of David, since kindness is not obligatory. A parallel to this is the judgment of Umar ibn al-Khattab against Muhammad ibn Maslama, that the water from al-'Uraid should pass over his land to the land of al-Dahhak ibn Khalifa. Umar said to Muhammad ibn Maslama: "Why do you prevent your brother from what benefits him, when it is beneficial to you as well?" Muhammad said: "No, by God." Umar said: "By God, it shall pass through it even if it be over your belly." So al-Dahhak did it. This was because Umar knew that both of them were people of merit, and that they would consent to what he resolved upon them. So the judgment of Solomon was the more preponderant.

This case resembles the judgment of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) between al-Zubayr and an Ansari concerning irrigation from the water-channels of al-Harra, when he first judged that al-Zubayr should hold back the water until it reaches the ankles, and then release the water to his neighbour. When the Ansari was not content, the Messenger of God judged that al-Zubayr should hold back the water until it reaches the walls, and then release it, and so al-Zubayr received his full right. The Prophet (ﷺ) began with the gentler option, and then, when neither of the two litigants was content, judgment was given between them by the decisive ruling. So the Prophet's judgment began with the better of the two options, in the manner of the judgment of Solomon.

As for the saying of God, exalted is He, "So We gave understanding of it to Solomon" [al-Anbiya: 79], its meaning is that He inspired him with another way of judging which was more preponderant, given what the form of the verb of understanding (al-tafhim) implies of the intensity of the occurrence of the act, more than the form of conveying understanding (al-ifham). This indicates that Solomon's understanding of the case was deeper. That is because it was gentler to both of them; and the matter was one in which two indications pull in different directions, so one resorts to preponderance (al-tarjih). The factors of preponderance are not confined, and they may not appear to the mujtahid. God, exalted is He, willed to manifest Solomon's knowledge to his father so that his joy in him would increase, and so that he would be consoled for the sons he had lost before Solomon was born. It suffices you that it agrees with the judgment of the Prophet in the case of al-Zubayr. There is room for ijtihad in the conflict of evidences.

This verse is a foundation for the difference of ijtihad, for acting upon the preponderant opinion, for the levels of preponderance, and for the excuse of the mujtahid if he errs in his ijtihad or does not discover the opposing evidence, in view of His saying, exalted is He, "and to each We gave judgment and knowledge" [al-Anbiya: 79], in the context of praising both of them.

In the remainder of the story there is what is suitable to be a foundation for a judge's retraction from his ruling, as Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-'Arabi said. However, the verse does not contain that, nor has the sound Sunnah brought it, so it should not be taken as a foundation; and what the two of them attempted in this regard was an oversight.

The attribution of "judgment" (حُكْم) to the plural pronoun is in consideration of the gathering of the judges and the litigants. As for the feminine pronoun in His saying "So We gave understanding of it" (فَفَهَّمْناها), with no feminine-form noun having preceded it to which it refers, it is according to the interpretation of "judgment" in His saying, exalted is He, "for their judgment" (لِحُكْمِهِمْ), in the sense of adjudication or dispute.

The clause "and to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge" [al-Anbiya: 79] is a concluding clause (تذييل) serving as a safeguard, to repel the supposition that David's judgment was an error or injustice, and that Solomon's judgment was only more correct.

The biography of David, peace be upon him, has already been given at His saying, exalted is He, "And We gave David a Psalter" [al-Nisa: 163] in surah al-Nisa, and at His saying, "and among his offspring, David" [al-An'am: 84] in surah al-An'am.

The biography of Solomon, peace be upon him, has already been given at His saying, exalted is He, "and they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon" [al-Baqarah: 102] in surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 79:

﴿And We subjected the mountains to celebrate Our praise along with David, and the birds too; and We were the Doers.﴾

This is a distinction specific to David: the subjection of the mountains to him. What explains it is the clause (yusabbihna, "they glorify"), so it is either an explanation (bayan) of the clause (sakhkharna, "We subjected") or a explanatory circumstantial clause (hal mubayyinah). Its mention here is digression (istitrad) and incorporation (idmaj). (Wal-tayra, "and the birds") is conjoined to (al-jibal, "the mountains"), or is a object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), meaning "along with the birds," i.e., the birds of the mountains. (Ma'a, "with") is an adverbial complement attached to the verb (yusabbihna), and it was placed before its complement for emphasis, to highlight the honour of David. The meaning is: when David glorified God among the mountains, he would hear the mountains glorifying in the same manner as his glorification. This is the sense of (ta'wib, "repeated returning") in His other verse, ﴿O mountains, echo with him [in praise]﴾ [Saba': 10], since ta'wib means repetition of the refrain, derived from (awb), which is return. Likewise the birds, when they hear his glorification, sing in a melody like his glorification; all of these are a miracle (mu'jizah) for him.

It must be that this subjection was granted to him after he was given prophethood (nubuwwah), as the context of its enumeration among the proofs of honour (karamah) God gave the prophets requires. Nothing is known of David, after he was given prophethood, practising the climbing of mountains or herding in them, although before prophethood he had been a shepherd. So perhaps this subjection occurred during his wandering (siyahah) in the mountain wilderness of "Zayf," which has a cave to which David would retreat with his companions who gathered around him during that wandering, at the time he went out fleeing from King "Saul (Talut)," when Saul turned against him through the slander of some of David's envious rivals, as is related in chapters 23–24 of the First Book of Samuel. This is the secret of the expression with (ma'a) attached to the verb (sakhkharna, "We subjected") here. In the verse of Surah Sad there is an indication that it was a subjection of accompaniment (tasakhkhur mutaabaah), not a subjection of service, unlike His later saying ﴿And to Solomon the wind﴾ [al-Anbiya': 81], where the verb of subjection, whose place is taken by the conjunction waw, is transitive by the lam of possession. Likewise the word (ma'a) came in the verse of Surah Saba': ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba': 10].

In this subjection of the mountains and birds, together with its being a miracle for him, there is also honour and care from God toward him, for it gave him companionship through those sounds in his solitude in the mountains and his distance from his family and homeland. The clause (﴿and We were the Doers﴾) is a parenthetical insertion between the report of what David was given, and (fa'il, "doer") here means "able" (qadir), to remove the improbability of the mountains and birds glorifying along with him. The use of the verb of being (kana) indicates that this is an established attribute of God from before, i.e., "and We were able to do that."

[p. 121]

God bestowed a favour through a craft He taught Dawud, from which people benefited, and it is the craft of armour, that is, coats of mail (durū' al-sard). It was said that armour before Dawud had scales of iron (dhāt ḥarāshif), so it was heavy on warriors (al-kumāh) when they wore it. God inspired Dawud to make coats of fine interlocking rings (ḥalaq), which are lighter to carry and better at protection.

In the seventeenth chapter of the First Book of Samuel, Goliath the Philistine went out to duel Dawud wearing scale armour (dir' ḥarshafī). Scale armour was therefore in use in the time of Dawud's youth, and the Arabs adopted coats of mail. This became well known among the Arabs, and Ka'b ibn Zuhayr described it well when he said:

Lofty-nosed heroes, whose garments in battle
Are of the weaving of Dawud, mail-shirts.

Bright, full-length, with rings sewn into them,
Like the rings of the qafā' (a plant), braided.

The Tubba'i armours were famous among the Arabs. Perhaps Tubba' borrowed them from the Children of Israel after Dawud, or perhaps the Tubba'i armours were of the scale type. al-Nabigha gathered them together when he said:

Every smooth Tubba'i coat of mail, and the weaving of Sulaym, every long-sleeved garment that trails.

By Sulaym he meant Sulayman, the son of Dawud, shortened as a diminutive form (tarkhīm). He attributed his father's work to him because he had been storing it.

"Libūs" (لَبُوس), with a fatḥa on the lām, originally is a name for anything worn. It is a fa'ūl in the sense of maf'ūl, like rasūl. Its use became dominant for the iron battle gear worn in war, namely the coat of mail. Therefore the coat of mail is not called libās, but it is called libūs, just as libūs is used for garments. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Libūs in the language means weapons; from it comes the spear, and from it is the saying of the poet, who is Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

And with me is a libūs for the wretched, as if it were
A horn on the forehead of a fleeing herd-owner of ewes."

[p. 122]

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read (لِيُحْصِنَكم) with the yā' (third-person masculine), taking the verb as referring to libūs as its implied subject. Attributing the protecting (iḥṣān) to the libūs is a figurative attribution (isnād majāzī). Ibn 'Amir, Ḥafs on the authority of 'Āṣim, and Abu Ja'far read it with the tā' (second-person), reading libūs as meaning the coat of mail, which is feminine. Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Āṣim, and Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub, read (لِنُحْصِنَكم) with the nūn.

The pronouns of address in (لَكم، لِيُحْصِنَكم، مِن بَأْسِكم، فَهَلْ أنْتُمْ شاكِرُونَ) are directed at the polytheists, following God's words before this: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder that We have sent down; will you then deny it?﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 50], because they neglected to thank God for His blessings, of which this is one, since they worshipped other than Him.

Iḥṣān means protection and defence. Ba's means war.

For this reason, the interrogative in God's words ﴿So will you be thankful?﴾ is used to express surprise at the lack of gratitude, and it is a metaphorical way of commanding gratitude. The departure from placing the interrogative (hal) before a verbal sentence to a nominal sentence, although hal has a greater affinity with the verb, is notable: he did not say "fa-hal tashkurūn" ("will you give thanks"), but moved to ﴿fa-hal antum shākirūn﴾, so that the shift from the verbal to the nominal form would indicate what the nominal form implies of firmness and continuity, meaning: "Has your gratitude been established and confirmed?" This is because repeated gratitude is what is expected in return for this blessing, like God's words ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 91] in the verse on the prohibition of wine.

[p. 123]

This is a coordinated clause (ʿaṭf, grammatical conjunction) following the sentence ﴿And We subjected the mountains to celebrate Our praises along with Dawud﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79], because both narratives contain an extraordinary subjugation of nature as a miracle for the two Prophets, peace be upon them.

The land that Allah has blessed is the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). The subjugation of the wind is its subjugation to what suits it, which is the sailing of ships on the sea. The meaning is that it flows toward al-Sham, returning from the regions it went out to for the interests of Sulayman's kingdom, whether for military campaigns or trade. This is indicated by the fact that it is subjected to Sulayman, so it must be moving for the benefit of the community of which he is king.

From the statement that it flows toward the land that Allah has blessed, it is understood that it leaves that land carrying the troops, or exporting the goods that the kingdom of Sulayman exports to the lands of the earth, and it returns with provisions, supplies, materials for manufacturing, and weapons for the army, to the land of Filastin (Palestine). Thus, in the speech there is an elision (iktifaʾ, omission of what is understood), relying on the contextual indicator (qarina). The same has been stated explicitly in the verse of Surat Saba, where the omitted part is mentioned: ﴿And for Sulayman, the wind: its morning course is a month's journey and its evening course is a month's journey﴾ [Saba: 12].

Its description here as ʿasifa (عاصفة), meaning strong, and its description in Surat Sad as rukhaʾ (رخاء), gentle, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We subjected to him the wind, flowing gently by his command wherever he directed﴾ [Sad: 36].

Rukhaʾ means the mild breeze suitable for the motion of ships. This varies according to conditions: when he wished to speed the journey, it moved strongly (ʿasifa), and when he wished gentleness, it moved gently (rukhaʾ). The context is an indicator that the intended meaning is compliance with Sulayman's will, as indicated by His saying, ﴿flowing by his command﴾, in both verses. This suggests that his purpose from it varies, as when he himself was riding on the sea, he wished it to be gentle so that it would not disturb him, and when his kingdom was exporting goods or importing them, it moved strongly. This is clear upon reflection. The expression "by his command" (bi-amrihi) refers to his desire and what suits the voyages of his ships. These are regular seasonal winds (riyah mawsimiyya, monsoon winds) that Allah subjected for him.

The command of Sulayman is his supplication to Allah that He make the wind move as Sulayman wishes. It is either a general supplication, like His saying: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾ [Sad: 35], which includes everything by which the affairs of the kingdom and its changing circumstances are kept in order; or it is a specific supplication at every journey for the ships of Sulayman. So Allah made the seasonal winds in the seas of Filastin during the reign of Sulayman, as an honour to him and a support, since his concern was to spread the religion of truth on earth.

Allah made the wind move by the command of Sulayman and did not make it move for his ships alone, because Allah subjected the wind to all the ships in which there is an interest of the kingdom of Sulayman. There came to him the ships of Tarshish, which he thought were Tartusha in al-Andalus or Qartajanna in Ifriqiya, and the ships of Hiram, king of Sur (Tyre), carrying gold, silver, ivory, monkeys, peacocks, and gifts of vessels, robes, weapons, perfume, horses, and mules, as in the tenth chapter of the First Book of Kings.

The sentence ﴿And We were, of all things, Knowing﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) between the sentences put forward to mention Allah's care for Sulayman. The connection is that the subjugation of the wind for the interests of Sulayman is one of the effects of Allah's knowledge of the varying conditions of nations and regions, and of what among them is suitable for the interest of Sulayman. So He directs affairs according to the wisdom that He willed, exalted is He, when He said: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾ [Sad: 20].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 82:**

﴿And among the devils were those who dived for him and performed other work besides that. And We were their guardian.﴾

This is a mention of a miracle and a mark of honour (karamah) for Sulayman (Solomon). It is that God subjected to him the immaterial powers (al-quwa al-mujarradah, i.e. unembodied beings) from among the classes of jinn and devils, who were capable of carrying out great works, such as diving into the seas to extract pearls and coral, and other works that were summarised in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they performed other work besides that﴾. Some of these were detailed in other verses, such as His words, exalted is He, (﴿They made for him whatever he wished: sanctuaries, statues, bowls like water-troughs, and fixed cooking pots﴾ [Saba: 13]). These are well-known kinds of work. Sulayman was singled out for their greatness, such as the building of the Temple of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and for the speed with which they were completed.

The meaning of ﴿And We were their guardian﴾ is that God, by His power, subjected them to Sulayman and prevented them from escaping from him or disobeying him. He made them work in secrecy and not harm anyone among the people. Thus God, in His wisdom, combined their subjection to Sulayman with His knowledge of how to govern them, make use of them and keep them obedient. He made them submissive to him and engaged in his service without hardship to him, and He stood between them and the people so that they would not harm them. When Sulayman died, God did not subject the jinn to anyone else, in response to his supplication when he said, ﴿Grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾ [Sad: 35]. When "God empowered the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ over the jinni who nearly ruined his prayer and who intended to tie him up, he recalled the supplication of Sulayman and released him," God combined for him empowerment over the jinn with the fulfilment of Sulayman's desire. The phrase (lahum) is connected to (hafizin), and the lam is the lam of reinforcement (lam al-taqwiyah, the emphasising lam). The underlying construction is: "guarding them," that is, preventing them from [harming] the people.

[Page 126]

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with Dawud and Sulayman, meaning: "And We gave Ayyub wisdom and knowledge when he called out to his Lord." Singling him out with the mention of what was mentioned before is because of the patience he was specially known for, to the point that he became a proverbial example of it. The biography of Ayyub has already been given in Surat al-Anʿam.

[Page 127]

As for the story to which this verse alludes, it is detailed in the book named after Ayyub among the Israelite prophetic books (asfar al-anbiyaʾ). Its summary is that he was a prophet, possessed of vast wealth and a righteous, enduring family. Then he was afflicted with calamities that struck his property one after another until they consumed it. He lost his seven sons and three daughters on a single day, and he received all of this with patience and submission. Then he was afflicted with sores on his body, and he received all of that with patience and wisdom, while he devoutly called upon God with glorification and supplication for the removal of the harm. He also received the lamentation of his companions over his condition with words of profound wisdom and knowledge of God. God revealed to him admonitions. Then God restored his health, gave him more wealth than he had before, and his wife bore him sons and daughters equal in number to those who had died before. His story has been mentioned in more detail here in Surat Sad. The storytellers (ahl al-qaṣaṣ) have exaggerations in it that are not fitting for the station of prophethood.

The word (idh) is an adverbial time expression (ẓarf) restricting the granting to Ayyub of steadfastness of heart and the wisdom of patience, because that time was the clearest manifestation of his knowledge and wisdom, as the story indicates. A similar usage appeared a little earlier at His saying ﴿ونُوحًا إذْ نادى مِن قَبْلُ﴾ (al-Anbiyaʾ: 76). Thus Ayyub became the proverbial example of patience.

As for His saying ﴿أنِّي مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ﴾, the hamza is opened (anna) on the assumption of a preposition bāʾ, meaning: he called upon his Lord that harm had touched him.

The word (massa) means a light touch. Using it is a narration of the courtesy Ayyub observed toward God in his supplication, since he treated the harm that befell him as a light touch.

The word (ḍurr), with a ḍammah on the ḍād, means whatever a person is harmed by in his body, such as illness or emaciation, or in his property, such as loss and the like.

[Page 128]

In His saying ﴿وأنْتَ أرْحَمُ الرّاحِمِينَ﴾ there is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to asking for the removal of the harm without an explicit request. He described himself with what calls for mercy toward him, and he described his Lord with being the most merciful, as an allusion to his request, just as Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"When a man praises you one day, the praise itself suffices him from having to ask."

That God is the most merciful of the merciful is because His mercy is the most perfect mercy, since everyone who shows mercy to another either does so seeking praise in this world, or reward in the Hereafter, or to relieve a passing tenderness of the soul at seeing one who deserves mercy, and so he is not free of seeking some benefit for himself. As for God's mercy toward His servants, it is free of seeking any benefit for His exalted Essence. Because Ayyub's praise was an allusion to supplication, God followed it with His saying ﴿فاسْتَجَبْنا لَهُ فَكَشَفْنا ما بِهِ مِن ضُرٍّ﴾. The sīn and tāʾ (in istajabnā) are for emphasis in answering, meaning: We answered his implicit supplication immediately after his words, and We removed the harm that was upon him, indicating the speed with which the harm was removed from him. Sequence (taʿqīb) is according to the nature of each thing. This is what custom requires regarding recovery from illness, the arrival of provision, and the birth of children.

The word (kashf) is used for swift removal. The removal of established illnesses and harms, which customarily do not go away except after a long time, is likened to removing a covering from a thing in its swiftness.

The relative (mā) in His saying ﴿ما بِهِ مِن ضُرٍّ﴾ is intended to be vague. Then it is explained by (min) used as explicative (bayāniyya), in order to magnify that harm because of the multitude of its kinds, to the extent that enumerating them would be long. A similar usage is His saying ﴿وما بِكم مِن نِعْمَةٍ فَمِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (al-Naḥl: 53), indicating its abundance. Do you not see how it is contrasted with its opposite in His saying ﴿ثُمَّ إذا مَسَّكُمُ الضُّرُّ فَإلَيْهِ تَجْأرُونَ﴾ (al-Naḥl: 53), to convey that they rush to God at the slightest harm and forget to be grateful for great blessings? That is: We removed what had befallen him of harm in his body and his property, so his health and his wealth were restored.

[Page 129]

The (ītāʾ) is giving, meaning: We gave him his family. The word (ahl) of a man means the members of his household and his kin. From the definiteness of (ahl) by its being in construct form, it is understood that the granting is the return of what had been taken from him of family, namely by the death of his sons and daughters. This is on the assumption of a clear omitted noun from the context, meaning: the like of his family, by his being granted children equal in number to what he had lost, and God added to him the like of them. Thus he was granted fourteen sons and six daughters from his wife, who had already reached the age of barrenness.

The word (raḥmatan) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). Mercy is described as being from God in order to exalt its status by mentioning the "nearness" (ʿindiyya), which indicates closeness, meaning here special favour. The mercy intended is mercy to Ayyub, when he said: "And You are the most merciful of the merciful."

The word (dhikrā) means reminder: reminding of what is likely to be forgotten or neglected. It is conjoined to (raḥmatan), so it too is an object of purpose, meaning: and as a reminder to the worshippers that God does not abandon His care for them. And by the generality contained in (al-ʿābidīn, the worshippers), the sentence becomes a concluding generalization (tadhyīl).

Do you not see how it is contrasted with its opposite in His saying ﴿ثُمَّ إذا مَسَّكُمُ الضُّرُّ فَإلَيْهِ تَجْأرُونَ﴾ (al-Naḥl: 53), to convey that they rush to God at the slightest harm and forget to be grateful for great blessings? That is: We removed what had befallen him of harm in his body and his property, so his health and his wealth were restored.

[Page 129]

The (ītāʾ) is giving, meaning: We gave him his family. The word (ahl) of a man means the members of his household and his kin. From the definiteness of (ahl) by its being in construct form, it is understood that the granting is the return of what had been taken from him of family, namely by the death of his sons and daughters. This is on the assumption of a clear omitted noun from the context, meaning: the like of his family, by his being granted children equal in number to what he had lost, and God added to him the like of them. Thus he was granted fourteen sons and six daughters from his wife, who had already reached the age of barrenness.

The word (raḥmatan) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). Mercy is described as being from God in order to exalt its status by mentioning the "nearness" (ʿindiyya), which indicates closeness, meaning here special favour. The mercy intended is mercy to Ayyub, when he said: "And You are the most merciful of the merciful."

The word (dhikrā) means reminder: reminding of what is likely to be forgotten or neglected. It is conjoined to (raḥmatan), so it too is an object of purpose, meaning: and as a reminder to the worshippers that God does not abandon His care for them. And by the generality contained in (al-ʿābidīn, the worshippers), the sentence becomes a concluding generalization (tadhyīl).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verses 85–86:

﴿And Ismail, and Idris, and Dhu al-Kifl; each of them was among the patient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy. Indeed, they were among the righteous.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon (Ayyub); that is, "And We gave Ismail, Idris and Dhu al-Kifl judgment and knowledge." He grouped these three together in one thread because they share the distinguishing quality of patience, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿each of them was among the patient﴾. This arose because of the connection with the mention of the most famous example of patience, Ayyub.

As for the patience of Ismail (peace be upon him), it is established through his patience in accepting the sacrifice, when Ibrahim said to him, ﴿Indeed, I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you﴾ [al-Saffat: 102], and he said, ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. It is also established through his dwelling in a valley without vegetation in compliance with the command of his father, who had received it from Allah, Exalted is He. The biography of Ismail has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for Idris, he is, according to the most probable opinion, the one named "Ukhnukh" (Enoch). Ukhnukh is mentioned in the Torah, in the Book of Genesis, as the grandfather of Nuh. His biography has already been discussed in Surat Maryam, where he was described as a truthful prophet (ṣiddīq nabī). Here Allah, Exalted is He, described him so that he would be counted among the patient. The apparent meaning is that his patience was in pursuing wisdom and knowledge and in the hardships he endured on his journeys. Stories have been related about his patience, among them that he would forgo food and sleep for long periods so that his soul would be clear for attaining wisdom and knowledge.

It has been said that he is "Ilyas," called in the books of the Jews "Elijah," and it has been said that he is the successor of al-Yasaʿ (Elisha) in the prophethood of the Children of Israel. The apparent view is that he is "ʿUbadya" (Obadiah), who has a book among the books of the Jewish prophets, the fourth of the twelve books known as the Books of the Minor Prophets.

He was given this title because he took charge of the affairs of the Children of Israel on behalf of al-Yasaʿ. This is because when al-Yasaʿ grew old, he wished to appoint a successor over the Children of Israel and said: "Whoever will take on for me three things, I will appoint him: that he fasts by day, stands in prayer by night, and does not become angry." No one undertook this for him except a young man named "ʿUbadya," and he remained firm in what he had undertaken, so he was among the greatest of the patient for this. ʿUbadya is generally counted among the prophets of the Children of Israel, as mentioned in the account in the First Book of Kings, chapter 18. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verses 87–88:

﴿Remember Dhu'l-Nun, when he went off in anger, thinking that We would not constrain him. Then he called out in the darknesses: "There is no god but You; glory be to You! Indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and delivered him from distress. Thus do We deliver the believers.﴾

This is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon "wa-Dhā al-Kifl" (and Dhu'l-Kifl). The mention of Dhu'l-Nun among those Prophets who are singled out for mention is because of what the verses narrate of his turning to God, his remorse over what had proceeded from him of impatience (jaza'), and God's answering of him.

"Dhu'l-Nun" (Possessor of the Fish) is a descriptive epithet, meaning the companion of the fish. It was given as a title to Yunus ibn Matta, peace be upon him. His biography has already been given in the commentary on Surat al-An'am, and his story with his people has already been given in the commentary on Surat Yunus. As for his going off in anger: it has been said that it was his departure, angry at his people, the people of Nineveh (Ninawa), when they refused to believe in what he had been sent with, while they were angry at his call. Thus the word "mughadaba" (going off in anger together) is of the form of mufa'ala. This is what is implied by what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said that it was revealed to him that the punishment was descending upon them after a period of time; when that period was about to end, they believed, and he went out angry at the fact that what he had warned them of had not come to pass. In that case, "mughadaba" is for intensification of anger, because it was a strange anger. This is what is implied by what is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Jarir chose it. The more correct view is that "mughadiban" is a circumstantial clause (hal) meant as a simile, i.e., he went out like one who is angry. This meaning will come in Surat al-Saffat.

God's words ﴿fa-zanna an lan naqdira 'alayhi﴾ imply that he went out without having been permitted by God to do so. He thought that if he moved far from the city to which he had been sent, God would send someone other than him to them.

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that Ezekiel (Hizqil), king of Israel, had in his time five prophets, among them Yunus; the king chose him to go to the people of Nineveh to call them, but he refused and said: "There are prophets here other than me," and he went out angry at the king. This is far from the Qur'an in other verses and from the books of the Children of Israel.

The point of the lesson in the verse does not depend on identifying the story.

As for the meaning of ﴿fa-zanna an lan naqdira 'alayhi﴾: it has been said that "naqdira" is the imperfect of qadara 'alayhi amran, in the sense of "to constrict," like His words ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills and constricts [it]﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26] and His words ﴿And whoever has his provision constricted for him, let him spend from what Allah has given him﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]. That is: he thought that We would not constrict upon him the obligation of residing with the people to whom he was sent, or the obligation of carrying out the conveyance of the message; and that when he left that place, the obligation of conveying the message would fall from him through his own ijtihad. Therefore he was reproached with what befell him, since it was incumbent upon him to seek guidance from his Lord regarding what he intended to do.

In al-Kashshaf: Ibn 'Abbas entered upon Mu'awiya, and Mu'awiya said to him: "The waves of the Qur'an struck me last night, and I drowned, and I found no deliverance for myself except through you." He said: "And what is it?" Mu'awiya recited this verse and said: "Does the Prophet of God think that God has no power over him?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "This is from qadar, not from qudra; meaning, constriction upon him."

It has been said that "naqdira" here means "nahkum" (We would judge), derived from qudra (power), i.e., he thought that We would not hold him accountable for leaving among his people without permission. This is narrated from Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi, and it is a report from Ibn 'Abbas; al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj chose it. On this view, Yunus made ijtihad and erred.

On this view, the sequence (tafri') is one of the occurrence of this thought in his mind after leaving had been a hasty act driven by anger, without reflection on its consequences and outcomes. They said: he had a nature of constricted breast.

It has also been said that the meaning of the speech is interrogative, with the interrogative hamza omitted; the estimate being: "Did he think that We would not have power over him?" This is attributed to Sulayman ibn al-Mu'tamir or Abu al-Mu'tamir. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said in his tafsir: "It has been read with this."

In my view there are two other interpretations: that he thought, while inside the belly of the fish, that God would not deliver him from the belly of the fish, since he regarded that as customarily impossible. On this view, the sequence is according to the actual event: he thought after the fish had swallowed him. As for his calling upon his Lord, that was a repentance that issued from him on account of his shortcoming, his haste, or his error of ijtihad. For this reason he said: ﴿Indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾, as an intensification of his acknowledgment of wronging himself. He ascribed to himself the verb of being (kana), which indicates the firmness of the attribute, and made the predicate that he is one of the group of wrongdoers, which is more indicative of the firmness of the attribute. Or [the other possibility]: he thought, according to the usual causes, that he would emigrate from the abode of his people, and did not think that God would prevent him from that, since no revelation from God had preceded it.

"Inni" (Indeed I) explains the verb "nada" (called out). Mentioning the acknowledgment of Tawhid before the glorification (tasbih) is a metonymy for God's singular management and His power over everything.

Al-Zulumat is the plural of zulma. It means the darkness of night, the darkness of the depths of the sea, and the darkness of the belly of the fish. It has been said: "al-zulumat" is an intensive form for the intensity of darkness, like His words ﴿He brings them out from the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqara: 257]. It has already been mentioned that we think the singular "zulma" does not occur alone in the Qur'an.

Al-istijaba is an intensification of ijaba (answering). It is the answering of his repentance for what he had neglected. The deliverance (al-injaʾ) occurred at the moment of the answer, since the correct view is that he remained in the belly of the fish only a short while. The conjunction here is with "wa" (and), unlike the conjunction of "fa-kashafna" upon "fa-istajabna." His deliverance was by decree and creation in the temperament of the fish, until the fish came near the shore and vomited him out, and he came out swimming to the shore.

This fish is of the kind of great fish that swallows large things and does not chew them with its teeth. Among people it became common to call a kind of fish "the fish of Yunus," by guesswork (rajman bi'l-ghayb).

The clause ﴿Thus do We deliver the believers﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil). The reference by "kadhalika" (thus) is to the deliverance by which Yunus was delivered; that is, like that deliverance We deliver the believers from distresses which those who fall into them think their deliverance is difficult. In this there is an allusion to the polytheist Arabs that God delivers the believers from the distress and vexation they encounter from the ill treatment of the polytheists towards them in their lands.

Know that the word "nunji" was written in the mushafs with one nun, just as it was written with one nun in His words in Surat Yusuf ﴿fa-nunji man nasha'﴾ [Yusuf: 110]. Abu 'Ali explained this orthography by saying that since the second nun was sukun and the letter jim following it requires its concealment (ikhfa'), because the sakin nun is concealed before the letters of the "shajariyya" (palatal letters): jim, shin and dad; when it was concealed it was dropped in pronunciation, so its concealment resembled the state of idgham (assimilation), and the scribe of the mushaf omitted it in the writing because of the hiddenness of its pronunciation in speech; that is, just as they omitted the nun of "in" with "la" in such as "illa tafʿaluhu," since it is assimilated into the lam.

The majority of reciters read with both nuns pronounced, so the omission of one of the nuns in the writing is merely an indication of one of the considerations of recitation. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read with one nun and with the jim doubled, on the basis of assimilating the nun into the jim just as it is assimilated into the lam and the ra'. Abu Hatim and al-Zajjaj rejected this reading and said: it is a grammatical error (lahn). Abu 'Ubayd, al-Farra' and Tha'lab justified their reading by saying that the yā' of "nujji" was made sakin and not vocalized, according to the dialect of those who say "baqi" and "radi," making the yā' sakin, as in the reading of al-Hasan (wa-dharu ma baqiya mina al-riba) with sukun on the yā' of "baqi." From Abu 'Ubayd and al-Qutabi: the second nun was assimilated into the jim.

Ibn Jinni, following al-Akhfash al-Saghir, justified it by saying that the original of this reading is "nunajjī" with fatha on the second nun and shaddah on the jim, then the second nun was deleted because of the succession of two identical letters, so it became "nujjī." According to some grammarians, this reading is interpreted as "nujjiya" being a past verb in the passive voice, and that its deputy subject (nā'ib al-fā'il) is a pronoun referring to the deliverance (al-nijā') derived from the verb, or derived from the demonstrative in His words "wa-kadhalika." "Al-mu'minin" is in the accusative as the object, according to the opinion of those who permit the substitution of the verbal noun (maṣdar) in the presence of the object, as in the reading of Abu Ja'far (li-yujza - with fatha on the zay - qawman bi-ma kanu yaksibun), with the estimate li-yujza al-jaza' qawman. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: this justification is a cold and strained reading (bārid al-ta'assuf).
