Abu 'Ubayd, al-Farra' and Tha'lab justified their reading by saying that the yā' of "nujji" was made sakin and not vocalized, according to the dialect of those who say "baqi" and "radi," making the yā' sakin, as in the reading of al-Hasan (wa-dharu ma baqiya mina al-riba) with sukun on the yā' of "baqi." From Abu 'Ubayd and al-Qutabi: the second nun was assimilated into the jim.

Ibn Jinni, following al-Akhfash al-Saghir, justified it by saying that the original of this reading is "nunajjī" with fatha on the second nun and shaddah on the jim, then the second nun was deleted because of the succession of two identical letters, so it became "nujjī." According to some grammarians, this reading is interpreted as "nujjiya" being a past verb in the passive voice, and that its deputy subject (nā'ib al-fā'il) is a pronoun referring to the deliverance (al-nijā') derived from the verb, or derived from the demonstrative in His words "wa-kadhalika." "Al-mu'minin" is in the accusative as the object, according to the opinion of those who permit the substitution of the verbal noun (maṣdar) in the presence of the object, as in the reading of Abu Ja'far (li-yujza - with fatha on the zay - qawman bi-ma kanu yaksibun), with the estimate li-yujza al-jaza' qawman. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: this justification is a cold and strained reading (bārid al-ta'assuf).

[Page 135]

﴿And Zechariah, when he called out to his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone, though You are the best of inheritors." So We answered him and gave him John, and We made his wife fit for childbearing.﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 90]

The matter of Zechariah, to which His saying ﴿when he called out to his Lord﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 83] alluded, was a sign from the signs of God in His care for His devotees who devoted themselves to His worship, so he was singled out for mention for this reason. The discussion of the conjunction (ʿatf) of "and Zechariah" is the same as the discussion of its preceding counterparts. The clause ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone﴾ explains the clause "called out to his Lord." The word "alone" (fard) was applied to one who has no child, as a comparison to a person who is single with no companion. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾ [Maryam: 95]. It is similarly said: "the wāḥid (one)" for one who has no companion. Al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām said:

*"And I know that if I fight alone, I will be killed, and my presence will not harm my enemy."*

Thus one who has no child is likened to the single one (mufrad), because a child makes his father like a shaf‘ (a pair), since the child is like a part of him. One does not say of a man with a child that he has a zawj (spouse) or a shaf‘ (pair).

The clause ﴿and You are the best of inheritors﴾ is a praise intended to prepare the way for the answer, meaning: You are the true Inheritor, so decide for me something from Your exalted attribute. It has become common in the Book and the Sunnah to mention one of God's attributes when asking Him for something of its kind, as Ayyub said, "and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful." The mention of this indicates that he asked for a child so that the child would inherit from him, as in the verse of Surah Maryam: ﴿who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya‘qub﴾ [Maryam: 6]. This clause has been omitted here because the narrated context points to it. The implied meaning: "let him inherit from me the inheritance that cannot approach Your inheritance of Your servants," that is, the remaining of what they left in this world by the disposal of Your power; or "let him inherit my wealth and my knowledge, and You inherit my self"

[Page 136]

entirely through its eternal return to You. Your inheritance is the best inheritance because it is more comprehensive and more lasting, and You are the best of inheritors in the realization of this attribute.

As for "making his wife fit" (iṣlāḥ zawjihi): He made her capable of conceiving after she had been barren. The mention of Zechariah has already occurred in Surah Āl ʿImrān, and the mention of his wife in Surah Maryam.

This is a clause functioning as a justification for the preceding clauses praising the mentioned prophets, and for what they were granted: the granting of victory, the answering of supplications, the deliverance from the plots of enemies, and what followed from these, beginning with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48]. Thus the plural pronouns refer to those mentioned. The emphatic particle (inna) conveys the sense of causation and reason, meaning: they did not deserve what they were given except because of their eagerness toward the paths of goodness and their earnestness in attaining them. The verb "kana" (was/were) indicates that this was their constant habit and their unfailing custom.

Al-Musara'ah (hastening, vying): a metaphorical usage for keenness, the directing of resolve and earnestness toward the good deeds, i.e., toward doing them, likening constancy and concern to the hastening of a traveler toward the intended destination, striving earnestly along its paths.

Al-Khayrat (the good deeds): the plural of khayr (with a fatha on the kha' and a sukun on the ya'), and it is a plural with the suffix -at contrary to analogical rule, like surad?iqat, hammamat and istablat. Khayr is the opposite of sharr (evil), and it is that which contains benefit. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Therein are good things (khayrat) and beautiful﴾ [al-Rahman: 70], it may be like this, and it may be the plural of khayrah (with a fatha and then a sukun), which is the lightened form of khayyirah with a doubled ya', meaning a woman possessing good moral qualities. The discussion of (al-khayrat) has already been treated in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those—for them are the good things (al-khayrat)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 88], in the surah "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah).

He then adds that they call upon God out of desire for His reward and fear of His wrath, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He fears the Hereafter and hopes for the mercy of his Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. Al-raghab and al-rahab, with a fatha on their second letter, are two verbal nouns from raghiba and rahiba. They are a description of the verbal noun in "yad'unana" (they call upon Us), specifying the type of supplication by what is more general in its genus; or a noun is understood to be omitted, meaning "possessors of desire and fear," so the genitive noun was placed in its position and took its case inflection. The verb "kana" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they were humble before Us﴾ is mentioned in the same way as its mention in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they were hastening﴾.

Al-khushu': the fear of the heart arising from reflection, without agitation of the outward limbs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 91:

﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit, and We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾

When the mention of the excellence of some of the prophets (men) was concluded, he followed it with praise of a prophetess woman, indicating that the causes of excellence are not restricted, as Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35], and so on. This is Maryam, daughter of 'Imran. He expressed her with the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) to indicate that she was well known for the content of the relative clause (al-silah), as is generally the case with the relative construction, and also because of what the relative clause contains of the meaning of refuting the Jews who spoke against her with falsehood and slander. And so that there is built upon that relative clause what follows from it, the words of the Exalted, ﴿So We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾, which is also in the position of the relative clause. It is as if it were said: "And she whom We breathed into of Our spirit," because both matters necessitate praise. Allah intended to honour her by making her a manifestation of His great power in opposing the human norm, by the conception of a female child without the contact of a male, so that people may see an example of the first creation, as indicated by the words of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59].

Al-nafkh (breathing) in its literal meaning is the expulsion of air from the mouth by tightening the lips. Here it is used figuratively for the casting of the spirit of creation into the womb of the woman for offspring in a single instant, without the usual means, likening the manner of rapid creation to the manner of breathing. It has been said that the angel breathed from that which is for him like the mouth.

The sense of containment conveyed by (fi, "in") is that Maryam was a vessel for the spirit breathed into her, since she was its receptacle. For this reason it was said (fiha, "in her"), and it was not said (fihi, "in him"), to indicate that the foetus which was formed in her womb came into being by a means other than the usual way. It is as if it were said: "So We breathed into her belly." This is more emphatic in opposing the custom, because the indication of breaking the custom grows stronger in proportion to the vanishing of the usual means in it.

Al-ruh (the spirit) is the power by which there is life. The Exalted said, ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29], meaning: I made Adam a spirit, and he became living. The particle (min, "of") is partitive, and what was breathed is a spirit because it was made a part of the spirit of Allah, that is, a part of the kind of spirit by which Allah makes bodies possessed of life. The attribution of the spirit to Allah is an attribution of honour, because it is a spirit sent forth from the presence of Allah the Exalted without the intermediary of the animal developments of natural generation. Making her and her son a sign is among the causes of honouring them both and of praising them, since Allah made them a means to certainty of His power and of the miracles of His prophets, as He said in Surat al-Mu'minun, ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50]. In this respect, some created things were honoured, so that Allah swore by them, such as ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1], ﴿By the sun and its brightness, and by the moon when it follows it﴾ [al-Shams: 1]. The singular (ayah) is used because the genus is intended by it. Since the one mentioned is two persons, and He informed about them that they are a sign, it is known that each one is a particular sign. Among the subtleties of this singular is that between Maryam and her son there is a shared state which is one sign. Then in each of them there is another sign, independent, according to the differing condition of the observer who reflects.

(إنَّ) with a kasra on the hamza ("Inna") is read this way by all the readers. It introduces a new statement. The well-known readings agree on the nominative (رفع) of (أُمَّتُكم) ("ummatukum"). The more apparent view is that the sentence is reported speech governed by an omitted verb of saying, which the context indicates. Omitting the verb of saying in such a construction is common in the Qur'an.

The address is to the prophets mentioned in the preceding verses. In that case, the most suitable reading is that the omitted verb of saying is in the form of the active participle (اسم الفاعل) in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (حال). The implied sense is: "saying to them, 'Indeed, this community of yours is...'" and so on to the end. The statement is reported in meaning: that is, saying to each one of Our messengers and prophets mentioned what the sentence "Indeed this community of yours" contains. The plural form is therefore intended to address them collectively, which is a common way of speaking about groups. An example is the saying, "The people rode their animals." Thus this verse follows the same style as its counterpart in Surah al-Mu'minun. That passage clarifies this further, for there a number of prophets are mentioned both in detail and in summary, as they are mentioned in this surah. Then it is followed by the words of the Exalted: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds; indeed I am Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 51]. (And "anna", with a fatha on the hamza)

Page 140

and with a kasra: ﴿This community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52]. The apparent conjunction requires that the words of the Exalted ﴿And indeed this community of yours is one community﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52] be included in the speech addressed to the messengers. The emphasis in this reading is merely to give importance to the report, so that the prophets receive it with firm resolve. Alternatively, it takes into account the situation of the nations to whom the messengers convey it, because the report that differing circumstances are unified is strange and may raise doubt about its meaning, since it may be taken figuratively; so it is emphasized by affirming it. Although it is addressed to the messengers, one of its intended purposes is that they convey it to their followers, so that they know that the religion of God is one. This helps every nation accept what its messenger brought, because it is supported by the testimony of those messengers who came before him.

It is also permissible for the sentence to be a fresh resumption (استئناف), with the address directed to the community of Muhammad ﷺ. That is: this religion, which is Islam, is one religion for all the messengers; that is, its foundations are one, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura: 13], and so on. The emphasis on this is to refute the denial of those who deny it, such as the polytheists.

The demonstrative in the words of the Exalted (هَذِهِ) refers to what the predicate in the words (أُمَّتُكم) explains, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿He said, "This is the parting between me and you"﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. So the demonstrative refers to the state in which they are, meaning in matters of religion, as is the case with the states of the prophets and messengers. Therefore, what the demonstrative conveys of distinguishing the thing pointed to is intended to encompass everything upon which the messengers stand of the foundations of the laws, namely tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness) and righteous action.

The word "ummah" here means religion (ملة), as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community (ummah), and indeed we are following in their footsteps"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. Al-Nabigha said:

I swore, and I left no doubt for you [to hold against me], and can one who has a religion (ummah) sin while he is obedient?

The original meaning of "ummah" is a group whose condition is one, and it was then applied to the religion that the group follows, by the indication that nations are not one.

(أُمَّةً واحِدَةً) is a circumstantial clause (حال) from (أُمَّتُكم), emphasizing what the demonstrative conveyed, and the demonstrative is the governing element of the one who has the circumstance. It conveyed the distinguishing and specifying of the state of the laws upon which the messengers stood, or to which Muhammad ﷺ called. The meaning of their being one is that they affirm God the Exalted, so there is no god besides Him. This is the situation of the laws of tawhid. By contrast, the religions of polytheism, because of the plurality of their gods, split into many religions, since every idol has its worship and followers. Although they are gathered under the description of polytheism, that is a general genus. This is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿and I am your Lord﴾, that is, none other than Me. The discussion of the Arabic grammar of this construction will be fully expounded in the commentary on Surah al-Mu'minun. The words of the Exalted ﴿and I am your Lord﴾ convey exclusivity (الحصر), that is, I am Lord and none other, by the indication of the context and the conjunction with (أُمَّةً واحِدَةً), since the meaning is: "and I am your Lord, a single Lord." For this reason He made the command to worship Him a consequence of it, that is, "so worship Me" to the exclusion of others. This command takes into account the starting state of the listeners from the nations of the messengers, so the meaning of worship here is worship of God alone and the maintenance of it.

This is a continuation of the verse, with ﴿And they divided their affair among themselves, each to Us will return﴾ [21:93] coordinated with the preceding clause ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me﴾ [21:92]. That is, they turned away from Our word. The verb (تَقَطَّعُوا, taqattaʿū, "they cut themselves into pieces/factions") and the pronouns of absence refer to something understood from the context, namely those who, in the Meccan Qur'an, are regularly described with such blame, that is, the polytheists (al-mushrikūn). Pronouns of this kind referring to the polytheists are common in the Qur'an. It is also possible that the pronouns refer to the nations of the prophets. On the first interpretation, which we gave earlier for the pronouns of address in ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾ [21:92], the discourse shifts from narrating about the prophets to narrating about the condition of their nations during their lives, or of those who came after them, such as the Jews and Christians, who broke the injunctions of their prophets.

[Page 142]

On the second interpretation, the pronouns of absence are an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person). It is also possible that the wāw (و) is coordinating one narrative with another, for a clear connection, just as its counterpart was coordinated with fā' (ف) in Surat al-Mu'minun. It may also be that the wāw is circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning: We commanded the messengers with the religion of Islam, which is the one religion; so it was from the misguidance of the polytheists that they divided their affair, opposed the messengers, and deviated from the religion of monotheism, which is the law of Ibrahim, their forefather. This interpretation is supported by the fact that the counterpart of this verse in Surat al-Mu'minun came with the coordinating particle of consequence, fā' (ف).

The tafaʿʿul-form verb (تَقَطَّعُوا) is the reflexive (muṭāwiʿ) of qaṭaʿa (قَطَعَ, "he cut"), meaning they became divided into groups. The act of dividing is attributed to them because they made themselves into factions, worshipping many gods; each tribe took for itself a god of idols alongside God. Thus their action was likened to "cutting apart."

In Jamharat al-Ansab by Ibn Hazm: Husayn ibn Ubayd al-Khuza'i, who was the father of Imran ibn Husayn, met the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Messenger of God said to him: "O Husayn, how many do you worship?" He said: "Ten gods." He said: "And where are they, and what are they?" He said: "Nine on the earth and one in the heavens." He said: "Then whom do you turn to for your need?" He said: "The one in the heavens." He said: "Then whom do you turn to for your request?" He said: "The one in the heavens." He said: "Then whom do you turn to for such-and-such? For such-and-such?" He would say each time: "The one in the heavens." The Messenger of God said: "Then discard the nine." In the Book of Supplications (Kitab al-Da'awat) of Sunan al-Tirmidhi, it is reported that he said seven: six on the earth and one in the heavens.

The word al-amr (الأمْرُ) means the state or affair. What is meant by it is the religion, as indicated by the verse ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion﴾ [6:159] in Surat al-An'am. Since (تَقَطَّعُوا) implies the meaning of "they dispersed," it is made transitive to (دِينَهُمْ, dīnahum, "their religion") and governs it in the accusative (فَنَصَبَهُ, fa-naṣabahu). The underlying form is: "they cut themselves apart in their religion and dispersed it."

[Page 143]

The addition of (بَيْنَهم, baynahum, "among themselves") serves to convey that they cooperated and supported one another in the fragmentation of their affair. For a tribe would adopt an idol that another tribe had not worshipped; then they would embellish to their neighbours and allies that they should worship it, and so they would add it to their gods. In this way, there came to be in the Ka'ba a number of idols and images, because the Ka'ba was the destination of all the tribes of the Arabs. It has been reported that 'Amr ibn Luhayy, who was nicknamed "Khuza'a," was the one who brought the idols to the Arabs.

The clause ﴿each to Us will return﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), answering a question that stirs in the mind of the hearer of His words ﴿And they divided their affair﴾, namely: what will be the outcome of this division?

The tanwīn (تَنْوِينُ, nunation) on (كُلٌّ, kullun, "each") is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the genitive complement omitted, meaning "all of them," that is, the bearers of the pronouns of absence, who are the polytheists. The statement conveys an indirect threat. This is indicated by the consequential connective in His words ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds﴾ [21:94] and so on to the end of the verse.

It is a wonderful consequence (tafri') drawn from the threat alluded to in His saying ﴿And all to Us they will return﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:93). It explains the nature of what they were threatened with, and this runs from His saying ﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:97) onward. He placed first the promise to believers of the reward for their righteous deeds, out of concern for it, and because it comes right after the threat, to hasten the joy of the believers before they hear the terrifying details of the threat. So it is not the primary aim of the consequence, but it resembles digression (istitrad) as a way of honouring the believers, just as they will be cared for after the details of the threat to the disbelievers, in His saying ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:101) to the end of the surah.

[Page 144]

Kufran is a verbal noun whose original meaning is not acknowledging a favour; it is the opposite of shukran (gratitude). Here it is used figuratively (majaz) for the denial of reward for a righteous deed, because acknowledging good customarily entails rewarding it, as in His saying ﴿And whatever good you do, it will not be denied you﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:115). So the meaning is that they will be given the reward of their righteous deeds. He emphasised this with His saying ﴿And indeed We are recording it for him﴾, emphasised by the emphatic particle (harf al-ta'kid) for the sake of its importance.

Writing (al-kitaba) is a metonymy (kinaya) for its certainty and for not losing it, because caring for the realisation of a thing entails guarding it against neglect and denial. Among the means of this is writing it down so that it may be mentioned even if time is long. This is a customary implication (luzum 'urfi), as al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Can desires undo what is in the scrolls?"

This is while writing is also used in its original meaning, as the apparent texts of the Book and the Sunnah indicate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 95:

﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should not return.﴾

This is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'tariḍa), and what is meant by "the town" (al-qarya) is its people. This covers every town of disbelief, as Almighty God said: ﴿And those towns — We destroyed them when they did wrong.﴾ [al-Kahf: 59]. Al-ḥarām (the forbidden) is that which is prevented. 'Antara said:

Forbidden to me she has become, would that she had not been forbidden,

i.e., she was prevented; that is, her people prevented her.

Page 145

That is, it is prohibited for a town whose destruction We have decreed that they should not return. So (ḥarām) is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿that they do not return﴾ is in the sense of a subject noun-phrase (mubtada') of a verbal noun. The predicate of (an) and its complement cannot occur except when placed first, as Ibn al-Ḥājib mentioned in his Amālī in discussing this verse.

The verb (ahlaknāhā) is used with the sense of intending the occurrence of the act, i.e., We intended its destruction.

Al-rujū' (return) is going back to the state in which a person was. It is possible that what is meant is their return from disbelief; in that case the (lā) in His saying "lā yarji'ūn" must be taken as an emphatic extra particle, because (ḥarām) carries the sense of negation, and (lā) is a negating particle, and the negation of a negation is an affirmation. The meaning would then become: prevention of their not returning to faith, which reverts to the sense that they are returning to faith, and this is not the intended meaning. So it is determined that the meaning is: it is prevented for a town whose destruction We have decreed that they should return from their error, since the decree of its destruction has already preceded.

This is an informing about the custom of God Most High in His dealings with the earlier nations, intended as an allusion to the despairing of a group of the polytheists from turning to faith, and a threat to them of destruction. These are the ones whose destruction God decreed on the day of Badr by the swords of the believers.

It is also permissible that what is meant is their return to the Hereafter through resurrection, and this is the more fitting, given that it follows His saying ﴿Each to Us will return﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 93]; in that case (lā) is a negating particle. The meaning: it is prohibited that their not returning to the Hereafter, which they claim, should happen; that is, their claim is false, i.e., they indeed return to Us and are recompensed for their disbelief. This is then an affirmation of resurrection by negating its opposite, and it is more eloquent than explicit affirmation, because it is an affirmation by way of implication, as though it were the affirmation of a thing by proof. It also serves as emphasis for His saying ﴿Each to Us will return﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 93].

The clause "(ahlaknāhā)" is an inclusion (idmāj) of a warning of worldly punishment before the punishment of the Hereafter.

The verb (ahlaknāhā) is used in its basic meaning, i.e., our destruction of it occurred. The meaning: no town We have destroyed and which has perished from the world, but they will return

Page 146

to Us through resurrection. It has been said that (ḥarām) is a homonym shared between the forbidden and the obligatory. They cited al-Khansā's verse:

And indeed, I do not see that, through time, one weeping for a grieving woman but that I weep for Ṣakhr.

In Lisān al-'Arab, in the ḥadīth of 'Umar: "In (al-ḥarām) there is the expiation of an oath": it is that a man says, "Ḥarām of God, I will not do it," just as he says, "Oath of God, I will not do it," and this is the dialect of the 'Uqaylīs. End.

I saw in an old literary collection from the books of the Zaytuna Mosque, numbered 4561, that the Banū 'Uqayl say "Ḥarām of God, I will surely come to you," just as it is said, "Oath of God, I will surely come to you." End. He explains the words of Lisān al-'Arab that this oath is not restricted to swearing for negation, as in the example of Lisān al-'Arab. Accordingly, a third interpretation becomes possible for His saying ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they do not return to Us﴾, i.e., "and an oath from Us upon a town," so the particle (ʿalā) enters upon that which the oath is directed at, as you say: "I have resolved upon you" (ʿazamtu ʿalayka), and as one says: "I swore upon so-and-so that he should not speak," as in the verse of al-Rā'ī:

Indeed I have sworn upon a pious oath, I will not conceal today the Caliph's words.

The opening of the hamza of (anna) in the oath is one of two possibilities in such a context of swearing. The meaning of "lā yarji'ūn" on this interpretation: they do not return to faith, because God knew this of them and therefore decreed their destruction.

Al-Jumhūr read (wa-ḥarām) with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and an alif after the rā'.

Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Bakr from 'Āṣim read (wa-ḥirm) with a kasra on the ḥā' and a sukūn on the rā', and it is a noun with the meaning of ḥarām. The word is written in the Mushaf without an alif, and it is transmitted in the readings of the qurrā' in two ways; the omission of the alif of the lengthened fatḥa is common in the mashāhif.

[Page 147]

﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose, and they swarm down from every mound.﴾ ﴿And the true promise draws near, and suddenly the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly. "Woe to us! We were certainly heedless of this. Rather, we were wrongdoers."﴾

(Ḥattā) is *ibtidā'iyyah* (inceptive, introducing a new statement). The sentence after it is a resumed statement (*kalām mustaʾnaf*) with no grammatical position (*lā maḥalla lahu min al-iʿrāb*, i.e., it is not in a place governed by any case), but *ḥattā* gives it a connection to the preceding speech. The apparent meaning of al-Zamakhsharī's words is that the notion of a limit (*al-ghāyah*) never leaves (*matā*, "when") when it is used for beginning. For this reason he and those who followed him among the exegetes (*mufassirūn*) were concerned to seek a limit for it here. In *al-Kashshāf* he made it a limit for his statement "and it is forbidden" (*wa-ḥarām*), saying: "*Ḥattā* is linked to *ḥarām*, and it is a limit for it, because the impossibility of their return does not cease until the Resurrection comes." End of quotation.

That is, it is a case of attaching a ruling to something that does not happen, like His saying: ﴿Nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 40]. Upon his statement are built the two interpretations that were mentioned earlier regarding the meaning of "return" in His saying ﴿that they will not return﴾, namely: they will not return from their disbelief until the world ends; or the negation of their return to Us in their belief ceases at the end of the world. So the intended meaning is to report the perpetuation of their disbelief under both interpretations.

On this interpretation, the opening (*fatḥ*) of Gog and Magog is the opening of the barrier (*al-sadd*) that stands between them and their spreading across the regions of the earth with corruption. This is what is mentioned in the story of Dhū al-Qarnayn in the Surah of al-Kahf. The timing of the promise of the Hour by the emergence of Gog and Magog is because their emergence is the first of the signs of the approach of the Resurrection.

The exegetes have counted it among the minor signs (*al-ashrāṭ al-ṣughrā*) of the establishment of the Hour.

[Page 148]

The approach of the promise has been explained as the approach of the Resurrection. It was called a promise because God named the resurrection a promise in His saying: ﴿As We initiated the first creation, We will repeat it. A promise upon Us; indeed, We are ever doing it.﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 104]. On this basis too, they took the pronoun in ﴿and they swarm down from every mound﴾ as referring to Gog and Magog, so that the clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from His saying "Gog and Magog".

According to this interpretation, this verse describes the spreading of Gog and Magog in a wondrous manner before their emergence by five centuries. Therefore we count this verse among the scientific and unseen miracles of the Qur'an. Perhaps the singling out of this event for timing, rather than other signs of the nearness of the Hour, was intended, together with the timing, to incorporate a warning to the Arabs addressed, so that this would be before their eyes as a caution to their descendants against the calamities of the appearance of these two groups. The collapse of the Arabs' established rule, the decline of their civilisation and their power, came at the hands of Gog and Magog, who are the Mongols and the Tatars, as the Prophetic warning explained at one of the moments of revelation. Zaynab bint Jaḥsh narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her in alarm, saying: "There is no god but God. Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near! Today an opening has been made in the barrier of Gog and Magog, like this," and he made a ring with his thumb and the finger next to it.

The approach, on this reading, is a relative approach, in relation to what remains of the lifespan of the world compared with what has passed of it, like His saying: ﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split﴾ [al-Qamar: 1]. It is also possible that the intended meaning of the opening of Gog and Magog is a parable for the bringing forth of the dead to the gathering, so that "opening" means "splitting," like His saying: ﴿The Day the earth will split from them swiftly; that is a gathering, easy for Us﴾ [Qāf: 44], and the name Gog and Magog would be a eloquent metaphor. Their being singled out for mention is due to the well-known abundance of their number among the Arabs, from the story of Dhū al-Qarnayn. This is supported by the ḥadīth of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God will say to Adam on the Day of Resurrection, 'Bring forth the group for the Fire.' He will say:

[Page 149]

'O Lord, what is the group for the Fire?' God will say, 'Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine.' They said, 'O Messenger of God, and which of us is that one?' He said, 'Rejoice, for among you is one man, and from Gog and Magog are nine hundred and ninety-nine.'"

Or the name Yājūj and Mājūj is used as a proverb for multitude, as in the saying of Dhū al-Rummah:

"Even if Gog and Magog were together, and ʿĀd returned, and they sought to muster the Tubbaʿ..."

That is: until the dead are brought out like Gog and Magog, after the manner of His saying: ﴿They will come forth from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7]. Then this is a eloquent metaphor, of the type of comparing an intellectual notion to an intellectual notion. It is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid, "*jadath*" (with a *jīm* and a *thāʾ* with a dot, meaning "grave"), i.e., "from every grave," in line with His saying: ﴿And when the graves are scattered﴾ [al-Infiṭār: 4]. Then the two pronouns in ﴿and they swarm down from every mound﴾ refer to a notion understood from the context, indicated by the clue of "return" in His saying "they will not return", i.e., the people of every town that We destroyed.

"Approach," on this aspect, is extreme nearness, which is imminence, i.e., the promise that the polytheists were promised has drawn near, namely the punishment, by their seeing the Fire and the reckoning. The feminine marker in the verb "were opened" (*futiḥat*) is because Gog and Magog are interpreted as a nation. Then a noun is understood, namely "barrier" (*sadd*), so the feminine is acquired from the genitive noun.

Gog and Magog are two tribes of one nation, like ʿĀd and Thamūd, or Ṭasm and Jadīs. [Note: the text states "مثل طسم وجديس", which are two extinct Arab tribes.]

The attribution of the verb "were opened" to Gog and Magog is by way of an understood genitive, i.e., "their barrier or their wall was opened." The verb "opened" is an indication of the object.

[Page 150]

Al-Jumhūr (the majority of readers) read "*futiḥat*" with a light (single) *tāʾ* after the *fāʾ*. Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb read it with a doubled *tāʾ*. The discussion of Gog and Magog has already been presented in the Surah of al-Kahf.

*Ḥadab*: an elevated spot of land, that is, what is raised from it.

*Yansilūn*: they walk the *nasalān* (a quick, light stride) with two *fatḥah*s, and its verb is of the pattern *ḍaraba*; its origin is the walking of the wolf. The intended meaning is quick walking. Choosing this expression here is one of the unseen subtleties of the Qur'an, because when Gog and Magog spread across the earth they spread like hungry wolves, causing corruption.

This is the summary of what has been scattered among the exegetes' statements and of the aspects they devised, and they all revolve around the axis of holding that inceptive *ḥattā* indicates that what follows it is a limit for what precedes it, with the object of "were opened" understood to be "the barrier of Gog and Magog," and with Gog and Magog taken in the literal sense of their name. This has driven them into a narrow place where the coherence of the sentence became difficult for them, so they were obliged to specify the thing limited (*al-mughayyā*) and to specify a limit suitable to it and to these interpretations, as you have learned from what has preceded. I do not see following them in these three matters. As for the indication of inceptive *ḥattā* of the meaning of limit, that is, that what follows it is a limit for the content of what precedes it, I do not consider this necessary. For some reason the Arabs distinguished between its use as a preposition (*jārrah*), as a conjunction (*ʿāṭifah*), and its use as inceptive. Did not the grammarians explicitly state that after inceptive *ḥattā* the speech is a resumed sentence? That was a statement that became correct on their tongues, yet they did not observe it as it deserves. The meaning of limit in *ḥattā* as preposition, which is the original use of this particle, is clear, because it means "*ilā*" (until). In *ḥattā* as conjunction, because it indicates sharing in the ruling, it is necessary that what is conjoined with it is the end of what it is conjoined to, in the intended meaning.

[Page 151]

As for inceptive *ḥattā*, the presence of the meaning of limit with it in its positions is not regular or consistent. Since what follows it is an independent statement, it is necessary that its presence between the two statements is merely to link the two statements. It has been transferred from the meaning of ending the sense of what precedes it by what follows it, to indicating that the speaker is ending the purpose of his speech by what he brings after *ḥattā*, and he does not intend to end the sense of what precedes *ḥattā* by what occurs when what follows it takes place (which is the original meaning of limit). Look at the use of *ḥattā* in several places in the Mu'allaqa of Labīd.

And in His saying: ﴿And they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], the saying of the Messenger is not a limit for the shaking, but it arises from it. Here the state of the disbelievers at that time has been depicted in the most eloquent depiction and its most striking effect on the listener's soul, since it is made to follow from the opening of Gog and Magog and the approach of the true promise, to indicate the swiftness with which that state comes upon them. Then by beginning the sentence with the particle of surprise and conditional (*idhā*), which indicates occurrence all at once, without gradualness or delay, and then by bringing in the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-qiṣṣah*) so that the listener acquires a general knowledge which is then detailed by what explains the pronoun of the matter, He said: ﴿Then suddenly the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly﴾, to the end of the verse.

*Shukhūṣ*: fixing the gaze without movement, as happens to one who is stunned.

The clause "*Yā waylanā*" ("Woe to us!") is the spoken content of an omitted verb of saying, as is evident, i.e., they will say at that time, "Woe to us!" The particle "*fī*" indicates that heedlessness has taken firm hold of them, as though it encompasses them like a container encompasses what it contains, i.e., we had a great heedlessness, namely the heedlessness of turning away from the proofs of recompense and resurrection.

"*Yā waylanā*" is a supplication against themselves because of the severity of what has befallen them. "*Bal*" is for the retracting, nullifying transition, i.e., "we were not in heedlessness, because we were called and warned, and we were only wrongdoers to ourselves through our obstinacy and turning away." The thing referred to by "*hādhā*" ("this") is the whole of those circumstances: the gathering, the reckoning and the recompense.

﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides Allah, are fuel for Hell; you will arrive at it﴾. ﴿If these had been gods, they would not have entered it; and all of them will abide therein﴾. ﴿For them therein is groaning, and they therein will not hear﴾.

The sentence ﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides Allah, are fuel for Hell﴾ is a response to their words ﴿Woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:97], and so on to the end of the verse. It is therefore a quoted statement with an omitted introductory phrase, in the manner of conversational discourse. The implied meaning is: it will be said to them, "Indeed you, and what you worship besides Allah, are fuel for Hell." This is an escalation in their destruction. They had said, "Woe to us! We were heedless of this," and so they were informed that their gods, who were dearer to them than their own selves and further in their view from being touched by any harm, are going to the same fate of disgrace and humiliation as they are. For this reason the report is emphasized with the particle of emphasis (inna), because they were in a state of denying it.

The word (ma) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and its most common use is for things whose referent is not rational. It is used here for their objects of worship, namely idols, jinn and devils, by way of taghlib (semantic prevalence of the non-rational), and also because (ma) is used very frequently in Arabic speech for what is more general than the rational and the non-rational.

Their idols and objects of worship were present at that scene, as the demonstrative indicates in ﴿If these had been gods, they would not have entered it﴾.

The word haseb (ḥaṣab) is a noun meaning "that which is thrown," i.e., that which is cast into something. From it comes the word ḥaṣbā' (small pebbles), because they are stones that are thrown. The meaning is that they will be thrown into Hell, as the Most High said: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:24], meaning the disbelievers and their idols. The clause ﴿you will arrive at it﴾ explains the clause ﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides Allah, are fuel for Hell﴾. Its purpose is to bring the fuel close to them in Hell, by what the word (wāridūn, "arriving") indicates of the attribute of entering the Fire in the present, as is the case with the predicate in the form of the active participle, which is literal (ḥaqīqah) for the present and metaphorical (majāz) for the future.

Their mistake in worshipping those idols was further made apparent to increase their distress, by making them witness the idols being brought to the Fire, and it was said to them: ﴿If these had been gods, they would not have entered it﴾. This is followed by the words of the Most High ﴿and all of them will abide therein﴾, meaning they and their idols.

The zafīr (groaning) is the breath that comes out from the depths of the two lungs due to the compression of air caused by being affected by grief. Here it is among the states of the polytheists, not of the idols. The reference of the pronouns is clear from context. The conjunction of the clause ﴿and they therein will not hear﴾ is required by the phrase ﴿for them therein is groaning﴾, because the nature of groaning is to be heard, so God informs that from the intensity of the punishment they lose hearing for this reason. The verse's context is clear regarding its intended meaning and does not need forced interpretation.

Ibn Ishaq related in his Sirah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once sat with al-Walid ibn al-Mughira in the Sacred Mosque, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith came and sat with them in a gathering of men of Quraysh. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to them ﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides Allah, are fuel for Hell; you will arrive at it﴾. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, and Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ara al-Sahmi came, before he embraced Islam. al-Walid ibn al-Mughira told him what had taken place in that gathering. Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ara said: 'By Allah, if I had found him I would have debated him. Ask Muhammad: is everything that is worshipped besides Allah in Hell along with those who worshipped it? We worship the angels, the Jews worship Uzayr, and the Christians worship Isa ibn Maryam.' This was related to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Whoever loves to be worshipped besides Allah is with the one who worships him. They are only worshipping the devil, who commanded them to worship him.' Then Allah revealed ﴿Indeed those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us, those will be kept far from it﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:101]." End quote.

Something similar is found in the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) by al-Wahidi, and in al-Kashshaf (by al-Zamakhshari) with additions: "Ibn al-Zib'ara met the Prophet (ﷺ), mentioned this, and added: 'You have been refuted, by the Lord of this temple! Do you not claim that the angels are honoured servants, that Isa is a righteous servant, and that Uzayr is a righteous servant? And these are the Banu Mulayh who worship the angels, these are the Christians who worship the Messiah, and these are the Jews who worship Uzayr!' So the people of Mecca cried out" — meaning in joy — "and said: Muhammad has been refuted." The story is also related in some Arabic grammatical works: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ibn al-Zib'ara: 'How ignorant you are of the language of your people! I said (what you worship) [wa-ma ta'budūn], and (ma) is for what does not reason, and I did not say (whom you worship) [wa-man ta'budūn].'" End quote.

The verse narrates what will happen on the Day of Gathering (yawm al-hashr), and its context is not a warning to the polytheists, so that the words ﴿Indeed those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:101] would be a specification of it, or so that the story would be the cause of its revelation.

﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (reward) has already been decreed from Us, they will be kept far away from it.﴾ ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound, and they will abide forever in whatever their souls desire.﴾ ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them: "This is your Day which you were promised."﴾

The sentence ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (al-husna, the good reward) has already been decreed from Us﴾ is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), prompted by the contrast between the account of the disbelievers and what is said to them on the Day of Resurrection, and the account of what the believers encounter on the Day of Resurrection and what is said to them. Those for whom al-husna has been decreed are the group opposite the people of the town whose destruction was already determined in God's knowledge. Since the people of the town were polytheists, the group opposite them are the believers. This sentence has no connection with the sentence ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98], nor does it specify the generality of the words of the Exalted ﴿what you worship besides God﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98]. Rather, the words of the Exalted ﴿those for whom al-husna has been decreed from Us﴾ are general, encompassing every believer who died in faith and righteous deeds.

As for al-sabq (precedence), its literal meaning is passing others in travel to a specific place, from which comes the racing of horses (sibaq al-khayl). It is used here metaphorically for the establishment of good fortune in the past. One says, "This happened in former ages" (al-'usur al-sabiqa), meaning those whose times have passed, because of the close connection between precedence and advancement. That is, those for whom al-husna was realized in this world, that is, faith and righteous deeds were realized for them from God, by His grace and decree, just as destruction was realized for their opposites through the forsaking that had been decreed for them.

Al-husna means the good state in religion. The Exalted said ﴿For those who did good is the best (husna) and more﴾ [Yunus: 26]. Or it means the good promise, that is, God's promise to them of good treatment has been established. This was discussed in the surah of Yunus.

This is a resumptive sentence (jumla musta'nafa), by which the mention of resurrection is repeated. It is used to establish and argue for its occurrence and possibility, refuting the polytheists' claim that it cannot occur on the ground that the bodies said to be resurrected have undergone great annihilation ﴿They say: "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:5).

The connection (munasaba) of this transition lies in what preceded it concerning the gathering, punishment and reward, namely His saying ﴿For them therein is a groaning﴾ (Al-Anbiya' 21:100) and His saying ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾ (Al-Anbiya' 21:101) and so on. The structure of the sentence has been arranged by means of anteriority and posteriority (al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir) for eloquent purposes. The original form of the sentence is: "We shall repeat the creation as We originated the first creation, on the day We fold the heaven like the folding of the scroll for the writing, as a promise upon Us." The order was then altered: the adverbial phrase was placed first, at the head of the sentence, to arouse anticipation, and it was connected to its governing element. There is also, in the sentence to which the adverbial phrase is attached, a strangeness and an antithesis, in that the beginning of a new creation, which is resurrection, is timed to the moment of the dissolution of an old creation, which is the folding of the heaven. ﴿As We originated the first creation﴾ was placed first, although it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in the accusative position in (nu'iduhu), in order to hasten the presentation of the proof before the claim, so that it may settle in the soul with greater firmness. All of these are aspects of concern for establishing the occurrence of resurrection. Therefore, His saying ﴿On the day We fold the heaven﴾ is not connected to what precedes it, His saying ﴿and the angels will receive them﴾ (Al-Anbiya' 21:103). He then followed this with what confirms the realisation of the resurrection, by describing it as a promise upon God, the word "promise" being construed to imply obligation. It is therefore followed by the preposition (ʿalā) in His saying ﴿as a promise upon Us﴾, that is, a truth that is binding.

The clause ﴿Indeed We have been doing﴾ is emphasised by the particle of emphasis, in order to treat the addressees as one who denies God's power. Since they negated resurrection on the ground that it is impossible to repeat bodies after they have perished, it follows that they are obliged to deem it impossible in relation to God's power. The meaning of His saying (fāʿilīn) ["doers"] is that He is the doer of what He promised, that is, the capable one. The meaning is: "Indeed We have been capable of that." Mentioning the verb of being (kāna) conveys that His power has indeed been realised, as indicated by the evidence in His saying ﴿as We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾.

[Page 159]

Al-tayy (folding) is the returning of one part of a soft, extended body onto another part of it; its opposite is al-nashr (unfolding).

Al-sijill (the scroll), here with a kasra on the sīn and a kasra on the jīm, has several dialectal forms. It is applied to the sheet on which writing is done, and it is also applied to the scribe of the document. Perhaps it is a designation by way of an omitted genitive construction, meaning "the owner of the scroll". It has also been said that sijill is the name of an angel in heaven to whom the records of people's deeds are raised, and who preserves them. It is not appropriate to interpret it here in the sense of "document", because that does not fit the attribution of folding to it, nor does it serve as a synonym for it given His saying (lil-kitāb) or (lil-kutub) ["for the writing" / "for the books"]; nor is it appropriate to interpret it in the sense of an angel charged with the records of deeds, because that was not well known, so how could it be used as a comparison with his action? The correct view is that by al-sijill is meant the scribe who writes the document and then folds it when he finishes writing, and this is a known practice. Thus the comparison with his action is elegant.

Al-Jumhur read (lil-kitābi) in the singular. Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (lil-kutubi) with a ḍamma on the kāf and a ḍamma on the tā', in the plural form. Since the definiteness of al-sijill and the definiteness of al-kitāb are generic definiteness, both the singular and the plural are equally valid for what is defined. As for reading them in the singular, it contains the embellishment (muḥassin) of observing parallelism (murā'āt al-naẓīr) in form. As for reading al-kutub in the plural while al-sijill is singular, it contains the elegance of variation (tafannun) through contrast. Its orthography in the Qur'anic codex, without an alif, admits both readings, since the alif is often omitted in such a form. The lām in His saying (lil-kitābi) serves to strengthen the governing element, and so it is attached to the object of (ṭayy) ["folding"].

The meaning of the folding of the heaven is the change of its bodies from one position to another, or the drawing of some of its parts close to others, as the edges of an unfolded sheet change when it is folded so that the scribe may write

[Page 160]

on one of its two faces. This is a manifestation of the extinction of the present order, an extinction which has many states, some of which are described in other sūrahs of the Qur'an.

The verse contains no evidence for the dissolution of the heavens themselves, but rather for the disruption of their order. In Surat al-Zumar ﴿and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾ (Al-Zumar 39:67). The question of the effacement (dathūr) of the heavens, that is, their annihilation, was raised by the earlier philosophers (al-ḥukamā' al-mutaqaddimūn), and the view of their eventual annihilation was favoured by Anaximenes of Miletus (Anaksimā'is al-Malṭī), Pythagoras and Plato.

Al-Jumhur read (naṭwī) with the nūn of majesty, a kasra on the wāw, and (al-samā'a) in the accusative. Abu Ja'far read it with a ḍamma on the tā' of the feminine present prefix, a fatḥa on the wāw, in the passive voice, and (al-samā'u) in the nominative.

Al-bad' (beginning) is an action whose like has not preceded it with respect to an agent, or to a time, or the like. The beginning of creation is that it did not exist before, that is, "as We made it a creation originated, not preceded by its like in its kind."

Khalq (creation) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used in the sense of the thing created (maf'ūl).

The meaning of the repetition of the creation is the repetition of its like in its form. The creature, considered as an individual of a genus, when it perishes, it is said that only its like is repeated, because genera have no actual existence outside except within their individuals. As God said ﴿We shall return it to its former state﴾ (Ṭā-Hā 20:21), that is, "like its former state in its genus", namely that it is a staff among staffs. The apparent meaning of the comparison conveyed by the particle of comparison (ka) in His saying ﴿as We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾ is that the repetition of the creation of bodies is compared to their initial creation. The point of comparison is the possibility of both and the power over both, and this is what the speech was brought to convey,

[Page 161]

although the comparison is capable of resembling in other respects as well. Muslim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood among us to admonish and said: 'O people, you will be gathered to God barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, as We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it, a promise upon Us, indeed We have been doing it.'" [He then related] the hadith in full. This is an explanation of some of what the comparison conveys, and it comes by way of revelation, and the wording does not refuse it, so it must be considered a meaning of the particle (ka) alongside the meaning indicated by the apparent context. This is among the ramifications of the ninth introduction among the introductions of this our commentary.

(Wa'dan) ["a promise"] is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, a cognate accusative) of (nu'īduhu) ["We shall repeat it"], because the report of the repetition carries the sense of a promise of it, so it is in the accusative to specify the kind of repetition. It is also permissible for it to be an emphatic absolute object, emphasising the content of the clause ﴿as We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾.

[p. 162]

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*) on Surah 21, verses 105–106:

﴿And We certainly wrote in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship.﴾

If the intended meaning of "the earth" is the earth of Paradise, as in His saying, exalted is He, in Surah az-Zumar: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups﴾ [az-Zumar: 73], up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the earth, that we may settle in Paradise wherever we will."﴾ [az-Zumar: 74], then the connection of this verse with the one preceding it is clear. It is also connected with His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts?﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ: 44].

If, however, the intended meaning is an earth of this world, that is, that its governance will be in the hands of God's righteous servants, then this verse is directed toward promising the believers the inheritance of the land in which they suffered harm, which is the land of Makkah and its surroundings. It would then be good news of the improvement of their condition in this world, following the good news of their good end in the Hereafter, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely give him a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ [al-Naḥl: 97].

Moreover, in the use of the name "the earth" there is something suitable for the meaning that the dominion of the world will be in the hands of the Muslims as long as they remain steadfast in faith and righteousness. God has fulfilled His promise in both cases and under both possibilities. In the ḥadīth transmitted by Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī from Thawbān, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God gathered the earth for me, so I saw its east and its west, and indeed the dominion of my community will reach what was gathered for me of it."

The majority of readers (al-Jumhūr) read *fī al-Zabūr* in the singular form, and it is the name of the written book, that is, *al-mazbūr* (the written), a form of *faʿūl* with the meaning of *mafʿūl*, like *nāqah ḥalūb* (a milch camel) and *rakūb* (a riding camel). Ḥamzah read it in the plural form: *Zubūr*, on the pattern of *faʿūl*, the plural of *zibr* (with a kasrah and then a sukūn), meaning *mazbūr*. Its pattern is like *qishr* and *qushūr*, meaning "in the scriptures." According to the reading of the majority, it is predominantly used as a designation for the Book of Dāwūd. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave David the Psalms﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 55], in Surah an-Nisāʾ and in Surah al-Isrāʾ. So the specification of this promise to the Book of Dāwūd is because no general promise to the righteous of this inheritance was mentioned in the heavenly books before it. As for what came in the Torah, in what the Qurʾān relates of the saying of Mūsā, peace be upon him, (﴿Indeed, the earth belongs to God; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 128]), that is specific to the Holy Land and the Children of Israel.

*Al-Zabūr* is the Book of Dāwūd, and it is scattered within the book called *al-Mazāmīr* (the Psalms) among the books of the Jews. I have not yet mentioned the sentence that contains this promise in the Psalms. I found in a lecture by the Italian Arabist "Fuwīdū" (Fuido?) that the text of this promise from the Zabur in Hebrew is thus: (*ṣiddīqīn yarshūn ʾaraṣ*), with a shīn dotted in *yarshūn* and a ṣād undotted in *ʾaraṣ*, meaning: "the righteous will inherit the earth." The purpose is the testimony to this promise from the earlier books, before there came a promise like this in the Qurʾān, in Surah an-Nūr, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the earth, as He made successors those before them﴾ [an-Nūr: 55].

According to the reading of Ḥamzah, this promise was repeated for groups of the righteous servants. The meaning of (*min baʿd al-dhikr*, "after the Reminder") is that this promise appeared in the Zabur after a reminder and admonition to the community. Thus, after the commands were delivered to them, they were promised the inheritance of the earth. It is also said that the intended meaning of "the Reminder" (*al-dhikr*) is the Book of Law, which is the Torah. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave Mūsā and Hārūn the Criterion, and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ: 48]. Then the adverbial phrase in His saying, exalted is He, (*min baʿd al-dhikr*) would be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the Zabur. The purpose of this circumstantial clause is to indicate that the promise spoken of here is other than the promise God made to the Children of Israel through Mūsā, of giving them the Holy Land. That is the promise mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, quoting Mūsā: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 21]. It is also other than the inheritance of kingship and dominion that God bestowed upon the Children of Israel, because that was a promise made before Dāwūd, since the kingship of Dāwūd is one of its manifestations. Rather, the purpose is to indicate that it is a promise God made to a righteous people after the Children of Israel, and they are none other than the Muslims, whom God made true in His promise, so they possessed the earth through the blessing of their Messenger (ﷺ) and his Companions, and their dominion expanded and their authority grew, in accordance with what their Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, foretold in the ḥadīth mentioned just above. The sentence ﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*) to the promise, and an announcement that its time has come and its appointed moment has arrived. For after Dāwūd, no believing people inherited the earth in this way, so when Islam came and people believed in Muḥammad (ﷺ), he had delivered the message to them.

The indication in His saying, exalted is He, (*Indeed, in this*) refers to the promise that was promised in the Zabur and conveyed in the Qurʾān.

By "a people who worship" is meant those whose nature is worship, not deviating from it even by the width of a fingertip, as the attachment of the description "those who worship" to the word "people" (*qawm*) suggests, indicating that worship is the foundation of their peoplehood, as we have mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe﴾ [Yūnus: 101], at the end of Surah Yūnus. It is as if He is saying: "I have indeed conveyed the promise to you, so strive to attain it." The people who worship are the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), may God be pleased with them, and those present at that time, and those who came after them.

*ʿIbādah* (worship) is adhering to the limits of the Law. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in God﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 110]. They inherited this great inheritance and left it to the community after them, and they vary in it in stages, like the varying conditions of wisdom and foolishness in managing the legacies of ancestors. What resembles this promise mentioned here and its linking with worship is the promise that this community was given in the Qurʾān: ﴿God has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the earth, as He made successors those before them, and He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and He will surely change their state after their fear into security, worshipping Me, not associating anything with Me. And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Nūr: 55], ﴿And establish prayer, give zakāt, and obey the Messenger, that you may receive mercy﴾ [al-Nūr: 56].

[p. 162]
