[Page 165]

This surah is built on establishing the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and confirming his call. It opens by warning the deniers that their reckoning is near and that God's promise is about to fall upon them, and by establishing that the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) was no novelty among the messengers. The messengers were mentioned in general terms, then a group of them was mentioned in detail. This was interspersed with admonitions and proofs. This sentence is connected to all that preceded it concerning the prophets who were given wisdom and knowledge, and the mention of the honours they were given. So this verse came comprising a comprehensive description of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). Its distinction over the other laws is a distinction that suits its universality and its permanence, namely that it is "a mercy to the worlds." Thus this sentence is a conjunction to the sentence ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 91], as a conclusion to the virtues of the prophets, and what lies between them is an interjection and a digression. This sentence has a connection with the verse ﴿And the wrongdoers conspired in secret: "Is this not but a human like you? Will you then submit to magic while you see?"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 3]. Its parallel, in describing the law of Muhammad (ﷺ), is the parallel of the verse ﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion﴾ [al-Anbiya: 48], the verse ﴿And We certainly gave Abraham his right judgement﴾ [al-Anbiya: 51], and the verses after it, describing what the earlier messengers were given. It was formulated in the most eloquent arrangement, for this verse, with the brevity of its words, includes praise of the Messenger (ﷺ), praise of the One who sent him, the Exalted, and praise of his message, in that it was a manifestation of the mercy of God the Exalted to mankind as a whole, and that it is the mercy of God the Exalted to His creation. It consists of twenty-four letters, without the conjunction letter by which it is joined. In it are mentioned the Messenger, the one who sent him, those to whom he was sent, the message, and the descriptions of these four, together with the indication of the generality of conditions, the encompassing of those to whom he was sent, the particularity of restriction, and the indefinite form of "mercy" (raḥmatan), which is for magnification. For there is no reason for choosing the indefinite form in this place other than the intention of magnification; otherwise it would have said: "except that We might have mercy on the worlds," or "except that you are the mercy to the worlds." The indefiniteness is not for singularity, clearly, since what is meant is the genus of mercy, and the indefiniteness of a genus is what is affected by the intention of magnification. So these are twelve specific meanings. It has surpassed the most comprehensive single expression of the eloquent Arabs, which is:

*Halt, let us weep at the remembrance of a beloved and a dwelling*

For that expression, at its utmost, as they said, is that he stopped, asked others to stop, wept, asked others to weep, mentioned the beloved and the dwelling, without any greater particularity than that, and so it gathered only six meanings, and these are not particularities; they are only an abundance of meanings. The indefiniteness of "beloved" (ḥabībin) and "dwelling" (manzilin) is only for unity, because he meant one specific individual from the genus of beloveds and one specific individual from the genus of dwellings, and these are his beloved, the owner of that dwelling, and his dwelling. Know that the accusative of "mercy" (raḥmatan), as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun of the addressee, makes him a description of its attributes; when the restriction of the described to this attribute is added to that, it becomes a restriction of the described to the attribute. In this there is a subtle allusion that the Messenger has become united with mercy and confined to it, and it is known that the title of messengerhood is constant for him in all his conditions, so his existence became mercy and all his being became mercy. The use of the attribute as a verbal noun (maṣdar) expresses hyperbole in this unity, such that mercy is an attribute firmly established in his being sent. What points to this meaning is what the Prophet (ﷺ) indicated in explaining it, with his saying: "I am only a mercy bestowed." The detail of this appears in two manifestations. The first is the character of his pure soul being shaped by the character of mercy; the second is mercy encompassing the variations of his law. As for the first manifestation, Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Tahir al-Qaysi al-Ishbili, one of the students of Abu 'Ali al-Ghassani and among those whom Abu al-Walid al-Baji licensed, from the men of the fifth century, said: God adorned Muhammad (ﷺ)

*Page 167*

*with the adornment of mercy, so his being a mercy, all his traits were mercy, and his attributes were mercy to creation.* End of quotation. 'Iyad mentioned it from him in *al-Shifa*. I say: he means that Muhammad (ﷺ) was created upon the character of mercy in all the conditions of his dealings with the community, so that there would be a harmony between his pure soul and what is revealed to him of the law, which is mercy, so that his receiving of the law would come from an expansion of the soul, finding what is revealed to him suitable to his desire and his character. 'A'isha said: "His character was the Qur'an." For this reason God singled out Muhammad (ﷺ) in this surah with the description of mercy, and did not describe any other of the prophets with it; and likewise in the whole Qur'an. God the Exalted said: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; it grieves him that you suffer; he is keen over you; to the believers he is kind and merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. And God the Exalted said: ﴿It was by a mercy from God that you were gentle with them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], meaning: by a mercy with which He made you and created you, so you were gentle to them. In the hadith of Muslim: "When the face of the Messenger of God was wounded on the day of Uhud, this grieved his companions, and they said: 'If only you would invoke a curse upon them.' He said: 'I was not sent as a curser; I was only sent as a mercy.'" As for the second manifestation of his being a mercy to the worlds, it is the manifestation of the variations of his law, that is, what it contains of the constituents of mercy general to all creatures; because the words of God the Exalted "to the worlds" (lil-'alamin) are connected to the word "mercy" (raḥmatan). The definiteness in "the worlds" (al-'alamin) is for the comprehensiveness of everything to which the name "world" truly applies.

"The world" (al-'alam) is a class among the classes of those possessing knowledge, that is, humankind, or a kind among the kinds of living created beings, as was previously mentioned regarding the possibility of both meanings in the words of God the Exalted ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2]. If the meaning is the classes of those possessing knowledge, then the meaning of the Muhammadan law being confined to mercy is that it is the broadest of the laws in mercy toward people. For the earlier laws, although filled with mercy, the mercy in them was not general, either because it did not relate to all the conditions of the obligated persons, as the Hanifiyya (*al-Hanifiyya*), the law of Abraham (peace be upon him), was a mercy specific to the condition of the individual in himself, and there was in it no general legislation; and the law of Jesus (peace be upon him) is close to it in this respect; or because in most of its rulings it contains, in more than a few cases, a severity required by God's wisdom in governing the communities, which were legislated for, as is the case with the law of the Torah, for it was the broadest of the earlier laws in relating to most conditions of individuals and communities, and it was a mercy as God described it in His words ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book, complete for him who excels, and an explanation of all things, and a guidance and a mercy, that they might believe in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 154]. Yet many of the punishments of its community were placed in the imposition of arduous acts upon the community, with harsh obligations that were continuous. God the Exalted said: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa: 160], and He said ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54], and other numerous verses.

Undoubtedly God the Exalted singled out the Islamic law with the description of complete mercy. This was alluded to by the words of God the Exalted in what He related as an address from Him to Moses (peace be upon him): (﴿My mercy encompasses all things; so I shall ordain it for those who are mindful of God, and pay the zakat, and those who believe in Our signs, those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet﴾ [al-A'raf: 156]), the verse. In His words ﴿encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156] there is an indication that the meaning is a mercy that is general. The Islamic law was distinguished in that mercy is constant for people in all their conditions, and that it is attained by all people, not by a particular community only. The wisdom in distinguishing the Islamic law with this excellence is that the conditions of human souls passed through ages and stages, which were prepared by their developments to be governed by mercy, and for harm to be removed from them except by necessary measures without which the interests cannot be upheld. So what was in the earlier laws of the mixing of mercy with severity, and what is in the Islamic law of the pure mercy, did not occur at any time except in accordance with wisdom. But God made this law, and the one who brought it, and the community that follows it, fortunate, by its coinciding with the time and the stage for which God's wisdom in governing mankind required that legislation for them be legislation of mercy until the end of the world.

Thus the Islamic law was established on the pillars of mercy, gentleness, and ease. God the Exalted said: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and God the Exalted said: ﴿God intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was sent with the tolerant, easy *Hanifiyya*." As for what may be imagined of severity in such matters as retaliation (*qisas*) and the prescribed punishments (*hudud*), it is only for the sake of weighing the conflict between mercy and hardship, as His words the Exalted indicated: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179]. So retaliation and the prescribed punishments are severity upon the criminals and mercy toward the rest of people. As for the mercy of Islam toward non-Muslim nations, what we mean by it is its mercy toward the nations who fall under its authority, namely the *ahl al-dhimma* (protected people, non-Muslim subjects under Muslim rule). Its mercy toward them is that they are not compelled to abandon their religions, and that justice is administered among them in rulings, such that they have what Muslims have and are subject to what Muslims are subject to in general rights. This is if by "the worlds" in the words of God the Exalted ﴿except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ is meant the kind among the kinds of living created beings. For the law is concerned with the conditions of animals in human dealings with them and human benefit from them, since they were created for the sake of humans. God the Exalted said: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29], and God the Exalted said: ﴿And the cattle, He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat﴾ [al-Nahl: 5]. ﴿And in them there is beauty for you when you bring them home and when you drive them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]. ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves; indeed your Lord is kind and merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 7].

The Islamic law has permitted people to benefit from whatever animals provide benefit, and has not permitted other than that. For this reason hunting for mere sport was disliked, and torturing animals for other than eating them was forbidden; and our jurists considered horse racing a concession for the need of warfare and the like. The law encouraged mercy toward animals. In the hadith of the *Muwatta'*, from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "God forgave a man who found a dog panting from thirst, so he went down into a well, filled his leather sock with water, held it in his mouth until he climbed up, and gave the dog to drink, and God forgave him."

As for harmful and injurious animals, permission has been given to kill and drive them off, in preference of human mercy over the mercy toward beasts. Regarding the details of rulings of this kind there is abundance, which the jurist will not lack in tracing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 108:

﴿Say: It is only revealed to me that your god is one God. Will you then submit?﴾

He followed the description encompassing the message of Muhammad ﷺ, in terms of its effect upon the conditions of mankind, with a description encompassing the essence of the Islamic call itself, which is obligatory for every one who follows it, namely belief in the oneness of God, the Exalted, and the nullification of divinity for anything other than Him, to repudiate the polytheism (shirk) spread among the nations of that day. And for the importance of this matter, the sentence was introduced with the command that he say it to them, in order to draw their ears to listen. The sentence was framed in the form of restricting the revelation to him in its content, because its content is the greatest foundation of the Law (al-shari'ah), and everything the Law contains branches off from it. Thus the call to it is the leading principle for bringing people to the whole Law, since the root of the dispute that day between the Messenger and his obstinate opponents was the question of oneness. For this reason they said, ﴿Has he made the gods one god? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!﴾ [Sad: 5]. Their denial of resurrection (al-ba'th) was only because they did not find it in their religion of polytheism, since those who devised polytheism for them spoke to them only about their state in this world. Thus their obstinacy in denying resurrection was only a branch of the branches of polytheism. Therefore, the emphasis on establishing oneness was certainly to narrow the gap of disagreement between the Prophet and the polytheists who turn away, whose condition the surah opened by describing with His saying, the Exalted:

صفحة ١٧١
﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near, while they are in heedlessness, turning away﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1] ﴿No reminder comes to them from their Lord, newly revealed, but they listen to it while playing﴾ [al-Anbiya': 2] ﴿their hearts distracted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3]. The particle (innama), with the hamzah kasrah, and its being followed by the verb (yuha, "is revealed"), conveys the restriction of the revelation to the Messenger upon the content of the clause ﴿that your god is one God﴾. This is a restriction of an attribute to a qualified subject. The particle (anna-ma), with the hamzah fathah, is the sister of (inna-ma) with the hamzah kasrah in conveying restriction, because (anna-ma) with fathah is composed of "anna" with fathah and the restrictive "ma" (al-kafffah). Just as (inna-ma) with kasrah is composed of "inna" with kasrah and "ma" (al-kafffah). Since "anna" with fathah is the sister of "inna" with kasrah in conveying emphasis, likewise, when it is joined to "ma" (al-kafffah), it is its sister in conveying restriction. This was discussed earlier, at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear delivery﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 92], in the Surah al-'Uqud. And since (anna-ma) with fathah has been followed by the noun that encompasses the reality of God, and it has been predicated that He is one God, it conveys that the possessor of this reality is singular in oneness, so there is no plurality of individuals in this reality; thus it conveys a second restriction, namely the restriction of a subject to an attribute. The first restriction is relative (idafi), meaning: what is revealed to me concerning God is only that God is one God. The second restriction is also relative, meaning: concerning God in respect of oneness. Since the relative restriction is by its nature intended to repel the belief of the addressee, the restriction by the two clauses necessitates considering the repelling of the belief of the polytheists by both restrictions. Thus the first restriction serves to nullify what they confuse people with, that Muhammad ﷺ calls to monotheism and then mentions God and the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). They also confuse people at times by saying he is a sorcerer, because he calls to what cannot be comprehended. He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And the disbelievers said, "This is a lying sorcerer."﴾ [Sad: 4] ﴿Has he made the gods one god? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!﴾ [Sad: 5]. So the meaning of the verse is in the sense of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Say: I am not a novelty among the messengers﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9]
صفحة ١٧٢
and His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Merciful?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 45]. Then, both restrictions were a comprehensive word for the call of Islam, bringing near the gap of disagreement and its divisions. And upon all these considerations, the sentence ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ is built as a consequence.

The interrogative is genuine, meaning: will you submit after this clarification? It is also used in a figurative (kinayi) meaning, namely exhortation to abandon associating partners and to enter the call of Islam.

The active participle is used in its original sense of the present time, meaning: are you now submitting, as a sign of impatience at the delay of their submission. This was expressed in a nominal sentence, which denotes permanence, rather than saying "will you submit," to convey that what is required of them is firm submission. As if there were in it an implicit reproach to them that they are in doubt, wavering.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 109:

﴿Then if they turn away, say: "I have announced to you all equally, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far."﴾

I.e., if they turn away after this detailed and comprehensive clarification, then convey to them the warning of the descent of what Allah has promised them.

Al-iidhan (الإيذان) means informing (al-i'lam). It is on the pattern of af'ala from adhina li-kadhaa, in the sense of "he heard." Its derivation is from the noun udhun (الأذن), the organ of hearing. It was then used to mean knowing through hearing, and then its use spread to knowing in general. As for (adhana) (آذن), it is a transitive verb with the hamza, and both forms were commonly used in the sense of warning (al-indhar), which is informing mixed with caution. From the use of adhina is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So be informed of war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279]. From the use of (adhana) is the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

"Asma' has announced to us her parting."

The second object of (aadhantukum) is omitted, indicating what His saying, "what you are promised" (ما تُوعَدُونَ), refers to. Or it may be estimated as: "I have announced to you what is revealed to me," indicated by what precedes it. The more apparent estimate is one that includes both meanings, like His saying: ﴿If they turn away, then I have conveyed to you what I was sent with to you﴾ [Hud: 57].

As for His saying (ʿalā sawāʾ) (عَلى سَواءٍ): the (ʿalā) here is for the figurative elevation (al-istiʿlaa' al-majazi), which is the strength of association and the firm attachment of the attribute to its subject. And (sawāʾ) (سَواءٌ) is a noun meaning "equal." Al-istiwaa' is equivalence in something, and its plural is (aswā'). Its origin is a verbal noun (masdar), then it was treated as a noun, so they pluralized it accordingly, though its proper form is not to be pluralized. It is permissible that (ʿalā sawāʾ) be a stationary adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqirr) that is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun of address in His saying (aadhantukum), meaning: "I warned you while being equal in informing you of it, so that none of you may claim that the warning did not reach him." This is an excuse for them and a recording against them, like his saying in his sermon: "Have I not conveyed?" It is also permissible that the prepositional phrase be connected to the verb (aadhantukum). Abu Muslim said: "Iidhan ʿalā sawāʾ" means calling to war openly, based on His saying: ﴿Then throw back to them on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58]. End of quote.

He means that this is an analogy with the state of one who warns of war, since there was no call to actual war in the Qur'an revealed at Makkah. On this meaning, it is also permissible that (ʿalā sawāʾ) be a circumstantial state from the pronoun of the speaker. The object of (aadhantukum) is omitted, indicating His saying: ﴿and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far﴾, and because the context implies it, through His saying before it: (﴿until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96]) and so on. This was discussed previously at His saying: ﴿Then throw back to them on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58] in Surat al-Anfal.

His saying ﴿and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far﴾ includes everything they are promised of punishment in this world and the Hereafter, whether they live or die. (Inna) is negating, and the verb (adri) (أدري) is suspended from acting because of the interrogative particle, and the returning pronoun is omitted. Its estimate is: "what you are promised of."

This is a parenthetical clause inserted between the coordinated clauses. The pronoun of the absent party refers to God, Exalted, by the indication of the context. The purpose of the sentence is to give the reason for the warning, by affirming that the threatened punishment will certainly befall them, and to give the reason for their ignorance of its nearness or distance. He explained this by saying that God, Exalted, knows their open speech and their secret speech, and He is the One who will call them to account for it, and He is the One who knows when His punishment will descend upon them. The returning pronoun of the relative clause in His saying, Exalted, (ما تَكْتُمُونَ) is an omitted pronoun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 21, verse 111:

﴿And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿And I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 109]. The pronoun that is the subject of (laʿalla, "perhaps") refers to what is indicated by the words of God, Exalted is He, ﴿whether what you are promised is near or far﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 109], namely that it is a matter awaited in its occurrence and that it has been delayed beyond the existence of its cause. The sense is: "Perhaps its delay is a trial for you," or "perhaps the delay of what you are promised is a trial for you." That is, "I do not know the wisdom of this delay; perhaps it is a trial for you, which God intended in order to give you respite, since with the delay of the promise you increase in denial and turning away, and that is a trial."

Fitnah (trial): the disruption of conditions that leads to what is harmful.

Matāʿ (provision): that which is benefited from for a short duration, as was mentioned earlier in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Let not the going about of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you; it is a little provision﴾ [Al ʿImran: 196], in Surat Al ʿImran.

Ḥīn (time): a period of time.

[Page 176]

﴿Say: "My Lord, judge with truth. Our Lord is the Most Merciful, the One whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾

This is a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i) after the discussion of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), the summary of its foundations, the command to warn his people, and the recording of his delivery of the message. By this new beginning he intended to hint at the hoped-for future outcome of this religion, so that the account of this religion and its bearer would be complete in both its beginning and its end. This follows the pattern of the stories of the earlier messengers mentioned before it, from the words of God Most High: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48], up to this point.

In God's command to His Prophet, peace be upon him, to turn to Him and seek His help, after He had said to him ﴿But if they turn away, then say: "I have announced to you equally"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 109], there is a signal that they will certainly turn away, and that God will judge among them by requiting their crime, because judgement by truth will not leave them. God's help to him is because when God teaches His servants a supplication, He has guaranteed to them that it will be answered, as in His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make mistakes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and similar verses. God has indeed fulfilled His promise and responded to His servant, and He judged these obstinate people with truth on the day of Badr. The meaning is: say this in their hearing, as a public display of your challenge to them, that you have entrusted your affair to your Lord, so that He may judge among them with the truth, which is the breaking of their power and the nullification of their religion. For God hurls the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, so it vanishes.

The "bi" (ب) in His words (bi-al-haqq, "with truth") is for accompaniment (mulabasah). The second complement of the verb (uhkum, "judge") is omitted, to draw their attention to the fact that the Prophet is upon the truth: he did not ask for judgement with truth except because he wants it. That is, judge for us, or against them, or between us.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (qul) in the imperative form. Hafs read (qala) in the past tense, like His words: ﴿He said: "My Lord knows the word"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 4] at the beginning of this surah. In the Kufan codex the alif is not written. This is a report of the words of the Messenger (ﷺ). (Rabbi) is a vocative with a possessive suffix, from which the "ya'" of the first person has been dropped, and the kasrah remains as evidence of the "ya'".

The majority read (Rabbi) with a kasrah on the ba'. Abu Ja'far read it with a dammah on the ba', which is an Arabic usage for a vocative attached to the first-person pronoun, as if they treated it as a form of apocope (tarkhim). This is permissible when there is no risk of ambiguity.

The definiteness of the subject through the possessive construction in His words (wa-Rabbuna, "and our Lord") serves to magnify the status of the Muslims, by the pride of their being able to say that God is their Lord. The pronoun of the first person plural includes the Prophet and those with him among the Muslims. In it there is also an implicit rebuke to the polytheists, that they have no share in God's lordship, to the extent that they have turned away from worshipping Him to worshipping idols, as in His words: ﴿That is because God is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector﴾ [Muhammad: 11]. (Al-Rahman) is an explicative apposition (‘atf bayan) to (Rabbuna), because the word here is intended as a proper name, not as a descriptive adjective, as a rebuke to the polytheists, since they denied the name al-Rahman: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?" And it increased them in aversion﴾ [al-Furqan: 60]. The definiteness of (al-musta'an, "the one sought for help") serves to express restriction (qasr), that is: I seek help from none other than Him against what you describe, since no one helps us except our Lord. This refers to His words: ﴿It is You we worship, and You we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5].

In His words ‘ala ma tasifun ("against what you describe"), there is an omitted noun governed by ‘ala, that is: against the nullification of what you describe, by displaying your falsehood to the people, so that they will believe and not follow you. Or: against the nullification of what results from it of their harm to him and to the believers, and their inciting of the Arabs against him. The meaning of (ma tasifun, "what you describe") is what your statements produce of harm to us. Here "description" (wasf) means the statements that indicate the attributes, and this has been discussed previously in the surah of Yusuf. They described the Prophet (ﷺ) with derogatory attributes, such as their saying: "Mad" and "Sorcerer," and they described the Qur'an as "poetry" and "tales of the ancients," and they spread this among their common folk to incite people against him.

[Page 179]

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

Surah al-Hajj

This surah was called al-Hajj during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi reported from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: I said: "O Messenger of God, was the Surah al-Hajj given preference over the rest of the Qur'an with two prostrations?" He said: "Yes."

Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah also reported "from 'Amr ibn al-'As that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had him recite fifteen prostrations in the Qur'an, of which three are in the mufassal, and in Surah al-Hajj there are two prostrations." This surah has no name other than this.

The reason it is called Surah al-Hajj is that God mentions in it how He commanded Abraham, peace be upon him, to call people to the pilgrimage to the Sacred House, and mentions the rites prescribed for the people on that day, glorifying the pilgrimage and its virtues and benefits, and rebuking those who bar believers from the Sacred Mosque. This is despite the agreement that it was revealed before the pilgrimage was made obligatory on the Muslims; the pilgrimage was made obligatory only by the verses in Surah al-Baqarah and Surah Al 'Imran.

[Page 180]

There is disagreement about this surah: whether it is Meccan or Medinan, or whether much of it is Meccan and much of it is Medinan.

From Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata': it is Meccan except for three verses, from His words ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19] up to ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Naqqash counted what was revealed of it in Medina as ten verses.

Also from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Hasan: it is Medinan except the verses (﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet﴾ [al-Hajj: 52]) up to His words ﴿Or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day﴾ [al-Hajj: 55], and these are Meccan.

From Mujahid, from Ibn al-Zubayr: that it is Medinan. This was also transmitted by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The majority said: this surah is partly Meccan and partly Medinan, and it is mixed, meaning that the Meccan part cannot be identified specifically, nor the Medinan part specifically. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is the most sound view.

I say: this view is not like what is common when they say about a few verses from several surahs that they were revealed in a place other than where most of the surah in question was revealed. Rather, they meant that much of it is Meccan, and that a similar amount or close to it is Medinan, and that it is not determined which part is Meccan and which is Medinan. For this reason they expressed it by saying: "It is mixed." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it was reported from Anas ibn Malik that he said: "The beginning of the surah was revealed during a journey, so the Messenger of God called out with it, and people gathered to him," and he related the narration that will come. Ibn 'Atiyyah means that its revelation during a journey requires that it was revealed after the Hijrah. It seems that its beginning was revealed in Mecca, for its opening with (O mankind) follows the patterns of the openings of Meccan surahs. And in the stylistic structure of many of its verses

[Page 181]

there is something that suits the style of the Qur'an revealed in Mecca. Nevertheless, opening with "O mankind" does not necessarily make it Meccan, and Ibn 'Abbas's statement, "O mankind," is intended to mean the polytheists. Therefore it is permissible to direct this address to the polytheists in Medina at the early period of the Prophet's (ﷺ) settlement there, for His words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of God and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Hajj: 25] suit being revealed in Medina, where the polytheists barred the Prophet and the believers from remaining with them in Mecca. Likewise His words ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against because they were wronged, and indeed God is competent to give them victory, those who were expelled from their homes without right﴾ [al-Hajj: 39], which is explicit that it was revealed concerning the Hijrah.

al-Tirmidhi related with his chain from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the Prophet was expelled from Mecca, Abu Bakr said: "They have expelled their prophet; they are surely going to perish." Then God revealed ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against because they were wronged, and indeed God is competent to give them victory, those who were expelled from their homes without right, except that they say, "Our Lord is God"﴾ [al-Hajj: 39–40]. Likewise His words ﴿And those who emigrated in the way of God and then were killed or died, God will surely provide for them a good provision﴾ [al-Hajj: 58], in which there is mention of the Hijrah and mention of those among the emigrants who are killed, and this indicates a jihad expected to come, as will be discussed there.

I think it is not determined that a consecutive group of its verses was revealed in Mecca and what follows was revealed in Medina; rather its verses were revealed scattered. Perhaps their order was by the Prophet's (ﷺ) instruction, and there are many similar cases. It has been said about His words ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19] that it was revealed concerning the battle of Badr, because of what is in the Sahih from 'Ali and Abu Dhar: that they were revealed concerning the single combat of Hamzah, 'Ali and 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith against Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah on the day of Badr. Abu Dhar used to swear to this.

[Page 182]

For this reason I reckon that this surah, some of which was revealed at the end of the Prophet's (ﷺ) stay in Mecca, as its opening with (﴿O mankind﴾ [al-Hajj: 1]) indicates, since it is established that this is the prevalent pattern in the style of the Meccan Qur'an, and that the rest of it was revealed during the Prophet's (ﷺ) stay in Medina. al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan and sahih, related from Ibn Abi 'Umar, from Sufyan, from Ibn Ju'dan, from al-Hasan, from 'Imran ibn Husayn, that "when ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord; indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ [al-Hajj: 1] up to His words ﴿But the punishment of God is severe﴾ [al-Hajj: 2] was revealed upon the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: 'Were these revealed upon him while he was on a journey?' He said: 'Do you know?'" and he related a long hadith. His statement, "They were revealed upon him while he was on a journey," implies that this surah was revealed upon the Prophet (ﷺ) after the Hijrah, since his journeys were for military campaigns and the like after the Hijrah. In another report from him, that journey was the expedition to Bani al-Mustaliq of Khuza'ah, and that expedition was in the year four or five. So the apparent meaning of his words, "they were revealed while he was on a journey," is that 'Imran ibn Husayn only heard the verse on that day and thought it was revealed on that day. For 'Imran ibn Husayn did not embrace Islam until the year of Khaybar, which was the year seven. Or one of the narrators inserted the phrase "they were revealed upon him while he was on a journey" into the words of 'Imran ibn Husayn, and 'Imran did not say it. For this reason this wording is not found in what al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan and sahih, also related from Muhammad ibn Bashshar, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Hisham ibn Abi 'Abd Allah, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from 'Imran ibn Husayn, who said: "We were with the Prophet on a journey, and he raised his voice with these two verses, ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord; indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ [al-Hajj: 1] up to His words ﴿But the punishment of God is severe﴾ [al-Hajj: 2]

[Page 183]

up to the end." The narration of Qatadah from al-Hasan is more authentic than the narration of Ibn Ju'dan from al-Hasan, because Ibn Ju'dan, whose name is 'Ali ibn Zayd, was described by Ahmad and Abu Zur'ah as "not strong." Ibn Khuzaymah described him as "poor in memory," and he had become confused, so it is advisable not to rely on what he alone reported of this addition. Ibn 'Atiyyah related from Anas ibn Malik that he said: "The beginning of this surah was revealed upon the Messenger of God during a journey." Ibn 'Atiyyah did not give a chain for it.

al-Qurtubi mentioned from al-Ghaznawi that he said: "Surah al-Hajj is among the wonders of surahs: it was revealed by night and by day, on journey and at home, Meccan and Medinan, peaceful and warlike, abrogating and abrogated, clear (muhkam) and ambiguous (mutashabih)."

The surah has been counted as the hundred and fifth in the enumeration of the order of the revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an, in the transmission of Jabir ibn Zayd from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It was revealed after Surah al-Nur and before Surah al-Munafiqun." This implies that, in his view, it is entirely Medinan, because Surah al-Nur and Surah al-Munafiqun are both Medinan. So reliance on this should be held in reserve regarding it.

The verse-count variants of Surah 21 according to the people of Medina and Mecca: seventy-seven. The people of Syria counted seventy-four. The people of Basra counted seventy-five; the people of Kufa counted seventy-eight.
* * *
Among the purposes of this surah: addressing the people, commanding them to fear God and to dread the Day of Recompense and its terrors.

Argument against polytheism and address to the polytheists, bidding them to desist from obstinacy in acknowledging God's sole divinity and from disputation about it, following the whisperings of the devils. The devils cannot avail them anything, nor can they help them in this world or in the Hereafter.

Denunciation of the polytheists' disputation concerning the Oneness (tawhid), in that they rest on no knowledge, and that they turn away from proof in order to lead people astray.

That they doubt the Resurrection, though it is established and there is no doubt in it. How can they doubt it, on the pretext that bringing back to life after death is impossible, when they do not consider that God created man from dust, then from a drop of semen, then shaped him through stages?

And that God sends down water upon the barren earth, so it comes alive and brings forth various kinds of plants. God is capable of all that. He gives life to the dead, and He is powerful over everything. Their disputing the Resurrection stems from ignorance and arrogance against complying with the word of the Messenger (ﷺ).

Describing the polytheists as wavering in their stance regarding adherence to the religion of Islam.

Allusion to the polytheists' arrogance toward the sunnah of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), to whom they trace their lineage and whom they imagine to be the guardians of his religion and the trustees of his House, while they oppose him in the foundation of the religion. And a reminder to them of the benefits God bestowed upon them through the prescription of the Hajj, yet they disbelieved His favor. And a comparison of them, in receiving the call of Islam, with the bygone nations who received the call of the Messengers with aversion and disbelief, so punishment befell them.

That something like it is about to befall these people, so the delay of punishment should not deceive them, for it is a respite from God granted to them just as He granted respite to the nations before them. In this there is consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) and those who believed, and good tidings to them of the ultimate victory over those who persecuted them and drove them out of their homes without right.

That the difference among the nations between the people of guidance and the people of error is a matter for which people split into many creeds.

That the Day of Resurrection is the Day of Judgment between them, to witness the recompense of the people of guidance and the recompense of the people of error.

That the guided and the misguided are two disputants who have disputed concerning the command of God, and each party has its recompense.

God consoled His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers by informing them that Satan corrupts in the hearts of the people of error the effects of the Messengers' call, but God makes His religion firm and nullifies what Satan casts. Therefore you see the disbelievers turning away and denying the verses of the Qur'an.

In it: the honouring of the Qur'an and of those who receive it with fear and patience; the description of the disbelievers by their hatred of the Qur'an and their enmity toward the one it was sent down with; and the praise of the believers, that God made easy for them the following of the upright religion (hanifiyya), and named them Muslims.

Permission for the Muslims to fight, with the guarantee of victory and of establishment in the land for them.

The surah concludes with a reminder to people of God's blessings upon them, and that God chose from among the angels and from among mankind some creatures; then He turned to the believers with guidance toward what brings them near to God in closeness, and that God is their Protector (mawla) and their Helper.
